SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/3887969  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/3887969.json` (HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` read IN FULL) — the route that worked. Metadata: Weblate, "SSRF via URL Parser Differential in `normalize_request_url` (wlc)", weakness Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), severity high (reporter suggested Critical, CVSS 3.1 `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N` 9.3), reporter `dark_river`, submitted 2026-07-24, disclosed 2026-09-02, Closed. Target: github.com/WeblateOrg/wlc, `wlc/client.py` (`normalize_request_url`, `get_origin`, `list_factory`), commit reviewed `d0ddc3d2c16b727d4f8ec2b576d0b7d209a53770`.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no wlc instance or malicious API server was stood up this pass; the code, table and quotes below are verbatim from the report body).
CLASS: DELTA ENTRY (the bypass itself is RECORDED — see DEDUPE/DELTA) — SSRF (CWE-918) in an API CLIENT/CLI: the client follows SERVER-SUPPLIED navigation URLs (the paginated API `next` field) and guards them with its own origin check, so a malicious or compromised API server drives HTTP requests FROM THE MACHINE RUNNING THE CLIENT; the guard is bypassed by the already-recorded backslash-before-`@` URL-parser differential.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SURFACE (the direction flip): `wlc`'s `list_factory` follows `data["next"]` from paginated API responses verbatim — `path = data["next"]` -> `self.get(path)` -> `normalize_request_url(path)` -> `requests` dispatch. The attacker is the SERVER side (a malicious or compromised Weblate, or a user lured into pointing `wlc` at an attacker URL) and the fetcher is the developer/CI machine running the client. Report: "A malicious or compromised Weblate server can exploit this by returning a paginated API `next` URL crafted with this pattern."
  2. THE GUARD: `normalize_request_url` resolves `urlparse(urljoin(self.url, path))` and compares `get_origin(url)` = `(scheme, hostname, port)` against `self.api_origin`, raising "Server returned a URL outside the configured API origin." on mismatch.
  3. THE BYPASS (recorded differential, this parser pair): a `next` value of `http://<attacker-ip>\@<real-api-host>:<port>/…`. Report's verbatim table for `http://***@127.0.0.1:8000/latest/meta-data/`: `urllib.parse.urlparse` (used for origin validation) resolves host `127.0.0.1`, while `urllib3.util.parse_url` (via `requests`, the actual outbound connection) resolves host `169.254.169.254`. Mechanism, verbatim: "`urlparse` treats everything before the backslash as part of the userinfo component and correctly extracts the real host after `@`. `urllib3`'s parser instead treats the backslash as a path separator, so it extracts the *first* token as the host." The full `(scheme, hostname, port)` tuple check does not defeat it — "urlparse resolves both host *and* port from the segment after the backslash, so the computed origin (`http`, `127.0.0.1`, `8000`) matches the real API origin exactly, and the check passes."
  4. THE DISPATCH PROOF (the black-box oracle): at the `requests` layer a `PreparedRequest` for the same URL shows `prepared url: http://169.254.169.254/%5C@127.0.0.1:8000/...` with `connection pool host: 169.254.169.254   port: 80` — the validation parse and the connection-pool target are DIFFERENT hosts.
  5. THE IMPACT (report's own): the client issues requests to arbitrary hosts from wherever it runs — "Internal-network-only services otherwise unreachable from outside", "Cloud instance metadata endpoints (e.g. AWS IMDS at 169.254.169.254, GCP, Azure), potentially exposing IAM credentials or instance metadata", "Any other host reachable from the machine running `wlc`".
DETECTION SIGNAL: any API CLIENT / CLI / SDK / CI tool that follows server-supplied navigation URLs (pagination `next`/`links`/`cursor`, callback URLs, redirect/manifest targets) and implements its OWN origin/host validation before fetching; a client whose guard parses with a different library than its HTTP stack (`urlparse`/`urlsplit` guard vs `requests`/`urllib3`/`httpx` dispatch; own URI class vs curl; `java.net.URI` vs HttpClient). TELL: the guard raises on cross-origin `next` values — that guard is the only thing between a malicious API server and the client's internal network.
CHAIN: malicious or compromised API server (or a user pointed at one) returns a crafted paginated `next` URL (primitive: the client consumes server-supplied navigation URLs) -> the origin check parses it with `urlparse`, which resolves the host from after the `\@` and the `(scheme, hostname, port)` comparison passes (bypass: validator and dispatcher disagree on `\` before `@` — the recorded differential) -> `requests`/`urllib3` connects to the attacker-chosen host from the CLIENT machine (escalation: server-side-request semantics relocated onto the developer/CI host) -> internal-only services and cloud IMDS reachable -> IAM credentials -> cloud account compromise (impact; reporter-rated Critical 9.3). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = a client pointed at (or connecting through) an attacker-influenced API server + the client following pagination; gain = arbitrary-host requests from the client machine incl. metadata endpoints.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: when auditing any API client/CLI/SDK — or any feature consuming a server-supplied URL (pagination, webhook/callback registration, manifest or redirect following): (1) serve the client from a malicious or MITM'd API endpoint and return `next` = `http://<your-collaborator-ip>\@<the-real-api-host>/<path>` (plus `%5c@` / `@`-in-path variants — the recorded Dropbox variant table applies); (2) watch BOTH the collaborator and the client's real connection target (`PreparedRequest` connection-pool host, `ss`/`strace`, or a proxy) to prove which host the dispatcher resolved; (3) if the guard passed while the connect went elsewhere, replay with `next` = `http://169.254.169.254\@<real-host>/latest/meta-data/` and observe what the client's response handling returns or dispatches. Rule: **an origin check is only as strong as its parser — when the guard's parser differs from the HTTP stack's parser, `\@` splits them, and a client that follows server-supplied `next` URLs hands a malicious API server SSRF on the machine running the client.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `3887969`, `normalize_request_url`, `wlc`, `dark_river`, `list_factory`, `urllib3` = 0 hits across the three write targets. THE BYPASS IS RECORDED and is NOT re-recorded here: ledger 2425-2442 (Dropbox, HackerOne #1406938, "SSRF (full-response) via URL-parser differential between the validating library and the fetching library (CWE-918 + CWE-436)") carries the identical differential character (`\` before `@`), the same 2017 Black Hat "A New Era of SSRF — Exploiting URL Parser in Trending Programming Languages" lineage, the payload shape `<allowed-host>\@<internal-host>:<port>`, the full-read/exfil requirement and the metadata-credential escalation; §17.250 holds URL-notation/userinfo parser differentials (IP-literal forms). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the NAT64/IPv6 parser-differential SSRF entry (ledger 6735 — IP-literal parsing, not userinfo-vs-path-separator); the validator-vs-shell `?`/`#` authority-terminator entry (ledger 7018 — command injection, different class). NEW DELTA (what the Dropbox entry does not carry): (a) the DIRECTION FLIP — server-supplied navigation URLs (paginated `next`) consumed by a CLIENT library whose own origin check is the guard (evil-API-server -> SSRF FROM the developer/CI machine; the Dropbox entry is user-supplied URL -> server-side fetch), (b) the Python-INTERNAL parser pair `urllib.parse.urlparse` (guard) vs `urllib3.util.parse_url` (dispatch) — divergence inside one language/stack, and (c) the `PreparedRequest` connection-pool target as the black-box oracle for which host the dispatcher really resolves. Per the Concrete CMS precedent (ledger 10165): the general method is owned by the Dropbox entry, this delta is recorded without re-deriving it, and it gets NO new §17 slot.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2026-07-24 / disclosed 2026-09-02 — INSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; genuinely fresh material, read because assigned.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/3699522  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/3699522.json` (HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` read IN FULL) — the route that worked. Metadata: Monero, "`check_reserve_proof` counts duplicate entries: one output can inflate `total`", weakness Business Logic Errors, severity medium, reporter `bebensap`, submitted 2026-04-27, disclosed 2026-08-05, Closed. Target: monero-project/monero `src/wallet/wallet2.cpp` + `src/wallet/wallet_rpc_server.cpp`, snapshot `master @ 3ad4a5ee8` (`v0.18.1.0-3ad4a5ee8`).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Monero tree, daemon or wallet RPC was stood up this pass; the code, test and output below are verbatim from the report body, which ships a checked unit test `tests/unit_tests/reserve_proof.duplicateKeyImagesReuseValidEntrySignatures`).
CLASS: business-logic / accounting flaw with monetary impact (fraudulent proof-of-reserves) — a verifier checks PER-ROW signatures over an UNTRUSTED, prover-authored list but never enforces ROW UNIQUENESS, then flat-sums per-row amounts (`total += amount`), so a malicious prover inflates the aggregate by duplicating ONE entry N times (CWE-841 improper enforcement of behavioral workflow / double counting).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE VERIFIER SHAPE: `check_reserve_proof` walks a vector of `reserve_proof_entry`; per row it verifies signatures against a `prefix_hash`, then adds the row's output amount to `total` (and `spent` when the daemon says the key image is spent). The accounting loop, verbatim: `for (size_t i = 0; i < proofs.size(); ++i) { ... total += amount; if (kispent_res.spent_status[i]) spent += amount; }` — "Nothing in that loop requires each `key_image` or each `(txid, index_in_tx)` to appear only once."
  2. WHY THE SIGNATURE DOES NOT SAVE IT: `prefix_hash = cn_fast_hash(message || address || <every key_image in list order>)` — the same layout the honest `get_reserve_proof` uses. Verbatim: "If you repeat the same output N times in `proofs`, you also repeat N copies of that key image in `prefix_data`, recompute `prefix_hash`, and sign against that hash. The owner of the output already has the keys to produce valid `shared_secret_sig` and `key_image_sig` for each row; those checks are per-row and do not see 'this key image was already used.'" A signature over the whole list is not a uniqueness guarantee when the list's author is the prover.
  3. THE EXPLOIT: serialize the same output N times in `proofs` (stock `get_reserve_proof` emits each selected transfer once, but "nothing stops a custom prover from serializing duplicates"; `on_check_reserve_proof` just forwards into `check_reserve_proof`).
  4. THE PROOF (the report's unit test, observed output): `duplicate_count = 3` on a single 7,000,000,000,000-unit output -> "reported total without dedup: 21000000000000" -> "inflation vs one output: 3x". Live-RPC variant: duplicate `selected_transfers` in `get_reserve_proof` after it finalizes (simulated malicious prover, verifier untouched), regenerate, call `check_reserve_proof` — "`good` stays true while `total` jumps by the duplication factor. Remove the hack and `total` returns to the real balance."
  5. THE FIX (report's own): before hitting the daemon or summing, reject duplicates — `std::unordered_set<crypto::key_image> seen_key_images; std::set<std::pair<crypto::hash, uint64_t>> seen_outputs;`.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any verifier/aggregator consuming an untrusted LIST of entries with per-row signatures AND per-row amounts/counts that it sums with no uniqueness set — proof-of-reserves / solvency attestations / ownership proofs / balance statements / batch settlement or invoice lists / ticket manifests; validation inputs (prefix/hash/signature payload) BUILT BY THE PROVER over their own list; an accounting loop of the shape `total += amount` per row with no `seen` set. TELL: duplicating one row in the submitted list changes the signed prefix but not the verdict.
CHAIN: a malicious prover — e.g. an exchange presenting a reserve proof to verifiers/users (primitive: the entry list is prover-authored) -> repeat one owned output's proof row N times and sign the duplicated prefix with the output's keys (bypass: the per-row checks are blind to row reuse and the prefix is prover-computed) -> the verifier returns `good` while `total` is N× the real on-chain reserve (3x demonstrated; bounded only by N) -> a fraudulent proof-of-reserves is accepted as evidence of solvency (impact: monetary/fraud — false collateral against deposits; report's own framing: "the reported reserve scales with how many times the same row appears, not with how many distinct outputs exist on-chain"). Per doctrine §8: preconditions = the ability to author the proof list (any party asked to PROVE reserves/ownership of a set) + a verifier of this shape; gain = an arbitrarily inflated verified total.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any proof/attestation/aggregation consuming a list of entries with per-entry signatures and amounts (reserve proofs, ownership proofs, batch invoices, ledger summaries): (1) take a valid list and duplicate ONE entry N times (same key image / row id / (txid, index)); (2) if the prover signs a prefix over the list (message + ids in list order), recompute and re-sign it with your own keys — you own the duplicated entry, so the signatures stay valid; (3) submit and check whether the verifier returns valid AND the summed total/count grows with N; (4) grep the verifier for a `seen`-set / unique constraint on the row identity — its absence is the root cause. Rule: **per-row signature verification is not row uniqueness — if the prover authors the list, the signature covers the duplication; any verifier that SUMS an untrusted list needs a seen-set on the row identity before the amount is added, and a proof-of-reserves that counts rows instead of distinct on-chain outputs is inflatable at will.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `3699522`, `check_reserve_proof`, `reserve_proof_entry`, `seen_key_images`, `duplicateKeyImages`, `bebensap` (as author of THIS report) = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the Monero wallet-RPC exposure entry (ledger 13175/13437 — `on_get_reserve_proof`/`on_export_key_images`/`on_start_mining` reachable on the RPC surface; surface enumeration, not accounting logic); `bebensap`'s #3693636 (batch-181 note — `res.txs.front()` on an empty vector via a malicious daemon = crash/availability-only, out of class); the error-based SQLi `Duplicate entry` extractor (ledger 16945 — `FLOOR(RAND(0)*2)` GROUP BY, a different mechanism entirely); the coupon/benefit stacking family (V-09 race replay + Stripe #1849626 non-idempotent claim — those inflate a COUNTER via REPLAYED CALLS; this inflates a verified TOTAL via DUPLICATED ROWS inside ONE accepted, correctly-signed payload, defeating per-row cryptography); the Augur bond-inflation entry (ledger 3914 — a derived fee fed by an attacker-controlled metric, no signature layer); the GitHub Projects "duplicate entry triggers the field-update path" (ledger 10193 — dispatch confusion, not summation). NEW DELTA: the duplicate-row inflation of a prover-authored signed list (the signature covers the duplication) and the seen-set fix rule. New general method -> §17.600.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2026-04-27 / disclosed 2026-08-05 — INSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; genuinely fresh material, read because assigned. The pattern (per-row verification + flat summation over a prover-authored list) recurs in every proof-of-reserves / attestation / batch-aggregation verifier.

ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/2575105.json` = HTTP 200 but `visibility: no-content` (reporter body withheld) — the ROUTE THAT WORKED for the report text: `web_extract` on the live `https://hackerone.com/reports/2575105` page (report text read; quoted verbatim below); `r.jina.ai` = 401 IP-blocked; the browser tool = H1 error page ("Sorry, something went wrong") on 2 attempts; Wayback `.json` capture (20250213150706) also `no-content`. Corroborated this pass (both OPENED): Debian security-tracker CVE-2025-23083 (fix commit `51938f023aac90dc1dc0bc1f743501788613210e`, v23.6.1; introduced by nodejs/node PR #44710, backported to 20.x) and the Node.js advisory `https://nodejs.org/en/blog/vulnerability/january-2025-security-releases` ("Worker permission bypass via InternalWorker leak in diagnostics (CVE-2025-23083) - (high)", fixed releases v20.18.2 / v22.13.1 / v23.6.1; credit `leodog896`, fix `RafaelGSS`). Metadata: Node.js, "Worker permission bypass via InternalWorker leak in diagnostics", reporter `leodog896`, submitted 2024-06-26, disclosed 2025-01-21, resolved, H1 severity high, CVE-2025-23083 (CWE-863).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no vulnerable Node v20/v22/v23 stood up this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched report text or the opened vendor advisory).
CLASS: sandbox escape / privilege escalation — Node.js Permission Model (`--permission`) bypass: a DIAGNOSTICS instrumentation channel delivers live INTERNAL worker instances to any in-process subscriber; the subscriber grabs the instance's constructor and RE-INSTANCES it, and the reinstated constructor creates workers the permission model never mediates.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SANDBOX: Node v20/v22/v23 running with `--permission`; the model mediates user-facing APIs (fs/net/child_process) of the main thread — but only the main thread's mediated surface.
  2. THE HOOK (report verbatim): "With the aid of the diagnostics_channel utility, an event can be hooked into whenever a worker thread is created. This is not limited only to workers but also exposes internal workers, where an instance of them can be fetched, and its constructor can be grabbed and reinstated for malicious usage." — the channel fires for USER workers AND Node's own INTERNAL workers, and the payload is the LIVE INSTANCE, not a description of it.
  3. THE BYPASS: fetch the internal-worker instance from the event payload -> grab its constructor off the instance -> reinstantiate it (verbatim: "its constructor can be grabbed and reinstated for malicious usage") — the reinstated constructor spawns workers OUTSIDE the permission model's mediation, so code the main thread may not run (restricted file read/write, net, child_process) runs in the spawned worker.
  4. THE IMPACT (advisory verbatim): "This vulnerability affects Permission Model users (--permission) on Node.js v20, v22, and v23" — rated HIGH (CVE-2025-23083); the fix (v23.6.1 / v22.13.1 / v20.18.2) stops the internal-worker leak.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a Node process running `--permission` (or any in-process sandbox/policy layer) that ALSO exposes diagnostic/telemetry/instrumentation hooks delivering live internal objects (workers, handles, class instances) to subscriber callbacks; an event payload carrying an INSTANCE where a description would do. TELL: from ordinary in-process code, `.constructor` is readable off a delivered internal object and callable.
CHAIN: attacker-supplied code evaluated inside a `--permission` process (plugin / template / scripting / user-land extension surface) (primitive) -> subscribe to the worker-creation diagnostics channel (any in-process code can observe) -> receive an INTERNAL worker instance (leak: the channel is not scoped to user workers) -> grab + reinstate its constructor (bypass: the constructor itself is not permission-gated) -> spawn a worker that executes outside the permission model (escalation: the sandbox boundary is crossed) -> file read/write and local-service access denied to the main thread become reachable -> host-level data access / code execution (impact: High; chain = sandbox escape). Per doctrine §8: precondition = ability to run JS inside the permission-model process + a worker-spawn trigger; gain = code execution with fs/net capabilities the model denies to the main thread.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any Node app/tooling running `--permission` (unpatched v20.x <20.18.2, v22.x <22.13.1, v23.x <23.6.1) — or any in-process sandbox exposing diagnostic hooks: (1) from user-reachable code, enumerate `diagnostics_channel` subscriptions and hook every channel that fires on worker creation (trigger a worker-spawn feature or wait for an internal one); (2) inspect the delivered payload — if it is a live internal worker instance, take its constructor (`payload.constructor` / prototype chain) and reinstantiate it with an attacker-controlled entrypoint; (3) confirm the spawned worker performs an operation the main thread is denied (e.g. `fs.readFile` of a restricted path) — success = permission-model escape. General rule: **a sandbox that mediates APIs but hands raw internal objects to in-process observers is dead — the observer grabs a constructor off the leaked instance and re-enters through the unmediated class; whenever a diagnostics/telemetry hook delivers live objects instead of data, test what can be constructed from them.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `2575105`, `InternalWorker`, `diagnostics_channel`, `CVE-2025-23083`, `leodog896`, `51938f0` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.186 (HackerOne #2434811 — monkey-patching the built-ins the permission model's CHECK calls, `Buffer.prototype.utf8Write` rewrite; same target, different mechanism: intercepting the checker vs. constructing through a leaked internal class), the Node type-coverage-gap entry (#2256167 — `Uint8Array` not normalized by the guard; a forgotten type, not a leaked constructor), §17.455 (#3465156 — a UDS path outside the network-check's classifier; a classifier gap, not an object leak). NEW DELTA: the INTERNAL-OBJECT LEAK BYPASS — instrumentation that delivers live internal instances (not data) to subscribers, and the instance's constructor is an unmediated door back into capabilities the sandbox denies. New general method -> §17.601.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2024-06-26 / disclosed 2025-01-21 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~22 months); read because assigned. The method (diagnostic hooks leaking unmediated internal constructors) is runtime/telemetry-design-level and re-detectable wherever an in-process sandbox coexists with instrumentation.

Everything below is either the published wording or a CLEARLY-LABELLED generalisation — no report content is invented.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GHES instance or fine-grained PAT was exercised this pass)
CLASS: authorization bypass / broken access control (CWE-863) — PERMISSION-SCOPE CONFUSION ACROSS UNIFIED OBJECT TYPES: a token scoped to sibling object type A ("Pull requests") reads type B's objects (issue comments) because the two types share one storage/API surface while the permission model treats them as separate dimensions.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE PERMISSION MODEL: fine-grained PATs / GitHub App tokens grant per-repo, PER-TYPE permissions — "Issues" and "Pull requests" are separate grants; a least-privileged CI/bot token is routinely minted with ONLY "Pull requests" (PR workflows) and Issues: no access.
  2. THE UNIFIED SURFACE [LABELLED GENERALISATION of the published wording]: a pull request IS an issue in GitHub's data model — conversation comments live in one store and the comment-read routes serve both types.
  3. THE BUG (CVE-2023-51380, verbatim): "An incorrect authorization vulnerability was identified in GitHub Enterprise Server that allowed issue comments to be read with an improperly scoped token." The H1 title states the bypass verbatim: comments from issues can be leaked "without ANY 'Issues' repo permissions by utilizing 'Pull Request' permissions" — the comment-read path authorizes against the Pull-Requests dimension (or never re-checks the Issues dimension), so the token's missing Issues grant is never required.
  4. THE SIBLING PROOF OF MISWIRED PREDICATES (GHES release notes, verbatim, for the UPDATE twin CVE-2023-51379): "An incorrect authorization vulnerability was identified that allowed issue comments to be updated with an improperly scoped token. This vulnerability did not allow unauthorized access to any repository content as it also required `contents.write` and `issues.read` permissions." — both the read and the write comment routes had their permission predicates wired to the wrong grant dimensions.
  5. [LABELLED GENERALISATION — the exact endpoint is NOT public] The probe: mint a fine-grained PAT with Pull requests: read and Issues: No access on a repo whose plain ISSUE carries comments, then request the issue-comment reads with it (shape in TRANSFERABLE TEST).
DETECTION SIGNAL: an API whose token/role permissions are scoped per OBJECT TYPE while sibling types share storage, ids or routes (PR↔issue; task↔bug; post↔comment; ticket↔conversation); a comment/reaction/attachment route reachable under the sibling type's grant; a permission matrix documented per type but enforced per route. TELL: a token deliberately missing type B's grant still returns type B's objects.
CHAIN: a least-privileged token holder — CI bot, GitHub App installation, fine-grained PAT granted ONLY "Pull requests" (primitive: the token is deliberately Issues-less) -> request the issue-comment reads (bypass: authorization keyed on the wrong type dimension — the shared issue/PR comment surface never re-checks the Issues grant) -> read every issue comment in the repo: private vulnerability discussions, security reports, internal notes, pasted secrets (escalation: cross-permission data read; GHES advisory severity MEDIUM, H1 medium) -> any credential posted in issue comments chains to the recorded secret-to-internal-access entries (final impact is comment-content-dependent; the demonstrated impact is the cross-permission read itself). Per doctrine §8: precondition = possession of a sibling-type-scoped token, no user interaction; gain = issue-comment content the token's scope explicitly excludes.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any platform with type-scoped fine-grained tokens (GitHub/GHES/GitLab/Bitbucket/GraphQL APIs with typed nodes): (1) mint a token holding ONLY sibling type A's read (GitHub: fine-grained PAT, `Pull requests: read`, Issues: No access) on a test repo where a plain ISSUE has comments; (2) with that token call every comment/reaction/attachment read for type B — REST (`GET /repos/{o}/{r}/issues/{n}/comments`, `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/issues/comments`, `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/pulls/{n}/comments` pointed at an ISSUE number) and GraphQL (`pullRequest` vs `issue` node aliases); (3) any type-B content returned = the confusion; (4) run the matrix in BOTH directions and on write verbs (the CVE-2023-51379 twin shows writes were miswired too). Rule: **where two object types share one storage/API surface but the permission model scores them as separate dimensions, the check is only as good as its type detection — test every shared route with a token scoped to the WRONG sibling type.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `2184950`, `51380`, `improperly scoped`, `scope confusion`, `pull_requests` = 0 hits across the three write targets (the `51380` grep hits are the substring `b270151380e6` inside a Medium URL — false positive). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the Shopify coarse-vs-granular permission-predicate confusion entry (ledger ~8440 — a COARSE requirement satisfied by ANY single object-level GRANT; here grants are per TYPE and the confusion is type misdetection, not grant granularity); §17.378 (child-object endpoint leaking `repository.name` to a token with no repo access — metadata leak, not a scope-confusion read); the CVE-2026-14340 note (ledger ~10953 — an installation token checked for READ instead of an explicit repo grant; breadth of one scope, not cross-type). New general method -> §17.602.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2023-09-28 / disclosed 2024-01-03 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~22 months); read because assigned. The method (permission dimension vs shared surface mismatch) is API-design-level and re-detectable on every type-scoped token model.

ROUTE THAT WORKED: the credited vendor artifacts — the CVE record https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2023-39957 (OPENED in full) and the FIX PR https://github.com/nextcloud/talk-android/pull/3064 ("File util fixes", merged 2023-06-01; OPENED in full incl. both commit messages, the diff of `FileUtils.kt` / `UploadAndShareFilesWorker.kt` and the review comments). Metadata: Nextcloud, "Path traversal allows tricking the Talk Android app into writing files into it's root directory", weakness Path Traversal (CWE-22), H1 severity medium (41 votes), reporter `fr4via`, submitted 2023-05-22, disclosed 2023-08-14, resolved; asset GOOGLE_PLAY_APP_ID `com.nextcloud.talk2`; CVE-2023-39957 (GHSA-36f7-93f3-mcfj), Talk Android < 17.0.0, fixed 17.0.0; CVSS 3.0 7.2 `AV:L/AC:H/PR:H/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` (NVD variant 7.8 `AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R`).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no APK was instrumented this pass; the code below is verbatim from the opened fix PR)
CLASS: mobile path traversal / arbitrary file WRITE (CWE-22) — an UNPROTECTED (exported) Android Intent feeds an attacker-controlled FILENAME into `File(context.cacheDir, filename)`, and a `../` sequence escapes the cache directory INTO the app's private root data directory (app-file overwrite; sandbox scope change).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE CARRIER (CVE record, verbatim): "an unprotected intend [intent] allowed malicious third party apps to trick the Talk Android app into writing files outside of its intended cache directory." Any app on the device fires the Talk share/upload flow (`UploadAndShareFilesWorker`) with a content URI (the CVSS vector still records UI:R).
  2. THE SINK (fix PR, `FileUtils.copyFileToCache`, verbatim diff): `fun copyFileToCache(context: Context, sourceFileUri: Uri, filename: String): File { ... val cachedFile = File(context.cacheDir, filename)` — `filename` derives from the caller-supplied URI; in the vulnerable code there is NO containment check, so `filename = ../../<target>` resolves into `data/data/com.nextcloud.talk2/` — the app's ROOT directory per the report title (files written "into it's root directory").
  3. FIX BYPASS ATOM (a) — a basename split is not a traversal defense (commit `d49441e` message, verbatim): "get last part after '/' also for content uris … note that this doesn't prevent path traversal as uris can be decoded" — splitting on `/` before decoding is defeated by percent-encoded separators (`%2F`, `%252F`).
  4. FIX BYPASS ATOM (b) — the canonical-prefix check as shipped is a PARTIAL path traversal (PR review comment, verbatim): "getCanonicalPath returns a path string that is not terminated with a slash, which means that external input may still be copied to siblings of cacheDir, rather than just its children, such as 'data/data/package/cachexxxx'" + the CodeQL reference `java-partial-path-traversal`. The added guard `if (!cachedFile.canonicalPath.startsWith(context.cacheDir.canonicalPath, true))` (commit `bd23edc`) blocks `../escape` but a crafted name matching the `cacheDir`+suffix prefix still resolves OUTSIDE the intended children.
  5. THE ESCALATION (report title + CVSS `S:C`/`C:H I:H`): a write into the app's private root reaches the app's own databases / shared_prefs / config files — overwrite them and the next launch consumes attacker-controlled state (server URL, account/token material); the write is what crosses the sandbox scope.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an exported/unprotected Intent (or any IPC: deeplink, share target, content-provider callback) whose extra/URI names a FILE the app copies/writes into its cache/files dir; a `File(dir, filename)` concat where `filename` derives from a URI/extra without `basename()` + `..` rejection; a "fix" that either (a) splits the last path segment before decoding or (b) checks `canonicalPath.startsWith(dirCanonical)` WITHOUT a trailing separator. TELL: the copy routine writes while the resolved path leaves the intended directory.
CHAIN: a malicious third-party app installed on the victim device (primitive: the Intent is unprotected — the CVE record's own wording) -> fire the share/upload Intent with a URI whose filename is `../<target>` (bypass: no containment check on the concat; even the patched basename split dies to `%2F`) -> the file lands in the app's ROOT data dir instead of cache (escalation: app-private overwrite; S:C) -> overwrite a database/preference the app trusts -> attacker-controlled server/account state on next launch -> account/data compromise (impact per CVSS C:H/I:H; report rated medium on H1, 7.2–7.8 High in the CVE record).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every mobile app in scope: (1) `aapt dump xmltree <apk> AndroidManifest.xml` and list exported/unprotected components (`android:exported="true"`, missing permission); (2) fire each share/upload/save flow (`adb shell am start ...`) with a content URI whose display name / path segment is `../../databases/<db>` and encoded variants (`%2e%2e%2f`, `%252F`, `..%2F`); (3) check where the file lands (`run-as`/`adb shell ls` on the app's data dir) — outside the intended dir = traversal; (4) if a containment fix exists, attack THE FIX: URI-encoded separators against last-segment splits, and sibling-prefix names (`<dirName>xxx`) against `canonicalPath.startsWith(dir)` without a trailing `/`. Rule: **a filename from an IPC source concatenated into a private dir path is a write-traversal sink — and both stock fixes (basename split, separator-less canonical prefix check) are bypassable unless the name is decoded first and the prefix check is terminated with a separator.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `1997029`, `39957`, `copyFileToCache`, `cacheDir`, `partial path traversal`, `canonicalPath`, `GHSA-36f7`, `talk-android`, `UploadAndShareFilesWorker`, `d49441e`, `bd23edc` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.363 (same reporter `fr4via`, Basecamp #2553411 — a DEEPLINK `filename` param written to SHARED storage for cross-app READ; different carrier (deeplink vs unprotected Intent), opposite direction (outward to shared storage for disclosure vs inward to the app root for overwrite), and no fix-bypass atoms); the Slack Android #1378889 entry (ledger ~4572 — a server-supplied upload filename into the app's private config/prefs -> auth tokens; carrier is a server filename, no traversal-fix analysis); §17.74/§17.88 (desktop/client `dir + fileName()` concat and page-named temp file — no Android IPC, no fix-bypass pair). NEW DELTA: the write-INTO-app-root direction and the FIX-REVIEW pair (encoded URI defeats the basename split — from the commit message; partial path traversal defeats `canonicalPath.startsWith` without trailing separator — from the PR review comment). New general method -> §17.603.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2023-05-22 / disclosed 2023-08-14 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned. The fix-review atoms are library-level and timeless.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1636552  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/1636552.json` = HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 1,111 chars read IN FULL (cross-checked this pass: identical row in the HuggingFace `Hacker0x01/hackerone_disclosed_reports` mirror `/tmp/h1_train.parquet`, VI LEN 1111). Metadata: Khan Academy, "Email Verification Bypass Allows Users to Add & verify Any Email  As Guardians Email", reporter `shuvam321`, submitted 2022-07-14, disclosed 2022-12-17, resolved, H1 severity high, weakness Privilege Escalation (khanacademy.org).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Khan Academy account was created this pass; every step below is quoted from the fetched report body).
CLASS: privilege escalation / email-verification bypass — the verification TOKEN is bound to the ACCOUNT's pending email state, NOT to the address it was delivered to: re-target the pending email after the mail is issued and the stale link verifies the NEW address (CWE-287 / CWE-640).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE ACCOUNT SHAPE (report verbatim): "Go to https://www.khanacademy.org/signup and signup as learner keeping date of birth below 13 years." — a <13 learner account is gated on a guardian: "Your parent or guardian must approve your account or it will be deleted in 7 days".
  2. THE UNPROVEN GUARDIAN BINDING (verbatim): "Now keep victims email as parent's email for example here I am keeping info@khanacademy.org as parents email and click on signup." — the guardian field accepts any address with no proof of ownership at signup.
  3. MOVE THE VERIFICATION TO ATTACKER TERRITORY (verbatim): "Now go to https://www.khanacademy.org/settings/account and update your email to temporary email or any email you have access to."
  4. HOLD THE TOKEN (verbatim): "You will receive a verification email in your temporary email you have access to. But don't click on the email." — the mail is issued to attacker address A; its link carries the live verification token.
  5. RE-TARGET THE PENDING CHANGE (verbatim): "Now again change the email to info@khanacademy.org." — the pending email becomes victim address B while token A is still valid (nothing invalidates outstanding links on change).
  6. CLICK THE STALE LINK (verbatim): "Now open the verification email you received in your temporary email account in an incognito tab and refresh your child's account. We have successfully tied info@khanacademy.org as parent account with email verification." — a token issued for A verifies B: the check binds to the account's CURRENT pending email, and the victim's address now counts VERIFIED as the account's guardian without the victim ever acting. Report impact verbatim: "Attacker is able to bypass email verification."
DETECTION SIGNAL: an email-change/verification flow whose confirm link is a bare token with no signed binding to the address it was mailed to; a change-email step that does NOT invalidate outstanding verification mails (the tell: the old link still works after the second change); a "verified" attribute consumed downstream (guardian approval, invite accept, verified badge, role claim).
CHAIN: any account with a pending email change (primitive) -> request the verification mail to attacker address A and hold the link -> re-target the pending email to victim address B (the state the token will bind to) -> click the stale link (bypass: the token is not bound to its delivery address) -> B is marked VERIFIED and tied as guardian WITHOUT the victim's action (escalation: verification bypass + guardian/identity binding forgery; program rating high, weakness Privilege Escalation) -> every flow that trusts "verified email" (invite-accept/claim, guardian approval, verified-role gates — the recorded #1551176 pattern) treats the forged binding as proven. Per doctrine §8: precondition = ability to create an account and drive a change-email flow twice; gain = an arbitrary address marked verified and bound (guardian) without ownership. The invite/role ATO rung is the CHAIN TO TEST, not a claim.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any app with change-email + verification: (1) start an email change to an address you own and receive the verification mail WITHOUT clicking; (2) change the pending email AGAIN to a victim address; (3) click the original link — if the victim's address shows VERIFIED (and any guardian/invite/role trust consumes it), the token is not bound to its delivery address. Also diff: does changing the email at any point invalidate outstanding links? Rule: **a verification token not signed/bound to the address it was mailed to is a verification bypass — issue it to yourself, re-target the change, click the stale link.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `1636552`, `shuvam321`, `khanacademy`, `Khan Academy` = 0 hits across the three write targets (`guardian`'s 3 ledger hits are "Desync Guardian"). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: #1551176 Reddit (mass-assign `email` in a PATCH -> silently verified — assignment, not token re-targeting); §17.326 Shopify #229619 (the confirmation token LEAKED in a resend link, GET verifies — token exposure, not stale-state binding); ledger ~11642 (password-reset token not bound to `userId` — cross-user replay of one token, not address re-targeting of a pending change); ledger ~15148 (stale RESET token after the VICTIM changes email — opposite direction); #617896 GitLab/Salesforce (SSO trusts an IdP email claim). NEW DELTA: the verification token binds to the PENDING CHANGE STATE instead of the DELIVERY ADDRESS — re-target then click. New general method -> §17.604.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2022-07-14 / disclosed 2022-12-17 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~4 years); read because assigned. The method (unbound verification token) is flow-design-level and re-detectable on any change-email implementation.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1025881  2026-11-12
ROUTE: the report BODY is NOT public on any route tried — live `https://hackerone.com/reports/1025881.json` = HTTP 200 but `vulnerability_information` 0 chars (the HuggingFace mirror `/tmp/h1_train.parquet` confirms `visibility: no-content`, VI LEN 0); `web_extract` on the live page = keenable timeout ×2; `r.jina.ai` = 401 IP-blocked; Wayback HTML captures (20221029013604, 20260717084645) = ~3.5 KB SPA shells carrying only the program summary; the ajaysenr mirror prints "No vulnerability information available." ROUTE THAT WORKED: the CREDITED PUBLIC WRITEUP — Snapsec's own blog https://blog.snapsec.co/hacking-larksuite/ ("We Hacked Larksuite For 1 month and Here is what we found", published 2022-09-04; OPENED in full via `web_extract`; the program summary credits the team verbatim "We thank @snapsec for reporting this to our team" and the blog's findings table lists exactly this title at ID 1). Metadata: Lark Technologies (asset `larksuite.com`), "Accessing/Editing Folders of Other Users in the Orginisation.", reporter `imran0x01` (Snapsec), submitted 2020-11-04, disclosed 2022-10-29, resolved, H1 severity High (CVSS 7.1), weakness Improper Access Control - Generic.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Larksuite tenant stood up this pass; every request shape below is quoted from the credited writeup).
CLASS: broken access control / IDOR on a DELEGATED-ADMIN console API — a delegation invite scoped to "company information" still reaches a per-user folder API that accepts an ARBITRARY `userID` and returns that user's directory tree plus capability TOKENS -> cross-user folder READ, file DOWNLOAD and directory WRITE (CWE-285 / CWE-639).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SETUP (writeup verbatim): "Lark-suite allows highest privileged user(Primary administrator) to invite other admin's/users. The invited users are allowed to view/modify their folders in the lark app." The tester grants the invited user ONLY the company-info permission: "he was only able to access the company information but he lacked access on the files and directories of other members."
  2. THE IDOR READ (writeup verbatim: "a GET Request which takes user id in a parameter and returns the directories and tokens of that user in the response"):
     `GET /suite/admin/space_manage/user_folder?userID=6782777787976515850 HTTP/1.1` (Host: `<tenant>.larksuite.com`, `X-Csrf-Token: [Value]`, `Cookie: [Value]`) — the response lists the TARGET USER's directories and each directory's token.
  3. ENUMERATE DOWN (verbatim: "we appended another token in the parameter query and added a parentToken and we gave its value as the user's folder token we got in the response of the above request"):
     `GET /suite/admin/space_manage/user_folder?userID=[UserId]&parentToken=[PToken] HTTP/1.1` — returns "all of the files inside that parent directory as well as the unique `token` of each file inside that directory".
  4. FILE THEFT (verbatim): the per-file tokens "could be later used to download the whole file using this endpoint `https://internal-api-space.larksuite.com/space/api/box/stream/download/all/[token]/`".
  5. THE WRITE (verbatim): `POST /suite/admin/space_manage/user_folder` (same host/headers) with a leaked directory token — "the response was 200 ok and upon confirmation, we found new sub directory was created in that folder" — the delegate alters the directory STRUCTURE of users whose files they cannot legitimately access.
  6. Program summary (the impact, verbatim): "A vulnerability was found where users without Primary admin privileges were able to view/modify the directory structure of other users in their organization. This would occur after those users were invited to view/modify their folders by a Primary admin."
DETECTION SIGNAL: an admin/delegation console whose APIs take a `userID`/`owner`/`account` parameter alongside the caller's session — the parameter is the object selector and nothing checks the caller's DELEGATION SCOPE or relationship to that user; responses returning capability tokens (file/folder/share tokens) for objects the caller cannot access; sibling admin APIs (`chatSetting`, employee add, app audit) behind the same invite-based role.
CHAIN: Primary admin invites the attacker as a limited delegate (primitive: trust in the delegation scope) -> delegate calls `GET .../user_folder?userID=<victim>` (bypass: no scope/ownership check on the user selector) -> victim's directory tree + folder tokens returned (escalation: cross-user structure read) -> `parentToken` walk leaks every file token -> `GET /space/api/box/stream/download/all/[file-token]/` downloads each file (escalation: org-wide file exfiltration; the writeup's finding #6 shows the same download route also bypasses an explicit no-download permission) -> `POST .../user_folder` creates directories in the victim's tree (integrity impact) -> per the program summary: non-Primary-admin users "view/modify the directory structure of other users" (High, CVSS 7.1). Per doctrine §8: precondition = an accepted delegation invite with the lowest informational permission, no victim interaction; gain = read+write over other org members' folder trees and download of their files.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any tenant product with admin delegation/invite roles: (1) accept a delegation invite granted ONLY the lowest informational permission; (2) replay every admin console API with an ARBITRARY victim `userID`/`owner` parameter (keep your own session/CSRF); (3) if any response returns the victim's object tree or capability tokens, walk it (`parentToken`-style child queries) and replay every returned token at download/export endpoints; (4) try write verbs (create/move/delete) with the leaked tokens. Rule: **a delegation scope enforced only in the UI is no scope at all — the admin API's user selector is an IDOR, and the capability tokens it returns are the escalation.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `1025881`, `user_folder`, `parentToken`, `space_manage`, `larksuite`, `imran0x01`, `snapsec` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §3.1 generic IDOR ("swap the identifier in a path parameter, then enumerate") — here the selector is a QUERY `userID` on a delegated-admin API and the returned capability TOKENS are the chain; ledger ~2831 (counterpart reference without ACL check), ~5841 (one request lists identifiers twice), ~8111 (attach-without-view-check) — object-relation mistakes, not delegation-scope gaps. The sibling Snapsec writeup bugs (app-credential XSS via `?next=`, `chatSetting`/`tenant/chat` privilege escalation, helpdesk `worksheet_id` IDOR, sandbox `AddTestTenantMember` tenant-join, JSON-CSRF invite) are SEPARATE findings from the same credited source and were NOT imported. NEW DELTA: the delegation-scope gap — an invite-based role whose enforcement stops at the UI while the admin API accepts an arbitrary user selector and hands back capability tokens. New general method -> §17.605.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2020-11-04 / disclosed 2022-10-29 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~5 years); read because assigned. The method (delegation-scope gap + capability-token escalation) is API-design-level and re-detectable on any delegated-admin surface.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1212822  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/1212822.json` = HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 6,647 chars read IN FULL (cross-checked in the HuggingFace `hackerone_disclosed_reports` parquet mirror `/tmp/h1_train.parquet`, VI LEN 6647). Metadata: GitLab, "Stored XSS in Mermaid when viewing Markdown files", reporter `saleemrashid`, asset gitlab.com, submitted 2021-05-30, disclosed 2021-10-18, resolved, H1 severity high (42 votes), weakness Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - DOM.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GitLab instance or Mermaid build was exercised this pass; every code/quote below is verbatim from the fetched report body)
CLASS: XSS (stored) — renderer config-directive OVERRIDE of a nested render key missing from the "secure keys" blocklist, combined with a BOOLEAN-vs-STRING truthiness mismatch between the sanitizer gate and the render gate (CWE-79; type confusion CWE-843).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SURFACE: GitLab renders Mermaid inside Markdown (`README.md`, issues, any GFM field); Mermaid accepts config directives `%%{init: {<JSON_OBJECT>}}%%` in the diagram body. The app's own hardening (render_mermaid.js, v13.12.1-ee, quoted in the report) sets `securityLevel: 'strict'` and `flowchart: { useMaxWidth: true, htmlLabels: false }`.
  2. THE BLOCKLIST GAP (report verbatim): "Mermaid also supports directives to alter the configuration. For security reasons, these directives aren't able to override certain configuration options" — the protected set is `secure: ['secure', 'securityLevel', 'startOnDate', 'maxTextSize']` (verbatim key list: `['secure', 'securityLevel', 'startOnLoad', 'maxTextSize']`). The nested render-behavior key `flowchart.htmlLabels` is NOT in it.
  3. THE OVERRIDE + GATE MISMATCH (report verbatim): "While you can't override `securityLevel`, it turns out that overriding `flowchart.htmlLabels` to `"false"` (specifically the string, not the boolean) is sufficient to bypass the sanitization". The sanitizer gate (common.js, quoted): `if (config.flowchart && (config.flowchart.htmlLabels === false || config.flowchart.htmlLabels === 'false')) { htmlLabels = false; }` — the STRING `"false"` makes the sanitizer SKIP (its rationale: render as TEXT, no escaping needed). But the render gate, quoted verbatim: "the code that actually decides whether to render it as HTML or text always uses `if (config.flowchart.htmlLabels)`, which would succeed for the string `"false"` (because it's truthy). This means the sanitization is bypassed, but the string is still rendered as HTML, resulting in XSS."
  4. THE STORED PAYLOAD (report verbatim steps): a `.gitlab-ci.yml` job writes `exploit.js` (`echo 'alert(parent.document.querySelector("meta[name=csrf-token]").outerHTML)' > exploit.js`, `artifacts: paths: [exploit.js]`), and the Markdown carries the diagram: `%%{init: {"flowchart": {"htmlLabels": "false"}} }%%` / `flowchart` / `A["<iframe srcdoc='<script src=https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/<user>%2F<repo>/jobs/<jobid>/artifacts/exploit.js></script>'></iframe>"]` — `<iframe srcdoc>` is used "because you can't directly inject a `<script>` tag with `innerHTML`".
  5. THE CSP LEG (recorded material, quoted for the chain): the page CSP `script-src 'self' ... 'nonce-<nonce>'` kills inline handlers ("Using nonces causes the browser to ignore `'unsafe-inline'`"), so the payload loads attacker JS hosted SAME-ORIGIN by the project's own pipeline artifacts — Workhorse "will serve pipeline artifacts with an auto-detected `Content-Type` based on the file extension"; `Content-Disposition: attachment` "prevents this from being used for HTML/SVG-based XSS, but it still allows pipeline artifacts to be used as scripts or stylesheets. Because they are on the same domain, they satisfy `'self'` in the CSP policy." (This artifact-based `script-src 'self'` bypass is ALREADY recorded at §17.155 — cross-referenced, not re-recorded.)
  6. THE IMPACT (report verbatim): "Because the XSS leads to code execution as the authenticated user, this allows full account take-over without user interaction." (The PoC exfils `meta[name=csrf-token]`.)
DETECTION SIGNAL: a diagram/chart/DSL renderer whose content carries a CONFIG directive (Mermaid `%%{init}%%`, chart option blocks, doc front-matter) merged into the live config; a "secure keys" blocklist that protects SECURITY keys (`securityLevel` etc.) but not nested RENDER-mode keys (`htmlLabels`, `renderAsText`, `sanitize`); TWO gates reading the same config value with different semantics — strict equality (`=== false || === 'false'`) in the sanitizer vs truthiness in the renderer. TELL: the STRING form of a boolean ("false") changes sanitizer behavior but not render behavior.
CHAIN: any user who can post Markdown containing a diagram (primitive: one stored directive string) -> `%%{init: {"flowchart": {"htmlLabels": "false"}}}%%` overrides a nested render key the `secure` blocklist misses (bypass 1) -> the sanitizer gate treats string `"false"` as "skip escaping" while the render gate's truthiness check keeps HTML rendering ON (bypass 2) -> raw HTML in the label (`<iframe srcdoc>`) = stored XSS firing for every viewer of the page -> nonce-based CSP blocks inline script, so the payload loads attacker JS from the project's own pipeline artifacts served `application/javascript` same-origin (`script-src 'self'` bypass, §17.155 leg) -> script runs in the viewer's session and reads the CSRF token -> "full account take-over without user interaction" (report impact; the class the doctrine accepts).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every surface rendering a config-capable DSL (Mermaid, Chart.js/Plotly, PlantUML/Graphviz, doc front-matter): (1) turn on the strict/safe mode and enumerate the blocklisted "secure" keys; (2) via the content-embedded config directive, override EVERY nested render-behavior key with STRING booleans (`"false"`, `"0"`, `"no"`) and odd truthy values; (3) submit an HTML-bearing label — HTML rendering while safe mode is "on" = the gates disagree, sanitizer off; (4) if a nonce CSP blocks inline handlers, escalate through same-origin script hosting (CI/CD artifacts, user uploads served `application/javascript`) and load it via `<iframe srcdoc>`. Rule: **a "secure keys" blocklist that skips nested render-mode keys plus a sanitizer gate and a render gate that read one value with different truthiness semantics is a sanitizer-off switch — send the string form of the boolean.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `1212822`, `saleemrashid`, `htmlLabels` = 0 hits across the three write targets (`flowchart`'s 1 ledger hit is an unrelated OAuth chain diagram; `mermaid`/`srcdoc` hits are the recorded entries below). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.152 (Mermaid `%%{init}%%` + `__proto__` prototype pollution -> attribute gadget — a pollution SOURCE, not a gate mismatch) and §17.155 (Mermaid `fontFamily` -> `</style>` breakout + pipeline-artifact `script-src 'self'` bypass + `<title><iframe srcdoc>` — that entry OWNS the CSP/artifact leg used here and is cross-referenced; its injection primitive is CSS-context breakout, not an unsanitized HTML-label path left on by a truthiness mismatch). NEW DELTA: the config-directive override of a non-blocklisted NESTED render key + the boolean-vs-string SANITIZER-GATE/RENDER-GATE mismatch (`=== 'false'` skips escaping; truthy `"false"` keeps HTML rendering). New general method -> §17.606.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2021-05-30 / disclosed 2021-10-18 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~5 years); read because assigned. The method (blocklist-gap + gate-pair mismatch in config-merging renderers) is library-design-level and re-detectable on any config-directive renderer.

ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/807961.json` = HTTP 200 but `visibility: no-content`, `vulnerability_information` 0 chars (cross-checked in BOTH HuggingFace parquet mirrors: `Hacker0x01/hackerone_disclosed_reports` `/tmp/h1_train.parquet` and `cjxcat/hackerone_disclosed_reports`, VI LEN 0). ROUTE THAT WORKED: `web_extract` on the live page `https://hackerone.com/reports/807961` — the fetch backend rendered the DISCLOSED body (read in full; the same route 403'd for sibling URLs this pass, so the live-page route is flaky per-URL). Metadata confirmed at the ajaysenr mirror `reports/807961.md`: 8x8 (asset `*.easycontactnow.com`, WILDCARD), "Blind Command Injection #1", reporter `bugify12334`, submitted 2020-03-01, disclosed 2020-06-22, resolved, High — CVSS 8.4, weakness Command Injection - Generic; team summary verbatim: "OS Command injection on text-to-speech functionality API."
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no 8x8/easycontactnow TTS endpoint was exercised this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched report body).
CLASS: command execution (OS command injection) — a TEXT-TO-SPEECH API passes unsanitized user text to the CLI synthesizer `espeak` THROUGH A SHELL, so shell metacharacters in the text execute on the backend; the "blind" label in the title is wrong — the command OUTPUT is spoken through the speakers, i.e. the generated AUDIO is the exfiltration channel (CWE-78).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SINK (report verbatim): "This issue arised because of the generic text to speech conversion tool being used here in the web application & because of the fact that the user input data was not being sanitised before taking it to the server for output of the inputed data."
  2. THE SHELL-OUT (report verbatim): "it was observed that espeak a Ubuntu command line tool was being used at the backend, because of which it was quite generic to just use simple command injection payloads".
  3. THE PAYLOAD (report verbatim code block): "User Input: 2 3hey `whoami` 4 5At the backend: 7user1@ubuntu: espeak hey `whoami` 8 9On the frontend: 11output: hey user1" — the text-to-speak input is interpolated into an `espeak` command line, the backticks run `whoami`, and the RESULT is what gets spoken/rendered.
  4. THE EXFIL CHANNEL (report verbatim): "Because of this, it allowed a full access to the backend server which was running the command. Use of the speakers here was quite important as you could hear the output of the command injection through you speakers, which turned out to be pretty cool! :D" — the output comes back INSIDE the rendered audio; the HTTP response carries only the media.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any "speak this text" / text-to-speech / voice-note / IVR / read-aloud feature (or any render-into-media feature) whose parameter names suggest text (`text`, `msg`, `say`, `voice`, `content`) and whose response is a MEDIA artifact (audio file/stream) rather than echoed text; error text or banners naming a CLI tool (`espeak`, `festival`, `say`, `pico2wave`, `ffmpeg`); command-shaped latency (`sleep`) scaling.
CHAIN: any user who can feed text to the TTS API (primitive: unsanitized text parameter) -> backtick/`$()` subshell in the text (bypass: input is not sanitized before shell interpolation of the `espeak` invocation) -> arbitrary OS command executes on the backend host as the service user (escalation: "full access to the backend server which was running the command"; program rating High, CVSS 8.4) -> command output is read back from the synthesized audio (exfil with NO OAST collaborator needed) -> follow-on commands (file read, `curl` exfil, reverse shell) reach the doctrine's P1 RCE ceiling. Per doctrine §8: precondition = access to the TTS text input (an API call); gain = arbitrary command execution on the backend + output readout.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every text-to-speech / speech-synthesis / read-aloud / voice-note / render-to-media feature: (1) submit `hey \`id\`` and `hey $(id)` as the text; (2) LISTEN TO or TRANSCRIBE (whisper/ffmpeg) the generated AUDIO and look for the command output spoken in it — an HTTP-response grep finds NOTHING because the output is encoded in the media; (3) confirm with one benign step (`` `cat /etc/hostname` ``) and a time differential (`$(sleep 5)`). Rule: **when a feature renders user text into MEDIA via a CLI tool, the text is a shell argument and the MEDIA is the exfil channel — inject a subshell and transcribe the artifact.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `807961`, `bugify`, `espeak`, `text-to-speech`, `speech`, `festival`, `pico2wave` = 0 hits across the three write targets (the 1 `TTS` hit is "TTS Bug Bounty scope" = Technology Transformation Services, unrelated). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the consolidated playbook's "Command-injection differential templates" (Terminator+OOB, Subshell+DNS/HTTP OOB, time-based A/B, "Output-based: `; id #` -> Reflected uid") — those rows confirm through OAST, time, or output REFLECTED AS TEXT in the response; the recorded ffmpeg/server-side media-conversion entries (upload -> conversion -> OOB) are a different sink (file upload to ffmpeg) with a different exfil (OAST). NEW DELTA: the TTS/shell-out family (user TEXT -> CLI synthesizer through a shell) + the AUDIO artifact as the output channel. New general method -> §17.607.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2020-03-01 / disclosed 2020-06-22 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~6 years); read because assigned. The method (text-to-speech shell-out + media-encoded output) is feature-design-level and re-detectable on any voice/speech surface.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/800231  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/800231.json` = HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 5,077 chars read IN FULL. Metadata: HackerOne (asset hackerone.com), "GraphQL node interface for ActiveResource models lacks encoding for resource identifier, enabling parameter injection in Payments backend", reporter `jobert`, submitted 2020-02-20, disclosed 2020-05-11, resolved, H1 severity medium, weakness Information Disclosure.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no HackerOne GraphQL/Payments backend was exercised this pass; every request shape below is quoted from the fetched report body).
CLASS: sensitive information disclosure WITH PoC, via PARAMETER INJECTION into an internal REST client — a GraphQL global ID (`gid://…`) whose resource identifier is concatenated UNENCODED into the ActiveResource HTTP path converts a single-record `find` into a filtered `index` call on the internal Payments REST service, with a BLIND RTT ORACLE as the readout (CWE-88 argument injection / CWE-203 timing discrepancy).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SURFACE (report verbatim): "HackerOne exposes a small number of ActiveResource objects through its GraphQL `node` interface. … Four of these models, `TaxForm`, `Payout`, `Payment`, and `PayoutPreference` are fetched from an internal Payments backend system with a REST interface. Due to the lack of encoding the resource identifier, it is possible to inject additional parameters and point a `find` call to a difference resource endpoint."
  2. THE UNSANITIZED IDENTIFIER (report verbatim): `query { node(id: "gid://hackerone/PaymentsLibrary::Payment/something") { ... on User { id } } }` -> "Will result in the following HTTP request: `GET /payments/something`" — "Because ActiveResource does not have an opinion on identifiers, it won't encode it (e.g. it doesn't raise an exception when a string is passed instead of an integer)."
  3. THE PARAMETER SMUGGLING (report verbatim): "A global ID … uses forward slashes to separate the different components (i.e. it's a URI). This means that any URL encoded character in the identifier (last) part of a global ID should be URL encoded and will be decoded when uses" — so `node(id: "gid://hackerone/PaymentsLibrary::Payment/%3fcore_hacker_username%3djobert%26core_team_handle%3dsecurity%26")` "Will result in: `GET /payments/?core_hacker_username=jobert&core_team_handle=security%26.json`" — `%3f`/`%26` decode to `?`/`&`, turning the `find` into the INDEX endpoint with the controller's own filter parameters (report: "This particular controller … have a number of parameters that can be used to filter objects. There are 16 parameters").
  4. THE EXTENSION NEUTRALIZATION (report verbatim): "the trailing ampersand (`%26`) is used to let the router ignore the appended `.json` extension."
  5. THE BLIND ORACLE (report verbatim): "The timing difference between a response without objects and a response with objects is significant enough to distinguish the two" — `%3fcore_hacker_username%3djobert%26core_team_handle%3dsecurity%26` = 0 objects ~400ms vs `%3fcore_hacker_username%3dfransrosen%26core_team_handle%3dsecurity%26` = 2 objects ~2000ms; the BODY is useless (verbatim: "In all cases, the server will respond with a 500 internal server error because the index endpoints of the REST interface will return an array, while the code expects a single record to be returned") — only LATENCY tells the truth.
  6. THE IMPACT (report verbatim): "roughly how many payments a user has received (not the amount, only total count!); the existence of a private bug bounty program; the type of tax form a user has signed; the default payout preference type of a user" — and (verbatim) "HackerOne exposes a sitemap with programs and user handles (and their ID), it would be rather straightforward to enumerate these and determine the information shown in the impact section".
DETECTION SIGNAL: a GraphQL `node(id:)`/global-object resolver whose target objects are fetched over HTTP from an internal service (ActiveResource, internal REST client, gRPC-gateway); an object identifier that reaches the transport layer WITHOUT encoding (tell: send a STRING where an int is expected — if the backend path becomes `/payments/something`, the identifier is concatenated raw); backend 500s whose LATENCY correlates with the result-set size; internal controllers with filter-parameter surfaces visible in error messages or docs.
CHAIN: GraphQL `node(id:)` query with a crafted global ID (primitive: the resource identifier reaches the internal REST path unencoded) -> `%3f…%26` smuggles QUERY PARAMETERS into the internal `find` and the trailing `%26` swallows the appended `.json` (bypass 1: the encoding gap; bypass 2: extension neutralization) -> `find` becomes the internal INDEX endpoint filtered by the controller's parameters (escalation: the internal API's ENTIRE filter surface — 16 params here, incl. `core_hacker_username`, `core_team_handle`) is injectable through one GraphQL query -> the response is always 500 but the RTT is a boolean oracle (400ms = 0 rows vs 2000ms = 2 rows) -> enumerated disclosure: per-user payment counts, private program existence, tax-form type, payout-preference type (program rating medium, Information Disclosure). ESCALATION TO TEST on other targets (recorded as the chain to test, not a claim): when the smugglable filter surface carries role/tenant/state parameters, the same gap is an internal-API BOLA — cross-tenant read of the internal service's data, the P2 rung. Per doctrine §8: precondition = GraphQL access to the node interface (any authenticated API user); gain = oracle extraction of financial/membership metadata from the internal Payments service.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every GraphQL API whose node/global-id objects are backed by an internal REST client: (1) pass a non-numeric STRING as the identifier and check whether the backend path becomes `/resource/<string>` (ActiveResource-style unencoded concatenation); (2) URL-encode `?` and `&` (`%3f`, `%26`) inside the LAST segment of `gid://<app>/<Type>/<ID>` with filter parameters the internal controller might accept (`%3fuser_id%3d2%26state%3dactive%26`), appending a trailing `%26` to swallow any server-added extension; (3) run identical queries differing only in filter values and DIFF server-side latency (or any side channel: error variance, response size) — a repeatable RTT split is the oracle; (4) enumerate at scale from any public sitemap/id list. Rule: **an object identifier that reaches an HTTP path unencoded is not an id — it is a query string: smuggle `%3f…%26`, turn the internal `find` into a filtered `index`, and read it through a timing oracle.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `800231`, `ActiveResource`, `core_hacker_username`, `PaymentsLibrary`, `%3f`, "trailing ampersand", "find call", "index endpoint" = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: V-12 and the recorded GraphQL `node(id:)` global-ID SWAP entries (AUTHORIZATION: resolve an id the viewer may not access; the `Z2lkOi8v…` base64-decode note is recon for id swaps) — this entry is INJECTION THROUGH the identifier, not an id swap; the ledger's `parameter injection` hits are SQLi `list[]` arrays and second-order XSS; `gid://`'s 28 pre-existing ledger hits are all id-swap/representation-diff material. NEW DELTA: unencoded resource identifier -> query-parameter smuggling into the internal REST layer + extension neutralization via trailing `&` + RTT oracle on a response that is always 500. New general method -> §17.608.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2020-02-20 / disclosed 2020-05-11 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~6 years); read because assigned. The method (identifier-to-transport injection + blind timing oracle) is framework-design-level and re-detectable on any GraphQL-over-internal-REST surface.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/3954327  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/3954327.json` = HTTP 200, `vulnerability_information` 3,485 chars read IN FULL this pass. Metadata: Shopify, "Unauthenticated access to Checkout Blocks employee-only endpoints exposed merchant metadata", submitted 2026-08-19, disclosed 2026-11-03, resolved, H1 severity medium (the reporter deliberately left severity empty, verbatim: "I am not proposing a severity and have left the field empty. Please rate it on what is actually reachable from this bypass"), weakness Missing Authentication for Critical Function (asset checkout-blocks.shopifyapps.com); reporter handle not shown in the fetched JSON, so none is claimed.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Shopify merchant or checkout-blocks tenant was touched this pass; every request shape below is quoted from the fetched report body)
CLASS: broken access control / missing authentication — an access gate implemented as a URL-PATH-PREFIX TEXT MATCH at the edge is bypassed through the framework's ALTERNATE URL for the SAME route: Next.js serves every page also at `/_next/data/<buildId>/<route>.json`, which does not begin with the gated prefix (CWE-285 / CWE-706).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE GATE (body verbatim): `checkout-blocks.shopifyapps.com` has staff pages at `/internal` and `/api/internal/`; without an employee session the request is redirected to `minerva.shopifycloud.com` employee login — "That redirect is the only thing protecting them." and "The rule matches on the text of the URL."
  2. THE ALIAS (verbatim): "This app runs on Next.js, which serves every page at a second URL too: `/_next/data/<buildId>/<route>.json`. That does not start with `/internal`, so the rule ignores it, and Next.js hands the request to the same code."
  3. THE RESULT (verbatim): "Those pages then answer 200 and JSON to a request with no cookie and no authorization header. All four staff routes behave this way. The build id is not a secret either; it is printed in the public `/login` page."
  4. THE POC LOG (verbatim): `1 normal  /api/internal/shops      -> 302  https://minerva.shopifycloud.com/auth/minerva?...` / `2 bypass  /_next/data/ID/..shops   -> 200  628 bytes  application/json` / `3 ghost   /_next/data/NOPE/..      -> 404  (expect 404)` / `4 control /_next/data/ID/..admin   -> 302  .../login  (expect 302 login)` / `5 last page  -> {'total': 201520, 'pages': 40304, 'current': 40298} | shops returned: 5`. Line 4 is the control — "a route that checks its own session still refuses" — proving a BYPASS, not a public endpoint.
  5. FALSE-NEGATIVE TRAPS (verbatim): "The build id changes on every deploy, so a stale one returns 404 and looks fixed; read it from `/login` at run time as the script does." and "test something under `/api/internal/`, because `/api/admin/` is protected properly and will look like the boundary holding."
  6. THE IMPACT (verbatim): unauthenticated access returns "the app's merchant install list, which your server reports as 201,520 records across 40,304 pages, each with the shop domain, an internal shop id and the install date. It also returns which merchants have internal flags turned on, including `checkout_blocks_allow_plus_features` and `allowPaidUpgrade`. It includes non public staging stores belonging to identifiable brands, and it is live."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a gate that decides access by matching URL TEXT/prefix at the edge or proxy (rewrite rule, WAF path match, "redirect to SSO if path starts with /internal") in front of an app built on a framework that serves each route under a SECOND URL shape (Next.js `/_next/data/<buildId>/<route>.json` and App-Router `?_rsc=` payloads, Gatsby/Nuxt JSON payloads, Rails `.json`/`:format`, Django `?format=json`); the build id visible in public HTML (`/_next/static/<buildId>/`, `/login` source); a MIX of routes where some enforce sessions in code and some rely only on the edge rule. TELL: 302-to-SSO on `/path` but 200 JSON on the alias for the same handler.
CHAIN: unauthenticated internet user (no account, no clicks) -> reads the build id from the public `/login` page -> requests `/_next/data/<buildId>/api/internal/shops` with no cookie/header -> the text-match gate never sees a `/internal` path and forwards to the same staff handler (bypass) -> returns 200 JSON: 201,520 merchant install records (shop domain, internal shop id, install date), internal feature flags (`checkout_blocks_allow_plus_features`, `allowPaidUpgrade`), non-public staging stores of identifiable brands — merchant metadata exposure at scale from a staff console = Missing Authentication for Critical Function. Per doctrine §8: precondition = none; gain = full read of an employee-only console's data (write ceiling untested — the reporter stopped deliberately).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every framework app behind a path-prefix gate: (1) trigger the gate on a sensitive path (note the 302/403 target); (2) request the same route through each framework alias with NO cookies — Next.js Pages Router: `/_next/data/<buildId>/<route>.json` (buildId scraped live from any public page source or `/_next/static/`), App-Router: same route with `RSC: 1` / `?_rsc=<hash>`, other frameworks: `/route.json`, `?format=json`, `Accept: application/json`; (3) 200 where the gated URL 302s = bypass; (4) run the control (an alias of a route that checks its own session — it must still refuse) to prove bypass vs public; (5) sweep ALL sibling routes incl. write verbs, and re-read the build id per test run (a stale id is a false negative). Rule: **a URL-text access rule cannot see framework rewrites — reach the same handler through every URL alias the framework exposes.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `3954327`, `_next/data`, `buildId`, `checkout-blocks`, `minerva` = 0 hits across the three write targets (the `__next_f`/`Next-Action`/`text/x-component` hits are §17.218 Next.js Server-Action invocation and an SSR prop-leak line — content/invocation surfaces, not route-alias gate bypass).
