SOURCE: https://hoyahaxa.blogspot.com/2022/05/bygone-vulnerabilities-remote-code.html  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract` on the live URL — one pass (Blogger page rendered in full). Metadata: Brian (HoyaHaxa blog), "Bygone Vulnerabilities - Remote Code Execution in IBM Lotus SameTime Clients (CVE-2013-0553)", May 27, 2022.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no SameTime client stood up this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched article).
CLASS: HTML sanitizer/renderer PARSE DIFFERENTIAL -> XSS -> fully-automatic RCE in a desktop client's embedded browser — the filter (IBM Active Content Filter) and the renderer (Lotus Expeditor's Gecko) disagree on where an HTML comment ENDS: `<!-->` + payload is ONE comment to the filter (payload allowed) but a closed comment plus live markup to the renderer; compounded by sanitization performed by the SENDING client, which a custom SDK client simply skips (CWE-79 -> RCE).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE TRUST BUG (article verbatim): "much the HTML filtering was done by the _sending_ client. Different versions of the Sametime clients each validated and sanitized _received_ messages a little differently, but this was done with assumptions about what types of messages clients could send in the first place. I'm sure you can see the security flaw here." — using the Sametime SDK the author "wrote a Sametime client/bot that did no HTML encoding or modification of outbound messages, and started fuzzing away."
  2. THE FILTER TO BEAT (article verbatim): Sametime 8.5.1 added IBM's Active Content Filter which "allowed lots of HTML tags, but actively filtered out standard XSS payloads and other malicious primitives. But I now had my goal -- bypass ACF and I'd likely have my RCE."
  3. THE DIFFERENTIAL (article verbatim): the discovery `<!--><my exploit payload here>` — "a syntax that took advantage of a discrepancy and confusion between ACF and Expeditor's Gecko rendering. ACF treated the entire string like a single comment, and allowed the exploit payload; without the <!--> prefix, ACF would have stripped and blocked the exploit. But Expeditor treated <!--> alone as the comment, and then happy rendered my payload. With an XSS-type payload, I had achieved automated RCE!"
  4. WHY RCE (article verbatim): the clients "came bundled with Lotus Expeditor, which provided embedded web browser functionality to render HTML and other rich content in Sametime messages"; Expeditor includes "a Gecko-compliant browser, but in 2013, it did not include many of the security features that were baked into Firefox, IE, Chrome, and Safari" — message-renderer XSS in that browser = code execution on the desktop, fully automatic. IBM provided a custom patch + public fix after disclosure.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any product that sanitizes HTML in one component and renders it in a DIFFERENT parser (embedded browser/WebView, desktop client, preview pane, notification renderer, editor print view); comments are the classic disagreement point — probe `<!-->`, `<!--->`, `<!-->-->`, `<![if]>`, `<![CDATA[` prefixes against a payload the filter blocks and diff FILTER verdict vs RENDERER DOM; a chat/messaging product where the sending side does the sanitizing (client-side trust) is a standing red flag.
CHAIN: attacker builds a custom sender (SDK/bot/modded client) with no outbound sanitization (primitive: sanitization on the wrong side of the wire) -> sends `<!-->` + XSS payload as a chat message (bypass: filter/renderer comment-grammar differential) -> the receiving client's embedded Gecko renders the payload while the filter passed it (escalation: HTML filter fully bypassed) -> JS executes in the desktop client's embedded browser = fully-automatic RCE in the victim's desktop context (impact: RCE demonstrated by the author, confirmed by IBM's patch).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any product with an HTML pipeline split across components: (1) map WHERE sanitization runs — sender client, server, or receiver; if a client SDK or the sender controls it, ship raw HTML with a custom client; (2) prefix a filter-blocked payload with comment-shape sentinels (`<!-->`, `<!--->`, `<!-->-->`, `<!---->`, `<![if]>`) and compare what the FILTER allows with what the RENDERER executes (browser DOM / embedded view); (3) any sentinel the filter treats as an unterminated comment but the renderer closes early is the bypass — then chain to the product's richest sink (embedded browser = RCE, WebView = app-context XSS). Rule: **sanitizer and renderer must parse the same comment grammar — a `<!-->`-style differential is a filter bypass that lands as code execution wherever an embedded browser renders the content.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `SameTime`, `Sametime`, `Expeditor`, `Active Content Filter`, `<!-->` as a technique, comment-parse differential = 0 technique hits across the three write targets (the only `<!-->` hits are IE conditional-comment boilerplate in captured pages and one SAML payload line — not this technique). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED, NOT re-recorded: the write-time-vs-read-time sanitization ORDER gap (ledger ~98-145: a post-sanitizer transformer builds HTML) and the post-sanitization-transformer checklist — those are ordering bugs within one pipeline; THIS entry is a GRAMMAR differential between TWO parsers (filter vs renderer) plus sender-side trust. NEW.
FRESHNESS: article 2022-05-27 about 2013-era software (CVE-2013-0553) — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned; the parse-differential class is not version-bound (modern analog: the mXSS family).
HONESTY: the working exploit was never published — the article prints only the `<!--><my exploit payload here>` shape; the RCE outcome is the author's own account, corroborated by IBM's patch; no reproduction possible from the text alone.

Rule: **a site-unique name is not a secret — derive it from the public input and the shipped salt, and the unauthenticated handler answers with admin-class data.**

SOURCE: https://www.netspi.com/blog/technical/cloud-penetration-testing/azure-cloud-vulnerability-credmanifest/  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract` on the live URL — first pass truncated mid-sentence at 15,000 chars; the 60,000-char retry returned head+tail with middle segments elided ("...") but the TL;DR, root cause, extraction channel, automation and addendum all present. Metadata: Karl Fosaaen (NetSPI), "CVE-2021-42306 CredManifest: App Registration Certificates Stored in Azure Active Directory", published 2021-11-17.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Azure tenant exercised this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched article).
CLASS: sensitive information disclosure -> credential theft -> privilege escalation (Azure AD): private-key PFX certificates for service principals stored in CLEARTEXT in App Registration manifests in a slot meant for PUBLIC keys, readable by any AAD user with app-registration read ("typically most AAD users"), usable to authenticate as the App Registration — typically Contributor on the subscription (CWE-312 -> CWE-269; Microsoft rated the CVE critical).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE TELL (article verbatim): "seeing Base64 certificate data ('MII…' strings) stored with App Registration 'manifests' in Azure Active Directory."
  2. THE ROOT CAUSE (article verbatim): "Due to a misconfiguration in Azure, Automation Account 'Run as' credentials (PFX certificates) were being stored in cleartext, in Azure Active Directory (AAD). These credentials were available to anyone with the ability to read information about App Registrations (typically most AAD users). These credentials could then be used to authenticate as the App Registration, typically as a Contributor on the subscription containing the Automation Account." — "There appears to have been logic on the Azure side that stores the full PFX file in the App Registration manifest, versus the associated public key."
  3. THE READ + THE USE (article verbatim): "The 'value' parameter is the Base64 encoded string containing the PFX certificate file that can be used for authentication. Before we can authenticate as the App Registration, we will need to convert the Base64." — the run-as service principal is created with Contributor on the subscription ("we are assigning the Contributor role to the 'Run as' account").
  4. THE AUTOMATION (article verbatim): NetSPI's PowerShell script `Get-AzAppRegistrationManifest.ps1` (MicroBurst repo on GitHub) "uses the Graph API to gather the manifests from AAD and extract the credentials out to files."
  5. BLAST RADIUS (article addendum, verbatim): "NetSPI initially discovered this issue with Automation Account 'Run as' certificates. MSRC's blog post details that two additional services were affected: Azure Migrate and Azure Site Recovery. These two services also create App Registrations in Azure Active Directory and were affected by the same issue which caused private keys to be stored in App Manifests."

ROUTE: `web_extract` on the live URL — one pass (Medium page rendered in full). Metadata: Yukesh Kumar (@3th1c_yuk1 / "3th1c_yuk1"), "UNAUTHENTICATED ACCESS TO CLOUD PORTAL — A 🚪 WITHOUT 🗝️" (techiepedia); the article prints no on-page date (VPS-recon era, ~2021-2022 by style).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no target exercised this pass; the author himself states "I don't know how it works and how the developer created this subdomain", so the ROOT CAUSE is unexplained in the source; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched article).
CLASS: authentication bypass / unauthenticated admin-panel + internal-service access (§1 reportable class) — an auth/caching gate whose verdict depends on COOKIE STATE: the SAME portal URL that returns an error (and only briefly flashes the dashboard) under the tester's existing session serves a FULL ADMIN DASHBOARD to a clean, cookie-less incognito session.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE RECON (article verbatim): grep the subdomain inventory for environment keywords — "Staging / Stg / Dev / Portal / Admin …..etc" — then push the alive hosts through httpx and Eyewitness ("a tool designed to take screenshots of websites") + Notify for alerts.
  2. THE TELL (article verbatim): a "weird subdomain with the name "portal"" throws "an error message … 502 Proxy error"; "First time — Shows the error message. Second time — loaded for a second and showed up the error message. Third time — logged into the dashboard but after some seconds showed up the same error message." — i.e. the protected dashboard FLASHES then is replaced by the error.
  3. THE BYPASS (article verbatim): "I just opened the private tab ( In mobile it is incognito mode ) pasted the domain and boom 💥 ended up getting into the dashboard without any error messages." — a clean, cookie-less session renders the FULL admin dashboard with NO error.
  4. THE IMPACT (article verbatim): "Explored the whole application got some sensitive API keys and much more." — the unauthenticated dashboard is an admin cloud console ("in which I can able to do many things as an admin"), and the harvested API keys are the escalation leg.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an auth-gated / login-flashing / intermittently-502 portal whose behaviour DIFFERS between your normal (cookie-laden) session and a fresh incognito / cookie-less session; a protected page that "flashes" the real dashboard before an error/redirect lands (enforcement sitting in a response/cache/gateway layer, CWE-602 family); a `portal`/`admin`/`staging`/`dev` subdomain found by keyword grep whose response changes on refresh or on session reset.
CHAIN: keyword-grep recon finds a `portal` subdomain (primitive: exposed admin/staging host) -> the URL 502s / flashes a dashboard under the tester's existing session (signal: cookie-state-dependent enforcement) -> a CLEAN incognito session loads the FULL admin cloud dashboard with no auth (escalation: unauthenticated admin-panel access) -> "Explored the whole application got some sensitive API keys" (escalation: secret harvest from the console) -> the API keys drive the org's cloud services (impact ceiling: cloud-service compromise; the author stopped and reported, so the realized impact recorded here is unauth admin access + API-key disclosure with PoC).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every `portal|admin|staging|dev|dashboard|console` subdomain AND every URL that auth-errors, redirects to login, or intermittently 502s: (1) fetch it in your NORMAL session and note the verdict; (2) re-fetch the EXACT same URL in a fresh incognito / cookie-less client (`curl` with no Cookie header, or a clean browser profile) and DIFF the two responses — a full dashboard / admin page / API-key-bearing console in the CLEAN session that your normal session did not get IS the auth bypass (the gate is cookie/cache-state dependent, not real auth); (3) confirm the page is pre-auth by replaying with zero cookies and harvesting any secrets/API keys it exposes. Rule: **an auth verdict that flips between a cookie-laden session and a clean incognito session is not authentication — it is a cache/cookie-state gate; the clean session is the attacker, and the pre-auth admin page it reveals is the finding.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `incognito`, `private tab`, `502 Proxy`, `clean-session`-as-bypass, `cloud portal` admin = 0 technique hits across the three write targets (the only `3th1c_yuk1` hits are this author's unrelated NUCLEI template authorship; `clean session` in the ledgers is TESTING hygiene — "record the legitimate flow from a clean session" — never an auth-bypass vector). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED, NOT re-recorded: §17.540 (zer0dac "Bypass SSO Login" — a login redirect appearing AFTER the protected body already rendered is response-layer enforcement, proven by raw no-redirect replay + proxy swap, NOT the cookie-state flip). NEW DELTA: the cookie-state dimension — the SAME URL serves the admin page to a clean session and an error to a cookie-laden one — and the incognito/cookie-less retest as the detection+bypass move.

CLASS: sensitive-info-disclosure (leaked auth tokens) -> JWT/session replay -> IDOR / broken-object-authorization WRITE on user metadata (CWE-639 + CWE-522) — RECORDED AS A CHAIN per the CHAIN-ONLY rule: the leaked-token disclosure is the first link; the chain reaches unauthorised modification of another user's account metadata.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SINK (article verbatim): capture the profile request in Burp — "in the request, you can observe that for authorisation only JWT is been utilized in the `Authorization header` and authorisation jwt already contain a `user ID` in the payload section"; "you can use jwt.io for analysing the jwt" -> the JWT's payload names the user, so owning a token = acting as that user.
  2. THE LEAK (article verbatim): google/GitHub dorks found nothing, "after when I used the `waybackurls` tool … `waybackurls hacktoberfest.digitalocean.com` … I found URLs in the Wayback where `users auth JWT tokens` are being used" — the web archive holds historical URLs that carry still-valid user JWTs (leaked credential).
  3. THE REPLAY (article verbatim): "in the jwt analysing section I can easily get `user_id` in the `JWT payload` part and can be used in the request now. Now when I used this JWT and user_id in the `Authorization header` and `request URL endpoint` respectively then my request got a `200OK` response and victim `metadata` got changed." — the leaked victim JWT in `Authorization` + the victim `user_id` in the URL writes the victim's metadata.
  4. THE PROOF (article verbatim): "I even demonstrated it with a sample victim account it was working as same as with waybackurls JWT samples." — and the closing line: "POC shows the power of chaining multiple vulnerabilities and why reconnaissance is important sometimes."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a metadata/profile/update endpoint that authorises ONLY on a JWT in `Authorization` and resolves the target object from a `user_id`/id in the URL or body; any archived URL (wayback / gau / CDX) whose query string or embedded request carries an `eyJ…` JWT or `Authorization: Bearer` value; tokens that decode to a `user_id`/`sub` claim and are still accepted after the capture date.
CHAIN: passive recon `waybackurls <domain>` (primitive: web-archive harvest) -> archived URLs leak users' still-valid `Authorization` JWTs (primitive: credential/token disclosure — the CHAIN-ONLY first link) -> replay the leaked JWT in `Authorization` + its decoded `user_id` in the request URL (escalation: session/token replay = act AS that user) -> the endpoint trusts the token+id pair and writes the victim's metadata with a 200 (impact: unauthorised cross-user account-metadata modification = IDOR WRITE; ceiling = full session replay of any archived token -> account takeover).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any token-authenticated app: (1) `waybackurls <domain>` (and `gau`, the Wayback CDX API `web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=<domain>/*&output=json`) and grep the output for `eyJ` / `Authorization:` / `access_token=` / `token=`; (2) base64-decode each hit's payload, pull the `user_id`/`sub`; (3) replay the captured `Authorization: Bearer <token>` against the user-object endpoints (profile/metadata/update) with that `user_id` in the URL/body — a 200 + a state change on ANOTHER account is the finding; (4) also test the plain IDOR: send YOUR OWN valid JWT with a FOREIGN `user_id` in the URL and see whether the write lands. Rule: **a token in the web archive is a live credential until it expires — harvest it, decode the identity, replay it against the object endpoints, and the disclosure becomes an IDOR/ATO chain.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `3028f8ad`, `varmaanu`, `Anurag__Verma`, `hacktoberfest.digitalocean`, `waybackurls`+JWT-replay = 0 technique hits across the three write targets (the `varmaanu`/`Anurag__Verma` hits are a DIFFERENT writeup — the phone-OTP `uid`-swap §17.541 entry — and `waybackurls` appears only as recon tooling and as the capability-URL/invite-token leak channel). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED, NOT re-recorded: §17.541 (Anurag Verma's OTHER bug — OTP proven on `mobileNo` while the account resolves from `uid`, a field-mismatch IDOR; NOT token leakage); the Khan-Academy capability-URL entry (leaked `/join/<token>` via wayback -> join a class, a CAPABILITY token not a JWT auth token, unauthorized-join not metadata-write); the internal-signed-token-replay entries (a JWT leaked via PATH TRAVERSAL + a trusted `X-User-Id` header, a different leak channel). NEW DELTA: the leak channel is the WEB ARCHIVE (waybackurls/CDX) surfacing still-valid `Authorization` JWTs in historical URLs, replayed to a metadata WRITE endpoint.
FRESHNESS: HacktoberFest-2021 era, article prints no on-page date — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned; the "archive leaks live tokens -> replay -> IDOR" chain is version-independent.
HONESTY: target is the public `hacktoberfest.digitalocean.com` demo; the PoC is a YouTube/video link (payload not printed in text); the metadata-change request body is shown only in screenshots; no reproduction performed; the exact JWT claim names are described in prose ("user_id"/"user ID in the payload"), not printed verbatim.

SOURCE: https://blog.sonarsource.com/gocd-pre-auth-pipeline-takeover  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract` on the live URL — one pass, full article (TL;DR, code snippets, patch and timeline all present). Metadata: Simon Scannell (SonarSource), "Agent 007: Pre-Auth Takeover of Build Pipelines in GoCD", published October 27, 2021; CVE-2021-43287 (fixed in GoCD v21.3.0, affected v20.6.0–v21.2.0).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GoCD instance exercised this pass; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched article).
CLASS: authentication bypass (filter-chain responsibility shift) -> path traversal / arbitrary file read -> secrets + encryption-key disclosure -> worker registration / agent impersonation -> CI/CD pipeline takeover (supply-chain capability).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE ROOT CAUSE (article verbatim): GoCD routes requests through Spring's FilterChainProxy — ".addFilterChain(\"/add-on/**\", assumeAnonymousUserFilter)"; "all request paths that begin with `/add-on/` are filtered with the `assumeAnonymousFilter` in line 39. As the name suggests, this filter does not actually perform authentication and lets any request through. This means endpoints exposed by addons are responsible for ensuring correct authentication and permissions themselves". A breaking change (commit 291d3d3485da818cd9067e487850c8153c6ba1e7) moved that responsibility: "Prior to this commit, these endpoints were accessible to authenticated users only. We realized that this breaking change could lead to add-ons being vulnerable to unauthenticated attacks, as the developers of add-ons might not be aware of this transfer of responsibility."
  2. THE FILE READ (verbatim code): `GET /add-on/business-continuity/plugin?folderName=...&pluginName=...` — "The pluginName parameter, which can be controlled by an attacker, is passed into the constructor of a new File object. This file is then read and served to the user making the request. By setting the `pluginName` parameter to, for example, `/../../../../../../../../etc/passwd`, it is possible to read the contents of the `/etc/passwd` file of a GoCD server."
  3. THE SECRETS — two requests (verbatim): `GET /add-on/business-continuity/cipher.aes` — "leaks an encryption key that is used to encrypt sensitive secrets"; `GET /add-on/business-continuity/cruise_config` — "leaks the main configuration file of a GoCD server. This XML config file contains all environment variables for all pipelines. Some of the environment variables are encrypted and contain secrets, but can be decrypted with the leaked AES cipher." Summarized in the article: "an attacker can extract all secrets that are available to a GoCD server with two requests: one for stealing the encryption key and one for obtaining all the encrypted secrets."
  4.   2.   3. THE ENVIRONMENT-ROUTING PARAMETER (verbatim): "there is a parameter that gets added to the oauth request each time.   4. THE BYPASS (verbatim): "changing the value of the **?referer** to **dashboard** while using my **staging jwt session(user B)**. And guess what ! I got redirected to our victim's account."
  5. THE ROOT CAUSE (verbatim): "The developers used the same jwt secret to decode the session of the users. There is a limitation I couldn't bypass though, newlines are filtered out, so the user needs to press the enter after the cloud command.   5. SCOPE (verbatim): "The most recent versions of the most popular terminal emulators are patched against attacks that are known to execute commands" — but "depending on terminal, other features such as font size, colors, terminal size, character set, alternate screen buffers and more may be accessible though escapes"; recommended fix: mask escape characters "just like *cat -v* does" in the CLI rendering layer.

SOURCE: https://joranhonig.nl/stealing-info-using-ipfs-fuse/  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract` on the live URL — one pass, full article (PoC commands, kill chain, the original vendor report and timeline all present). Author: Joran Honig; disclosure timeline printed in the report: 2021-02-04 initial vendor disclosure, 2021-08-04 vendor "won't fix" (known since 2018 — go-ipfs#5161), 2021-08-24 full disclosure. No publication date printed on the page.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no go-ipfs mount exercised this pass; the source ships a complete Vagrant PoC; every quote below is verbatim from the fetched page).
CLASS: path traversal / arbitrary file read (CWE-22 / CWE-59) — SYMLINK ESCAPE THROUGH A FUSE MOUNT THAT DOES NOT JAIL SYMLINKS: attacker-published content-addressed (IPFS) file nodes are fetched and resolved by the mount, and a symlink node resolves OUTSIDE the mountpoint to any host path, readable with the privileges of whatever software consumes the mount.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE ASSUMPTION THAT FAILS (verbatim): go-ipfs mounts IPFS/IPNS on the filesystem through FUSE using the bazil ("brazil") Go library, which "does not provide secure by default settings and assumes that it's provided with safe input from the code calling into it. This assumption is not valid in IPFS's case for two reasons: 1. Any IPFS file node can be queried through the ipfs fuse mount. 2. An attacker can create a IPFS file node with a symlink pointing to any point in the filesystem."
  2. THE PRIMITIVE (verbatim): "if you `cat` an IPFS node, which is a symlink to `/etc/passwd`, through the mount then you'll end up catting the contents of `/etc/passwd`."
  3. THE POC (verbatim commands): `mkdir poc; ln -s /home/vagrant/secret_file ./poc/not_so_secret; ipfs add -r ./poc; ipfs pin add <hash of poc node>; cat /ipfs/<hash_of_poc_node>/not_so_secret` -> prints `secret`.
  4. THE KILL CHAIN (verbatim): any portal that serves IPFS nodes through the mount (example: nginx in front of `youripfsportal.com/QmYw…/readme`) — "an attacker might create a node with a cleverly crafted symlink that points directly where certbot would normally put your SSL private key": `certificate -> /etc/letsencrypt/live/youripfsportal.com/privkey.pem`. "Now all the attacker has to do is put that node on IPFS and query it through youripfsportal.com and NGINX will diligently get it for them!"
  5. SCOPE + FIX (verbatim): the bug arises "virtually every scenario where you have: 1. An application that provides access to IPFS to users 2. A user who (1) can influence file requests to the ipfs mount by the application and (2) has with fewer file system permissions than the application." Fix = jail symlinks (osxfuse `jail_symlinks` mount option) or "sanitise node data so that only symlinks pointing within the mount are accepted".
DETECTION SIGNAL: a service that serves user-influenced file nodes through a FUSE/user-space mount (IPFS/IPNS mounts, content-addressed stores, FUSE mirrors) where node METADATA (symlink entries) is attacker-controlled and the mount options show no symlink jailing; the consumer (web server, proxy, indexer) reads paths under the mount with higher privileges than the node publisher.
CHAIN: attacker publishes an IPFS directory node containing a symlink entry to a host path (primitive: node metadata is never sanitized — "path name parameters for these nodes are never sanitised") -> the victim app fetches and serves the node through the FUSE mount (primitive: the mount resolves symlinks OUTSIDE the mountpoint — bazil/fuse offers no jail) -> requesting the symlink entry through the service returns the TARGET file's content with the serving software's privileges (escalation: arbitrary host file read as the service user) -> in the nginx/certbot scenario the target is `privkey.pem` (impact: TLS private key theft -> MitM of every user of the site); the same test reads any config/credential the service account can read.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: wherever a service serves user-influenced file nodes through a FUSE/user-space mount: (1) build a directory with `ln -s /etc/passwd ./poc/not_so_secret` (and `ln -s /etc/letsencrypt/live/<host>/privkey.pem`), `ipfs add -r`, pin; (2) request the symlink entry THROUGH the consuming service (the portal URL / mount path), not just locally; (3) if the host file comes back it is arbitrary file read as the service — check the mount options (`jail_symlinks`) and which user the consumer runs as. Rule: **a mount that follows symlinks turns every node into a pointer to the host filesystem — the attacker only publishes, the privileged reader does the reading.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: `IPFS`, `FUSE`, `bazil`, `joranhonig`, `jail_symlinks`, `content-addressed` = 0 technique hits across the three write targets (the only `IPFS` hit is the unrelated curl #3366484 entry — SSRF via an unsanitized `ipfs://..%2F..%2Fapi/v0/shutdown` CID against a configured gateway; different class). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED, NOT re-recorded: V-11 / §17.13 (symlink planted in an UPLOADED tar/zip, dereferenced at load), §17.643 RubyGems (symlink write through the installer's realpath-prefix check), §17.197/§17.202 Semmle (symlink shipped as a repo file), §17.648 (sandbox path-check vs symlink resolution) — all require the victim to IMPORT the attacker's file; here nothing is uploaded to the victim: the symlink is fetched on demand from a public content-addressed network and resolved by the MOUNT layer itself.
FRESHNESS: full disclosure 2021-08-24 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned; the class (FUSE mount without symlink jailing + privileged consumer) is implementation-shape-level and version-independent.

SOURCE: https://habr.com/en/post/579714/  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract` on the live URL — one pass, full article (all four 0-day write-ups, Swift PoC snippets and per-vulnerability timelines present). Title "Disclosure of three 0-day iOS vulnerabilities and critique of Apple Security Bounty program"; the article's own timeline dates publication to Sept 24, 2021 ("September 24 - I still haven't received any reply so I publish this article"). Author handle is NOT printed in the fetched text (cited by PentesterLand) — not invented here.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no iOS device/App-Store build this pass; every quote and PoC line below is verbatim from the fetched article).
CLASS: sandbox escape / arbitrary file read + sensitive-info disclosure + entitlement (authorization) bypass — a PRIVILEGED SYSTEM XPC/MACH SERVICE REACHABLE BY ANY APP WITHOUT ITS REQUIRED ENTITLEMENT, whose methods return Apple-ID credentials and read arbitrary files outside the app sandbox, PLUS a caller-supplied PARAMETER (`sdk-version`) whose low value makes the entitlement check get SKIPPED.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE gamed ARBITRARY-FILE-READ + TOKEN THEFT (verbatim root cause): "XPC service com.apple.gamed doesn't properly check for com.apple.developer.game-center entitlement." Any App Store app opens `NSXPCConnection(machServiceName: "com.apple.gamed", options:.privileged)` and calls `getServicesForPID` to obtain `GKAccountService`/`GKUtilityService` proxies. `GKAccountService.authenticatePlayerWithExistingCredentials` returns "Apple ID of the user, DSID and Game Center authentication token (which allows to send requests to https://gc.apple.com on behalf of the user)"; `GKProfileService.getProfilesForPlayerIDs` returns "first and last name"; `GKUtilityService.requestImageDataForURL(_:subdirectory:fileName:handler:)` "allows to read arbitrary files outside of the app sandbox by passing file URLs."
  2. THE FILES READ (verbatim): `/var/mobile/Library/AddressBook/AddressBook.sqlitedb` (full Address Book), `AddressBookImages.sqlitedb` (contact photos), `/var/mobile/Library/CoreDuet/People/interactionC.db` (contacts from Mail/SMS/iMessage/3rd-party + interaction metadata/timestamps), `com.apple.mobilephone.speeddial.plist` (favorite contacts + numbers), `com.apple.MobileGestalt.plist`. `cacheImageData:inSubdirectory:withFileName:handler:` "might allow to write arbitrary data to a location outside of the app sandbox."
  3. THE nehelper PARAMETER-GATED ENTITLEMENT SKIP (verbatim root cause): "XPC endpoint com.apple.nehelper accepts user-supplied parameter sdk-version, and if its value is less than or equal to 524288, com.apple.developer.networking.wifi-info entiltlement check is skipped" in `-[NEHelperWiFiInfoManager checkIfEntitled:]`. PoC sets `xpc_dictionary_set_uint64(xdict, "sdk-version", 1)` ("may be omitted entirely") + `interface-name=en0` -> returns `SSID` + `BSSID` for any app holding location authorization.
  4. THE nehelper APP-ENUMERATION ORACLE (verbatim): `com.apple.nehelper` `cache-command=3` + `cache-signing-identifier=<bundleId>` returns `cache-app-uuid` if that app is installed, empty otherwise -> "determine whether any app is installed on the device given its bundle ID" (`-[NEHelperCacheManager onQueueHandleMessage:]`).
  5. THE analyticsd LOG READ (fixed in iOS 14.7): `com.apple.analyticsd` `command=log-dump` returns analytics logs carrying "medical information (heart rate, count of detected atrial fibrillation ...)", "menstrual cycle length, biological sex and age, whether user is logging sexual activity", per-app screen time + session counts, accessories, crashes, Safari page languages — "available to an attacker even if 'Share analytics' was turned off."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a privileged IPC service (XPC/Mach/D-Bus/system RPC) reachable by any low-privilege client; a method on it that (a) takes a FILE URL / path parameter and returns file bytes, or (b) returns credentials/tokens; an entitlement/authorization check GATED by a caller-supplied version/mode/flag parameter whose LOW/absent value SKIPS the check; a service that answers even when the "entitled" feature is disabled on the device.
CHAIN: any App Store app (no special entitlement, no user prompt) -> opens the privileged `com.apple.gamed` XPC (primitive: the service never enforces its entitlement) -> `requestImageDataForURL` with an arbitrary file URL -> full Address Book / CoreDuet / Speed-Dial read OUTSIDE the sandbox (escalation: sandbox escape / internal file read) -> `authenticatePlayerWithExistingCredentials` returns the Apple-ID email + Game-Center auth token (impact: identity disclosure + a token usable against `gc.apple.com`; Apple valued the class at $100,000 — "Broad app access to sensitive data normally protected by a TCC prompt or the platform sandbox"). Parallel branch: `sdk-version<=524288` skips the wifi-info entitlement -> SSID/BSSID with no authorization.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: (1) enumerate privileged IPC/RPC endpoints reachable WITHOUT their required entitlement/authorization and call any file-URL/path-accepting method for arbitrary read + any credential-returning method; (2) for every version/mode/flag parameter that GATES an entitlement/authorization check, replay with the LOWEST / absent value (`sdk-version=1`, `=0`, omit it) and see whether the check is SKIPPED. Web adaptation: any `api-version`/`sdk`/`legacy`/`mode`/`debug` parameter that turns OFF a server-side authorization/entitlement check — set it low and the check disappears. Rule: **a privileged service reachable without its entitlement is an arbitrary-file-read + token oracle, and a parameter that gates the entitlement check is a one-value authz bypass.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: 0 hits for `com.apple.gamed`, `nehelper`, `analyticsd`, `requestImageDataForURL`, `sdk-version`, `game-center entitlement`, `GKUtilityService` across the write targets. The only related XPC material (the desktop privileged-helper entry, ledger ~5853) is a DIFFERENT bug: a SMJobBless/helper RPC taking a CALLER-SUPPLIED source/destination PATH (path-injection privilege escalation). NEW here: (a) a system XPC service that never enforces its entitlement so a stock App Store app reads arbitrary sandbox-external files + steals the Apple-ID/Game-Center token, and (b) the `sdk-version<=524288` PARAMETER-GATED entitlement skip. Slot 17.675. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced). Mobile-platform-specific; the transferable core is the parameter-gated authz skip + the privileged-IPC-no-entitlement read.
FRESHNESS: published 2021-09-24 (article timeline) — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned; the method (privileged IPC without entitlement enforcement + parameter-gated check skip) is implementation-shape-level.
HONESTY: no reproduction this pass (needs an iOS device + App-Store build); the PoC snippets are the article's own Swift, reproduced verbatim; per the article's UPDATE 6 the gamed bug was "quietly patched" in iOS 15.0.2 and the other two were unpatched at publication; the author handle is not printed in the fetched text and is not invented here.

CORE METHOD:
  1. THE DORK (verbatim): while hunting the private VDP (`redacted.com`), "I just put in some random google dorking in its search box and nothing seems interesting to me until the one below: `site:redacted.com inurl:admin \"@gmail.com\"`" — the email-provider token (`"@gmail.com"`) is what surfaces a page that "exposed all user's email addresses of my target."

  4. THE OUTCOME (verbatim): reported to the program, "The issue was latter fixed but as this is a VDP program, bounty for this bug was zero."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a search-indexed (Google-discoverable / cached) admin or back-office page on the target's domain that LISTS user records (emails/names); a per-record EDIT/VIEW control whose response returns the full stored row — check whether secret fields (password, SSN, API key, security answer) come back in PLAINTEXT; EDIT/DELETE actions on OTHER users' rows; no auth, or an auth gate the cached/indexed page bypasses. Recon tell: `inurl:admin`/`inurl:manage`/`inurl:edit` combined with a common email-provider string (`"@gmail.com"`, `"@outlook.com"`) proves the page lists live user rows.
CHAIN: unauthenticated/low-priv attacker (primitive: the admin CRUD is search-indexed and directly reachable) -> google-dork `site:<target> inurl:admin \"@<email-provider>\"` surfaces the user-listing admin page (primitive: search-engine-indexed admin surface) -> open a record's EDIT view -> the full row including the PLAINTEXT PASSWORD is returned for ANY user (escalation: bulk sensitive-credential disclosure = §1 "sensitive information disclosure with PoC" + "admin panel access") -> EDIT/DELETE any of the 38k records (escalation: BAC / cross-user write) -> full user-table takeover (impact: P1 — mass credential disclosure + cross-account write).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any target — (1) google-dork the domain for indexed admin/user-listing pages: `site:<target> inurl:admin \"@gmail.com\"` (rotate the email token to `@outlook.com`/`@yahoo.com`/`@hotmail.com`, and try `inurl:manage`/`inurl:edit`/`inurl:users`/`inurl:staff`); (2) open a hit and click a record's EDIT/VIEW control while watching the response — if secret fields (password/SSN/key) return in plaintext you have a bulk credential-disclosure oracle; (3) test EDIT and DELETE on a row that is NOT yours for cross-user write; (4) check `robots.txt`/`noindex` but do not trust it — search engines often cache the page anyway. Rule: **a search-indexed admin CRUD page that lists users is a plaintext-credential + cross-user-write oracle — dork it with an email token, open the edit view, read the stored secrets.**

Related-but-distinct REVIEWED, NOT re-recorded as a §17 method: ledger ~6684 (dork the build/deploy estate + decorative-login-gate test — an auth-bypass-on-build-panel finding, not plaintext-cred disclosure in an admin CRUD); the CryptoCat "exposed log file, live admin sessions, and 50,000 records" entry (ledger ~6963 — a server-side LOG-FILE exposure carrier, not a search-indexed admin CRUD page). Author: AsterFiester ("Raidh"), Sep 2021 (snapshot Sep 11 2021; report timeline: Reported May 27 2021, Rewarded $3133.70 Jun 17 2021, Fixed Jul 5 2021). Google VRP, Dialogflow (dialogflow.cloud.google.com).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Dialogflow tenant/lab; every quote and the request body below are verbatim from the fetched Wayback article).
CLASS: authorization / IDOR / BOLA (cross-tenant object-level access) on a COMPOSITE RESOURCE NAME whose CHILD id is NOT a secret — it is DERIVED from a shared PREBUILT/TEMPLATE agent, so it is IDENTICAL across every account that instantiates the same template — while only the PARENT (agent) id differs, and that parent id LEAKS through the public web-demo share link / embed snippet. Swapping the parent-id segment of the fully-qualified resource name reaches the victim's objects.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE FEATURE (verbatim): "The dialogflow have 2 different versions of applications. Dialogflow Essentials and Dialogflow CX." Hunting broken access control, "Test Cases are empty and I tried to import them but it didn't work!" Reading the docs surfaced a "prebuild agent" feature — "There are so many pre build agents available and I just selected the first one" (an Agent "is just like a project to create everything"); creating a prebuild agent populated Test Cases.
  2. THE REQUEST (verbatim body): deleting a Test Case sends `{"names":["projects/agent-nameas-nqsq/locations/us-central1/agents/3fbab09c-d034-4f35-bb1f-1ab0837e8806/testCases/9a1c14e8-3dee-43a6-8e58-10d4a1fb8a70"]}` — "It have two different id's one agent id and the testCases id. It is hard to guess and hard to do bruteforcing."
  3. THE KEY INSIGHT — TEMPLATE-DETERMINISTIC CHILD IDS (verbatim): "why wouldn't you create a same prebuild agent in the victims account?" Importing the SAME prebuild agent into a SECOND account and deleting the same test case, "I saw the same test case id which is inside the attacker account"; the Burp-Comparer delta is "the `agents/3fbab09c-…` id that's the main difference in the both requests." So the `testCases/<id>` segment is IDENTICAL across accounts built from one template; only `agents/<agent-id>` differs.
  4. THE BYPASS (verbatim): "I just replace the attacker agent id to victims agent id and It successfully deleted the test case in the victim account." (the "ids are unguessable" objection is beaten WITHOUT guessing — the child id is a constant.)
  5. THE PARENT-ID ORACLE (verbatim): "To integrate the agent in any website you should need to paste this JavaScript Code" OR "you can share the agent link by enabling web demo. https://bot.dialogflow.com/be29c5bc-b4b7-4d24-b5ba-ec3d3cbe4ba1" — "That's the main way to get the agent id."
  6. THE IMPACT (verbatim): "we can select all test cases and able to delete with one click by changing the agent id" — cross-tenant delete of the victim's test cases. Reward $3133.70.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an API addressing objects by a COMPOSITE / HIERARCHICAL resource name (`projects/{p}/locations/{l}/agents/{a}/testCases/{t}`, `orgs/{o}/teams/{t}/items/{i}`, `.../{parent}/{child}`) whose object is INSTANTIATED FROM A SHARED TEMPLATE/PREBUILT/SEED; a child id IDENTICAL across two accounts that used the same template (diff your own object's child id against a second account's — a match means it is not a secret); the parent/container id disclosed via a share link, embed snippet, public web-demo URL, or mobile deep link. The author's tell: "import didn't work" until he used a prebuilt agent — templated objects are exactly the ones with deterministic sub-ids.
CHAIN: attacker instantiates the SAME prebuilt/template agent in their own account (primitive: sub-object ids are template-derived and predictable) -> creates/deletes a test case and captures the fully-qualified resource name -> obtains the victim's agent id from the public web-demo link `bot.dialogflow.com/<agent-id>` / the embed snippet (primitive: parent-id disclosure via the integration surface) -> re-sends the request with the victim's `agents/<agent-id>` segment while keeping the deterministic `testCases/<id>` (escalation: cross-tenant object access) -> delete/mutate ALL the victim's test cases (impact: cross-tenant data destruction / BOLA on a Google Cloud product — P1/P2).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any product that instantiates user objects from a shared TEMPLATE/PREBUILT/SEED (project templates, sample workspaces, prebuilt agents/bots, starter repos, demo tenants) — (1) create the SAME template in TWO of your own accounts and diff the child-object ids; any IDENTICAL child id is a constant, not a secret; (2) capture the fully-qualified resource name from a mutation (`{"names":[".../parents/<pid>/children/<cid>"]}`); (3) get the victim's PARENT id from any integration/share surface (embed snippet, `*.domain/<uuid>` share link, public demo URL, deep link); (4) replay swapping ONLY the parent-id segment to the victim's while keeping the deterministic child id — a 200 / state change on the victim's object is the cross-tenant IDOR. Rule: **a composite resource name is only as secret as its least-secret segment — if the child id is template-derived and the parent id leaks via an embed/share link, swap the parent segment and you own the victim's objects.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: 0 hits across the write targets for `dialogflow` (the only recorded Dialogflow entry, ledger ~11827 / 0x01alka, is the Share/invite 'Developer'-role privilege escalation — a DIFFERENT bug), `prebuild`/`prebuilt agent`, `bot.dialogflow.com`, `testCases`, "same prebuild agent in the victims account", template-deterministic sub-object ids. The recorded IDOR families (ledger ~3427 "swap the user/account identifier"; ~9595 parent-scope+child-id-not-revalidated) all swap a guessable/leaked user-or-object id — NONE carries the TEMPLATE-DETERMINISM insight that the child id is IDENTICAL across tenants, so the "ids are unguessable, IDOR is dead" objection fails WITHOUT guessing and only the leaked parent id must be swapped. NEW: template-derived deterministic child ids + parent-id-via-integration as a two-part IDOR bypass on composite resource names. Slot 17.677. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced).
FRESHNESS: published ~Sep 11 2021 (Wayback snapshot; report timeline May–Jul 2021) — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned; the method (template-deterministic sub-object ids + parent-id disclosure on composite resource names) is implementation-shape-level and still applies to any template/seed-instantiated multi-tenant product.
HONESTY: no reproduction this pass (no Dialogflow tenant/lab); the live article is 410-DELETED by the author and the body was recovered ONLY from the Wayback snapshot `web.archive.org/web/20210911154607/...` (route documented above); every quote and the request body are verbatim from that snapshot; the agent/test-case UUIDs are the article's own; the earlier writeup it links ("5000-google-idor-vulnerability-writeup-c7b45926abe9", its 1st Dialogflow IDOR writeup) was NOT read this pass.

SOURCE: https://valsamaras.medium.com/size-matters-cve-2021-0485-cfa0a291f903  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract` on the live URL — one pass, full article. Author: valsamaras, "Size Matters — CVE-2021–0485 (High)" (article undated on-page; it references the Android security bulletin 2021-05-01 as the fix, so it is a May–June 2021-era post).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Android lab this pass; the article's evidence is the manifest/snippet steps + screenshots + the linked PoC repo github.com/Ch0pin/CVE20210485, which was NOT downloaded or run this pass).
CLASS: privilege escalation / platform security-restriction bypass — an UNPRIVILEGED Android app (NO special permission) holds FOREGROUND state in an INVISIBLE 1x1dp Picture-in-Picture window, defeating every Android Oreo/Pie/Q restriction that keys on "the app is in the background / the UID is idle" (sensor access, camera/microphone, location throttling, background activity starts).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE RESTRICTIONS (verbatim): Android Oreo (2017) introduced "background execution limitations including the frequency of location updates"; Android Pie (2018) "disabled access to sensors for idle UIDs, thus an application being in the background for more than a certain amount of time shouldn't be able to use the camera, microphone or other sensors in general"; Android Q "imported new restrictions that prevent an application to start an activity from the background".
  2. THE FEATURE NEEDS NO PERMISSION (verbatim): PiP = "a special type of multi window mode"; declare `<activity android:name="VideoActivity" android:supportsPictureInPicture="true" android:configChanges="screenSize|smallestScreenSize|screenLayout|orientation" ...` and call `enterPictureInPictureMode()` — "…And as you probably noticed NO SPECIAL PERMISSION IS REQUIRED".
  3. THE SIZE KNOB: `setAspectRatio` "will not work in the particular case"; use the `<layout>` manifest element ("PiP is just a special type of multi window mode") — `android:defaultWidth`, `android:defaultHeight`, `android:gravity`, `android:minHeight`, `android:minWidth`.
  4. THE PAYLOAD (verbatim): `<activity android:name=".MainActivity" android:supportsPictureInPicture="true" android:theme="@style/Theme.AppCompat"> <layout android:defaultHeight="1dp" android:defaultWidth="1dp" android:gravity="top|end" android:minHeight="1dp" android:minWidth="1dp" />` — "This little 'dot' will maintain your application in the foreground bypassing the restrictions we described in the beginning of the article." (A transparent activity alone fails because "there is a shadow dropped in the window frame"; the 1dp window is "not visible or touchable".)
  5. THE RESULT (verbatim): "By using a very small PiP window it is possible for an application to maintain a foreground state without becoming perceived to the user" — camera/mic/sensor access, location updates and background activity starts persist. Fixed per https://source.android.com/security/bulletin/2021-05-01; PoC github.com/Ch0pin/CVE20210485.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any control that grants/denies a capability by a STATE the caller can hold artificially (foreground/visible/idle/unlocked) while the windowing layer lets an app hold that state in a window the user cannot perceive: a manifest declaring `supportsPictureInPicture="true"` with a `<layout>` min size of 1dp and an immediate `enterPictureInPictureMode()` in `onCreate`; web/mobile twins = API actions gated on "user active / tab visible / device unlocked" client flags.
CHAIN: unprivileged app from the store (primitive: `supportsPictureInPicture` + `enterPictureInPictureMode()`, no permission) -> 1x1dp PiP window (bypass: "no control of the minimum allowed window size while in PiP mode") -> app stays FOREGROUND invisibly (bypass: every Oreo/Pie/Q restriction keys on background/idle state) -> persistent hidden camera/microphone/location/sensor access + background activity starts + no idle throttling (impact: invisible surveillance-grade capability = platform privacy-restriction escape; the author's own framing: spyware/ad-fraud class impact).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: (1) list the target platform's restrictions that key on an observable STATE (background/idle/visible/unlocked); (2) list the OS features that can HOLD that state cheaply (PiP with `<layout android:minWidth="1dp" android:minHeight="1dp" android:defaultWidth="1dp" android:defaultHeight="1dp"/>` + `enterPictureInPictureMode()`; overlay/inset windows; invisible foreground services); (3) build the minimal holder and verify the denied capability (camera/mic/location/activity-start) now works while nothing is visible to the user; (4) port the shape to web targets: any API action gated on a client-held flag ("active session", "visible tab") — hold the state and re-test the denied action. Rule: **a state-based restriction is only as strong as the cost of holding the state — the smallest window that keeps you 'foreground' turns every background restriction into advice.**
WHY IT IS A NEW TECHNIQUE (A/B + §17 slot): 0 hits across the write targets for `CVE-2021-0485`, `Picture.in.Picture`/`enterPictureInPictureMode`, `1dp`/`minWidth` window tricks, `valsamaras`, "background execution limit"/"foreground state". The recorded mobile/platform material (§17.675 iOS XPC entitlement skip; the Nextcloud screen-lock entry; §17.546/§17.554 macOS trust/sandbox) attacks entitlements, signatures or brokers directly — NONE records defeating STATE-KEYED restrictions by holding the state in an unperceivable window. NEW: invisible-PiP foreground-hold as a universal state-restriction bypass. Slot 17.678. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced).
DEDUPE/DELTA: `tapjacking`/`TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY`/invisible-window/foreground-service = 0 relevant hits (only VRT list mentions of tapjacking). DELTA = the STATE-HOLD primitive (restriction keyed on background/idle defeated by a 1dp PiP window) rather than any overlay/entitlement attack.
FRESHNESS: 2021 (fix in the 2021-05-01 bulletin) — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned; the method (state-keyed restriction + cheap state-hold) is version-independent.

CORE METHOD:
  1. BUG A — THE FAKE ADMIN GATE (verbatim): `maconfig.exe` "is a tool that can be used to dump sitelist.xml, the only problem is it requires administrator privileges. If you try to run it from an account with low privileges you'll get 'Access is Denied'." — but "I noticed a problem with the permissions set on the parent folder which contains the executable maconfig.exe. A user with low privileges can copy and paste the parent folder to a different location and with that in mind, I copied the parent folder to my desktop and tried executing maconfig.exe and it ran!"
  2. EXPLOIT A (verbatim): "1. Copy the folder 'C:\Program Files\McAfee\Agent' to a location you have write access to (e.g. Desktop) 2. Run the following command: maconfig.exe -getsiteinfo [destination] 3. Use this tool to decrypt the passwords in sitelist.xml" (funoverip/mcafee-sitelist-pwd-decryption). sitelist.xml "contains UNC paths, usernames, server names, and encrypted passwords (which can be decrypted)". CVE-2021-31836, McAfee Agent < 5.7.4, "requires normal user privileges".
  3. BUG B — THE UNPROTECTED KEY (verbatim): "Most McAfee registry keys cannot be edited due to tamper prevention/HIPS. Fortunately, some keys are not protected by tamper prevention/HIPS and can be modified. Some of the unprotected registry keys contain paths to a McAfee DLL." — `Computer\HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\McAfee EndPoint Encryption\AppExtensions\MfeCryptoAdapter` "contains 'DllPath' and the value can be modified by anyone with local administrator privileges. Upon setting this to a custom DLL, it will run everytime the screen is locked or unlocked."
  4. WHY IT WORKS (verbatim): "the DLL isn't injected into a McAfee process, rather it's injected into the Logon User Interface (LogonUI.exe). And since LogonUI.exe runs with NT AUTHORITY/SYSTEM privileges, our DLL inherits those permissions."
  5. EXPLOIT B (verbatim): `reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\McAfee EndPoint Encryption\AppExtensions\MfeCryptoAdapter" /t reg_sz /v dllpath /d C:\path\to\malicious\dll\evil.dll` — trigger: "You can lock the screen with cmd prompt using rundll32.exe user32.dll,LockWorkStation"; demo DLL "launches Notepad.exe" and "notepad is launched with SYSTEM privileges" (McAfee Drive Encryption < 7.2.9.5; vendor reply verbatim: "We are not planning to put another CVE for the DLL Hijacking issue as fixing the registry keys will automatically get this resolved.").

CHAIN: (A) low-priv user on a managed host (primitive) -> copy `C:\Program Files\McAfee\Agent` to a writable dir (bypass: the folder ACL was the only admin gate) -> `maconfig.exe -getsiteinfo` dumps sitelist.xml (escalation: UNC paths, usernames, server names, encrypted passwords) -> decrypt with the public tool -> ePO/domain credentials (impact: sensitive info disclosure with PoC -> network foothold; P2 class). (B) local admin (prerequisite, stated) -> write `DllPath` in the tamper-exempt key (bypass: key not covered by HIPS) -> lock/unlock loads the DLL into LogonUI.exe as SYSTEM (escalation: admin->SYSTEM) -> arbitrary code execution as SYSTEM + persistence on every lock/unlock at the credential screen (impact: privilege escalation + persistence).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any managed Windows host — (1) run each vendor admin utility from a low-priv shell IN PLACE (note the failure), then `xcopy` its parent folder to %TEMP% and re-run: success means the "admin requirement" is a folder ACL — dump whatever it dumps (site lists, config, credential material) and look for decryptable secrets; (2) `reg query` the vendor's whole registry tree, attempt writes (as admin) and diff which keys are protected vs writable; for every writable key list `DllPath`/`Path`/`Image`/`Command` values and identify the CONSUMER process and its trigger; (3) point one at your DLL, trigger (`rundll32.exe user32.dll,LockWorkStation`, screensaver, logon) and check the executing process's integrity (`whoami /groups` — SYSTEM means the LogonUI-class payoff). Rule: **the FOLDER can be the only admin gate (copy the binary out and it runs), and a tamper-protection exemption list is an attack surface — a writable `DllPath` into a SYSTEM-process consumer at lock/unlock is admin->SYSTEM plus credential-screen persistence.**
WHY IT IS A NEW TECHNIQUE (A/B + §17 slot): 0 hits across the write targets for `maconfig`/`sitelist`/`MfeCryptoAdapter`/`DllPath`/`LogonUI`/`getsiteinfo`/McAfee/CVE-2021-31836 ("DLL hijack" hits = §17.343 Viber qwave traversal-write, #440963 missing-dir search-order, the Burp installer note; "ships" noise only otherwise). Related-but-distinct REVIEWED, NOT re-recorded: §17.628 (Monero Inno Setup `Permissions: users-full` on a directory holding an app-executed binary — a user-writable EXECUTION surface, not a fake admin gate); the OneDrive entry (ledger ~15894-15900, world-writable root daemon after an updater `chmod -R 777` — installer-mess aftermath, not a deliberate ACL gate); §17.182 (privileged helper installer paths). NEW: (1) folder-ACL-as-privilege-gate defeated by copy-out -> privileged credential dump; (2) tamper-protection-EXEMPT vendor registry key -> DllPath consumed by a SYSTEM HOST process (LogonUI) at lock/unlock -> admin->SYSTEM + persistence. Two new primitives in one source, one entry, one §17 slot (the batch-250 habr iOS precedent). Slot 17.679. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced).
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over §17.628/OneDrive = the AUTHENTICATION-vs-ACL confusion (the check IS the directory ACL; moving the binary dissolves it) and the tamper-protection-EXEMPTION axis (vendor security software explicitly exempts keys; the exempt set is the writable registry surface) with a cross-process load target (LogonUI, SYSTEM) at a lock/unlock trigger.

SOURCE: https://google.github.io/security-research/pocs/linux/cve-2021-22555/writeup.html  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract` on the live URL — first pass truncated mid-exploitation (ended at "the more we can vary"); a 60,000-char retry returned the FULL writeup (vulnerability, exploitation stages, PoC output, timeline). Author: Andy Nguyen (theflow@), Google Information Security Engineer; reported 2021-04-06, patched 2021-04-13, publicly disclosed 2021-07-07; kCTF pod-isolation break, $10,000 to charity.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no vulnerable kernel/lab run this pass; the linked PoC github.com/google/security-research/.../cve-2021-22555 was NOT compiled or executed; every quote and code fragment below is verbatim from the fetched writeup).
CLASS: sandbox/container escape + privilege escalation (kernel memory corruption) — a 15-year-old Netfilter COMPAT-mode heap out-of-bounds write (4 zero bytes, up to 0x4C past the object) reachable with only `CAP_NET_ADMIN` inside a user+network namespace (i.e. from an unprivileged k8s pod), turned into kernel code execution and a Kubernetes pod escape.
CORE METHOD:
  1. ENTRY (verbatim): "When `IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE` or `IP6T_SO_SET_REPLACE` is called in compatibility mode, which requires the `CAP_NET_ADMIN` capability that can however be obtained in a user+network namespace, structures need to be converted from user to kernel as well as 32bit to 64bit… Our vulnerability is in `xt_compat_target_from_user()` where `memset()` is called with an offset `target->targetsize` that is not accounted for during the allocation - leading to a few bytes written out-of-bounds".
  2. PRIMITIVE SHAPING (verbatim): "The `targetsize` is not controllable by the user, but one can choose different targets with different structure sizes by name (like `TCPMSS`, `TTL` or `NFQUEUE`)… the target size must _not_ be 8 bytes aligned in order to fulfill `pad > 0`. The biggest possible I found is `NFLOG` for which we can choose an offset up to 0x4C bytes out-of-bounds (one can influence the offset by adding padding between `struct xt_entry_match` and `struct xt_entry_target`)". "the minimum size is > 0x100 which means that the smallest slab this object can be allocated in is kmalloc-512".
  3. SLAB DISCIPLINE (verbatim): "it had something to do with the `GFP_KERNEL_ACCOUNT` flag… Jann Horn confirmed that before 5.9, separate slabs were used to implement accounting. Therefore, every heap primitive we use in the exploit chain should also use `GFP_KERNEL_ACCOUNT`."
  4. OOB -> UAF via `msg_msg` (verbatim design): spray `msgsnd()` PRIMARY messages + SECONDARY segments of 1024 bytes ("its structure `msg_msg` has surprisingly never been abused"); "we create some holes (in our case every 1024th) in the primary messages, and trigger the vulnerable `setsockopt(IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE)`"; overwrite two zero bytes of the adjacent primary's secondary-message pointer — "Since we allocate them with a size of 1024 bytes, we therefore have a 1 - (1024 / 65536) chance to redirect the pointer"; two primaries now share ONE secondary -> "we namely fetch the secondary message from the real message queue using `msgrcv()` and as such free it" = use-after-free.
  5. SMAP BYPASS + LEAK (verbatim): reclaim with `socketpair()` unix-socket sk_buff sprays "and imitate the `struct msg_msg` header"; `mlist.next` stays `41414141` ("not having a kernel address is crucial as it actually prevents us from freeing the block again"); inflate `m_ts` "to `DATALEN_MSG=4096-sizeof(struct msg_msg)`" to read past the message and "leak the `struct msg_msg` header of the adjacent message"; the circular list makes `mlist.next` point back to the primary -> re-craft `next` -> leak the secondary's address.
  6. BETTER UAF (verbatim): "This stale `struct sk_buff` data buffer is a better use-after-free scenario to exploit, because it does not contain header information, meaning that we can now use it to free _any_ kind of object on the slab."
  7. VICTIM + KASLR (verbatim): `struct pipe_buffer` ("allocated in kmalloc-1024", `alloc_pipe_info()` uses `GFP_KERNEL_ACCOUNT`) holds `const struct pipe_buf_operations *ops`; writing to pipes sets `ops` to the static `anon_pipe_buf_ops` in .data — leak it through the stale buffer ("anon_pipe_buf_ops: ffffffffa1e78380 / kbase_addr: ffffffffa0e00000") because "the difference between the .data segment and the .text segment is always the same".
  8. CODE EXEC (verbatim): reclaim the pipe_buffer with a fake one whose `ops` points at a planted fake `pipe_buf_operations` with a malicious `release`; "close all pipes in order to trigger the release which in turn will kick off the JOP chain… achieve a kernel stack pivot as soon as possible in order to execute a kernel ROP chain"; ROP = "call `commit_creds(prepare_kernel_cred(NULL))`… then call `switch_task_namespaces(find_task_by_vpid(1), init_nsproxy)`".
  9. CONTAINER ESCAPE (verbatim): "Arriving back in userland, we now have root permissions to change mnt, pid and net namespaces to escape the container and break out of the kubernetes pod": `setns(open("/proc/1/ns/mnt", O_RDONLY), 0); setns(open("/proc/1/ns/pid", O_RDONLY), 0); setns(open("/proc/1/ns/net", O_RDONLY), 0);` then `execve("/bin/bash", ...)`. Discovery heuristic (verbatim): "I started by looking at old vulnerabilities like CVE-2016-3134 and CVE-2016-4997 which inspired me to grep for `memcpy()` and `memset()` in the Netfilter code."
DETECTION SIGNAL: compat/32-on-64 conversion paths (Netfilter `xt_compat_*`, `compat_sys_*` ioctls) where the allocation size and a later `memset`/`memcpy` offset disagree — the smoking-gun shape is `pad = XT_ALIGN(target->targetsize) - target->targetsize; if (pad > 0) memset(t->data + target->targetsize, 0, pad);` with the allocation sized without `pad`/`off`; plus any container/pod that hands the workload `CAP_NET_ADMIN` in a user+network namespace (the default shape of an unprivileged Kubernetes pod).
CHAIN: unprivileged workload inside a Kubernetes pod (primitive: user+network namespace yields `CAP_NET_ADMIN`) -> compat-mode `setsockopt(IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE)` with an NFLOG target (offset tuned by match padding) -> 4-zero-byte heap OOB write up to 0x4C past `xt_table_info` (primitive: partial NULL of an adjacent pointer) -> two `msg_msg` primaries share one secondary -> `msgrcv()` frees it = UAF (escalation) -> `socketpair()` sk_buff reclaim + `m_ts` inflation leaks kernel heap addresses (SMAP bypass) -> the stale sk_buff frees ANY slab object -> reclaim with `pipe_buffer` -> leak `ops`->`anon_pipe_buf_ops` = KASLR/SMEP defeat -> planted fake `pipe_buf_operations.release` -> JOP -> stack pivot -> kernel ROP (`commit_creds(prepare_kernel_cred(NULL))` + `switch_task_namespaces(find_task_by_vpid(1), init_nsproxy)`) = kernel code execution -> `setns(/proc/1/ns/{mnt,pid,net})` = CONTAINER / KUBERNETES POD ESCAPE -> root shell (impact: P1/critical — kCTF pod isolation broken; $10,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any Linux container/k8s workload (an unprivileged pod suffices): (1) audit compat conversion paths for allocation-vs-memset offset mismatches — the author's own heuristic is "grep for `memcpy()` and `memset()` in the Netfilter code" (start: `xt_compat_target_from_user`/`xt_compat_match_from_user`); (2) with a 2/4-byte NULL OOB write: spray `msg_msg` (primary `msgsnd` + secondary segments sized 1024, `GFP_KERNEL_ACCOUNT` discipline), punch holes every Nth primary, land the victim object in a hole, NULL the low two bytes of the adjacent secondary pointer so two queues alias one segment, `msgrcv()` one copy to free it; (3) reclaim the freed segment with `socketpair()` sk_buff buffers carrying a fake `msg_msg` header, inflate `m_ts` to `DATALEN_MSG` and read out the adjacent header (`mlist.next` = heap leak); (4) re-claim with `pipe()` `pipe_buffer`s, leak `ops`->`anon_pipe_buf_ops` for kbase, plant a fake `pipe_buf_operations` and `close()` the pipes to fire `release`; (5) post-root escape with `setns(open("/proc/1/ns/mnt"|"pid"|"net", O_RDONLY), 0)` + `execve("/bin/bash")`. Rule: **a two-byte NULL OOB write is enough: alias two `msg_msg` queues on one segment for a UAF, leak through `m_ts`, hijack `pipe_buffer.ops`, and the pod dies at `setns(/proc/1/ns/*)`.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD: 0 hits across the write targets for `22555`/`xt_compat`/netfilter/`msg_msg`/`pipe_buffer`/`kCTF`/`IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE`/`theflow`/`Andy Nguyen` as a kernel-heap carrier (the `theflow0` PlayStation entries are a FreeBSD setsockopt race UAF and a BD-J chain — different bugs). The recorded kernel material (PlayStation `IPV6_2292PKTOPTIONS` UAF ~ledger 2756/2916; the Docker overlay2 file-capability privesc ~15850) and the recorded container escapes (§17.406 hot-patch host-agent binary substitution; V-10 HostPath) contain NOTHING of the msg_msg dual-queue UAF, the `GFP_KERNEL_ACCOUNT` slab-matching discipline, the `m_ts` inflation leak, the `anon_pipe_buf_ops` KASLR defeat, or the `setns(/proc/1/ns/*)` escape. NEW end-to-end: compat-conversion OOB -> msg_msg UAF -> pipe_buffer ops hijack -> ROP -> container escape. Slot 17.680. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced).
DEDUPE/DELTA: every atom above greps 0 except `setxattr` (§17.542 macOS broker — unrelated) and `user namespace` (V-10/Docker hardening text — unrelated carriers). DELTA = the whole pattern; no recorded entry teaches kernel-heap exploitation methodology at all.
FRESHNESS: disclosed 2021-07-07 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned; the pattern (compat conversions + `msg_msg` + `pipe_buffer` + `setns` escape) is implementation-shape-level and remains the canonical container-escape chain taught by this writeup.
HONESTY: not reproduced this pass (no kernel lab; the public PoC was NOT run); all quotes/code verbatim from the fetched writeup; the source page elides some middle passages and figures with "..." placeholders (present in the fetched HTML) — those gaps were NOT filled in from memory; the exploitation percentages and stage names are the writeup's own.

SOURCE: https://ertugrull.medium.com/unprivileged-user-with-read-write-permission-to-user-access-can-escalate-their-role-to-admin-a217d2d280a8  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract` on the live URL — one pass, full (short) article. Author: Ertugrul (@ertugrulphp), Jun 19 2021, first Medium post; private HackerOne program (target unnamed).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — private program, no lab; the article's evidence is the request screenshots (not renderable in the extract) plus the narrative steps quoted verbatim below).
CLASS: privilege escalation (vertical) — RBAC authorization bypass on a SELF-SERVICE role-edit request: the `roleId` parameter is documented/used as a UUID (custom roles), but the BUILT-IN admin role carries NO UUID, so sending the LITERAL NAME TOKEN `ADMIN` resolves outside the "switch to lower roles only" authorization set and promotes the caller to admin.
CORE METHOD:
  1. SETUP (verbatim): the program has "a team building feature"; the author "created a role that only allowed read/write to user data" and invited a second e-mail with that role — "all I could edit was my own role and name".
  2. THE REQUEST (verbatim): "When I inspected the role edit request, I saw a parameter named roleId= in the body of the POST request. It was in UUID format."
  3. THE BLIND SPOT (verbatim): "Except for the admin role, there was permission to switch from my own role to lower roles. Because each different role created was custom created, they all had a different UUID value, but no UUID for the basic admin role. I guess it didn't have the UUID value as it was already a role that existed when you created the account."
  4. THE BYPASS (verbatim): "When I realized that there was no UUID value for the admin role, I tried to continue the request by typing ADMIN in the roleId= parameter." — "I continued the request and when I refreshed the page, I was now an Admin, I could access all the panel content and could delete other admin accounts."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a role/membership EDIT request whose id field is a machine-generated UUID for user-created roles while built-in/system roles appear NOWHERE (no id in the dropdown, no id in the role-list API); a client-side restriction ("may switch to lower roles only") with no matching server-side comparison; any id parameter whose only validation is its FORMAT (UUID) — and the strongest tell: a role selector that cannot represent the built-in admin role at all.
CHAIN: team member holding only user-data read/write (primitive: the lowest custom role, self-service edit of own role+name) -> POST the role-edit with `roleId=ADMIN` in place of a UUID (bypass: the authorized set = the enumerable custom-role UUIDs; the built-in admin role is NAME-keyed and resolves outside that set) -> caller's role becomes Admin -> full panel access incl. deletion of other admin accounts (impact: vertical privilege escalation to full admin — §1 class).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any RBAC product with custom roles — (1) create a custom role, capture the self role-edit/membership-update request and note the id format (UUID/slug/int); (2) replay your OWN role-change with the LITERAL NAMES of built-in roles instead of ids (`ADMIN`, `admin`, `Admin`, `OWNER`, `owner`, `root`, `superuser`, `system`, `1`, `0`, empty) and with names of roles the UI will not offer you; (3) re-read session/permissions after each attempt (a role change may only apply at re-auth — re-login and re-check); (4) diff the UI's role list against the API's and against the built-in set: any privileged role with NO id is a name-resolvable blind spot. Rule: **when custom entities have generated ids but built-in ones have none, the id FORMAT is the authorization boundary — feed the literal name of the built-in superuser role and the boundary dissolves.**
WHY IT IS A NEW TECHNIQUE (A/B + §17 slot): 0 hits across the write targets for `roleId`/`role_id`, literal-name-token-in-id-parameter, "no UUID for the admin role", name-fallback role resolution, `ertugrull`. Related-but-distinct REVIEWED, NOT re-recorded: §17.413 (boomneroli — a LOWER role invoking ADMIN-ONLY GraphQL mutations via a STATIC client-supplied role id harvested from a temp org: id REUSE across contexts, not format confusion); ledger ~2251 (Teleport — a delegated owner writing RESTRICTED FIELDS `grants`/`owner_grants` in their own object: field-level authz); §17.676 (a privilege-granting boolean in one's own object); ledger ~2545 (tenant identity-header replay). NEW: the ID-FORMAT assumption as the authz boundary + the built-in-role-has-no-id blind spot (a value OUTSIDE the enumerable id set that a fallback resolver maps to the superuser role). Slot 17.681. UNVERIFIED (not reproduced).
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over §17.413 = VALUE-FORMAT confusion (literal name vs UUID hitting a different resolver path) versus STATIC-ID reuse; over ~2251/§17.676 = the privilege token is not a field/flag on the object but the IDENTIFIER FORMAT of a role reference in a self-edit.
FRESHNESS: Jun 19 2021 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; read because assigned; the test (literal role-name tokens in id parameters) is version-independent and cheap to run on every RBAC target.
HONESTY: no reproduction this pass (private H1 program, target unnamed in the article); quotes verbatim from the fetched article; the request screenshots ("Press enter or click to view image in full size") could not be rendered by the extractor — the request shape is recorded ONLY as the article's text describes it (`roleId=<UUID|ADMIN>` in a POST body; no endpoint URL is given); the CVSS figure is an image and its content is NOT transcribed.
