SOURCE: https://hackerone.com/reports/4126768 + https://hackerone.com/reports/4124549 + https://hackerone.com/reports/4016541 (curl VDP; reporters cyrax21_ / joumaaa / causalsecurity; disclosed 2026-10-19 / 2026-10-20 / 2026-09-14)  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live `web_extract` on all three report pages (summary + root-cause + PoC blocks read; each page's middle elided at ~8-8.2k chars, no method text missing from what was read).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no curl build or harness run this pass; every quote and code location is verbatim from the fetched reports; each report ships its own harness, described but not executed here).
CLASS: authentication bypass / identity confusion via an INCOMPLETE CONNECTION-REUSE OR SESSION-CACHE KEY — a security-relevant policy/identity dimension is enforced only in the connect state machine or lives outside the keyed struct, so a pooled/resumed transfer silently inherits another transfer's trust.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SHAPE (all three reports): the reuse/resume decision keys on a TUPLE; the security dimension in question is NOT in the tuple; its enforcement runs only when a NEW connection/session is established. A second transfer with DIFFERENT policy or identity rides the first transfer's state and its own policy is never evaluated / its own identity never presented.
  2. SSH HOST-KEY (#4126768, verbatim): "The core effect is a silent host-authentication bypass: a transfer whose configured SSH host-key policy would reject the server is served anyway, with exit code 0 and no warning, because it reuses a pooled connection established under a weaker or absent policy." `ssh_config_matches()` (`lib/url.c:569-579`) compares ONLY `priv_key`/`pub_key`; silently skipped on reuse: `CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS`, `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256`, `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_MD5`, `CURLOPT_SSH_HOSTKEYFUNCTION` (CLI `--knownhosts`, `--hostpubsha256`, `--hostpubmd5`, `-k`); protocols `sftp://`/`scp://`; both backends (libssh2, libssh). "curl sftp://host/a [policy A] --next sftp://host/b [policy B] reproduces the bypass with no unusual options." The TLS matcher DOES compare `pinned_key`, `CAfile`, `CApath`, `ca_info_blob`, `verifypeer`, `verifyhost`, `verifystatus` (`match_ssl_primary_config()`, `lib/vtls/vtls_config.c`) — "SSH compares none of its equivalents" (the asymmetry is the audit map). History: 1645e9b445 (CVE-2022-27782 fix, client keys only) -> removed 3e9817cd1b -> reinstated unchanged 0618ffe50d (June 2026); the 2026 connection-matching hardening commits each added parameters to the TLS/FTP/generic tuples and left `ssh_config_matches()` untouched.
  3. PROXY IDENTITY (#4124549, verbatim): `proxy_info_matches()` (`lib/url.c:540-549`) compares only `proxytype` + destination + `Curl_creds`; "`git grep proxyheaders lib/url.c` returns nothing"; `CURLOPT_PROXYHEADER` is sent once at tunnel-setup (`lib/http_proxy.c:63-83`) and is absent from the reuse path — the PoC transcript: two HTTPS-over-CONNECT transfers on one easy handle differing only in `Proxy-Authorization: Bearer TOKEN_A` / `TOKEN_B` -> "CONNECT requests the proxy received : 1 / Proxy-Authorization the proxy saw : ['Bearer TOKEN_A'] / transfer#2 reused the tunnel; its 'Proxy-Authorization: Bearer TOKEN_B' never reached the proxy"; the CONTROL (`CURLOPT_FRESH_CONNECT` on #2) shows both credentials. Impact (verbatim): "Cross-identity / cross-tenant confusion", "Privilege inheritance", "Silent credential non-presentation" (a rotated token is not presented until a fresh connection).
  4. TLS SESSION CACHE (#4016541, verbatim): the session-cache key `ssl_peer_key_build()` (`lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c:228`) is built from `struct ssl_primary_config`; the `CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION` callback (`fsslctx`, `lib/vtls/vtls_config.h:65`, outside `primary`) is not in that struct — "a client certificate installed through the callback is structurally incapable of entering the session key. Two transfers with different client identities produce byte-identical keys, and the second resumes the first's session." The documented remedy fails (verbatim): "`CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION`'s man page prescribes `CURLOPT_FORBID_REUSE` as the remedy for callback state leaking between transfers. That remedy does not work… the carrier here is the TLS session cache" (control: `CURLOPT_SSL_SESSIONID_CACHE=0`).
DETECTION SIGNAL: any client/SDK/pool where (a) policy or identity can differ between transfers, (b) enforcement lives in a connect/handshake state machine, and (c) the reuse-key builder visibly lists FEWER dimensions than the security options expose (diff the key builder fields against the full security-config surface); plus the fix-history tell — "the CVE fix added X to the key" (CVE-2022-27782 -> client keys; CVE-2026-3784 -> `Curl_creds`) while sibling identity channels feeding the SAME decision were left out.
CHAIN: two transfers in one pool with different trust configuration (primitive) -> the reuse/session key merges them (bypass: the policy/identity dimension is not keyed and is only enforced at connect time) -> transfer B's strict pin / its own proxy identity / its own client cert is silently replaced by transfer A's -> in a multi-tenant or privilege-separated client: tenant B rides tenant A's authenticated channel (impersonation / cross-tenant data), an unpinned host is accepted as pinned (host-auth bypass, exit 0), or a lesser identity inherits a privileged tunnel.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: (1) for every HTTP/DB/SSH client with pooling or session resumption on the target (SDKs, backend fetchers, service-mesh sidecars): run transfer A with identity/policy A, then transfer B with identity/policy B on the SAME pool, and diff what the SERVER logs (how many CONNECTs? which credentials? which client cert? which host-key policy applied?); use a forced-fresh-connection run as the control; (2) read the reuse/cache-key builder and list every security-relevant config field NOT in it; (3) whenever a CVE fix "adds X to the key", grep for sibling identity/policy channels in the same decision and re-test them. Rule: **anything enforced only at connect time is bypassed by reuse — the cache key IS the security boundary, and every dimension missing from it is a bypass.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD (A/B + §17.691): 0 hits across the three write targets for `4126768`, `4124549`, `4016541`, `ssh_config_matches`, `proxy_info_matches`, `ssl_peer_key_build`, `CURLOPT_PROXYHEADER`, `CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION`, `session resumption`, `connection reuse`/`connection pool` as a security-tuple carrier. Recorded nearest material REVIEWED and delta'd: the HTTP desync/connection-reuse entries (response-queue POISONING — the reuse lane's CONTENT ordering is the weapon; this entry's weapon is the reuse decision's own IDENTITY/POLICY tuple); the `unfurl_link`/`PrivateNetworkGuard` SSRF entries and §17.213 (URL/address parsing differentials — the request is mis-aimed; here the request is correctly aimed but rides the wrong trust). NEW: the reuse-key-tuple audit as a class (three independent carriers in one client), the "key builder vs security-option surface" diff, and the "fix keyed dimension A — check sibling dimensions B/C" heuristic.
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over the desync corpus = content-ordering vs identity-inheritance; over the parser-differential corpus = mis-addressed request vs correctly-addressed request on wrongly-trusted state.
FRESHNESS: disclosed 2026-09-14 / 2026-10-19 / 2026-10-20 — INSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window.
HONESTY: not reproduced this pass; the three reports' harnesses (`t1_matrix.sh` + paramiko SFTP listener; `poc_proxy_hdr_reuse.py`; the self-contained TLS server script) were NOT executed — their behaviour is recorded only as the reports describe; all quotes verbatim from the fetched pages.

SOURCE: https://medium.com/bugbountywriteup/unauthorized-access-to-odata-entities-2k-bounty-from-microsoft-e070b2ef88c2  2026-11-12
ROUTE: the Medium URL `web_extract` -> CRAWL_HTTP_403 and `r.jina.ai` -> http_error (both blocked); recovered via the AUTHOR'S OWN PUBLIC MIRROR `https://logicalhunter.me/unauthorized-access-to-odata-entities-msrc/` (opened live via `web_extract`) — every request shape below is quoted from that writeup. Microsoft Forms (forms.office.com), "Unauthorized Access to OData Entities – Microsoft Forms Vulnerability" — BAC / IDOR / cross-identity sensitive-info-disclosure; $2,000 MSRC bounty + Microsoft Hall of Fame; author/reporter Borna Nematzadeh; Medium post 2021-01-10 (per the MSRC writeups index), author mirror dated 2024-10-21.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Microsoft Forms/OData endpoint was exercised this pass; the `runtimeForms`/`createdBy`/`formID` detail and the request shapes are quoted from the fetched writeup).
CLASS: authorization bypass on an OData API — FIELD-LEVEL (projection) authorization is enforced PER ENTITY TYPE, so the denylist that blocks `$select=<sensitiveField>` on the primary entity is bypassed by selecting the SAME field on a SIBLING entity type that SHARES THE SAME ENTITY KEY, addressed with a key the attacker legitimately obtained.
CORE METHOD:
  1. ENUMERATE THE MODEL: fetch the OData metadata document — `http://forms.office.com/formapi/api/$metadata` (the data model / `information_schema`: entity types, properties, relationships, and each type's ENTITY KEY). The reporter fed it to `https://pragmatiqa.com/xodata` (a generic OData model visualizer) to see which entity types share properties and keys.
  2. OBTAIN THE VICTIM'S KEY LEGITIMATELY: through the product's own share flow (User A shares a form with User B; on submit the request `formapi/api/<ownerTenantID>/users/<ownerID>/forms(<formID>)/responses` fires), the attacker legitimately holds `ownerTenantID`, `ownerID`, `formID` — the victim's own addressing parameters. No enumeration needed.
  3. HIT THE SENSITIVE FIELD, GET DENIED: `.../forms(<formID>)?$select=createdBy` (createdBy = the user's email) -> 404. The field projection is BLOCKED on the `forms` entity.
  4. BYPASS VIA SIBLING-ENTITY KEY REUSE: find a SIBLING entity type that (a) exposes the same sensitive property (`createdBy`) AND (b) shares the SAME ENTITY KEY (`formID`) as the denied entity. The shared key is the crux — a sibling keyed by a random `accountID` would be unusable (you don't know the victim's accountID), but one keyed by `formID` is addressable with the key you already hold. The reporter found `runtimeForms` (has `createdBy`, keyed by `formID` like `forms`).
  5. RE-ISSUE $select AGAINST THE SIBLING: `formapi/api/<ownerTenantID>/users/<ownerID>/runtimeForms(<formID>)?$select=createdBy` -> returns the victim's email with NO user interaction (the reporter's first variant needed user interaction; removing that requirement is what earned the $2K).
DETECTION SIGNAL: an OData (or GraphQL/REST/ORM) API with a metadata/model endpoint that enforces field/property authorization PER ENTITY TYPE (the sensitive `$select`/`fields`/projection returns 403/404 on one entity) while the model exposes a SIBLING entity carrying the same sensitive property under the SAME key; the product's normal flow hands the attacker the victim's entity key (share/collab/reference). Oracle: the same `$select=<field>` works on the sibling but is denied on the primary entity with the same key.
CHAIN: product share flow leaks the victim's entity key (ownerTenantID/ownerID/formID — primitive: attacker legitimately holds the victim's addressing params) -> `$select=createdBy` on the primary `forms` entity is denied (field authorization holds there) -> re-issue `$select=createdBy` on the SIBLING `runtimeForms` that SHARES the `formID` key (bypass: authorization is entity-scoped, not property-scoped across sibling types) -> read the victim's email/PII with no user interaction (cross-identity sensitive-data disclosure — the exact class MSRC's M365 bounty pays a +20% "cross-identity sensitive data leakage" bonus for; here $2,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any OData/GraphQL/REST API with a metadata/model endpoint: (1) pull the model and list every entity type that carries the sensitive property (email/phone/SSN/createdBy) together with its ENTITY KEY; (2) get ONE legitimate key value through the product's own share/collab flow; (3) request the sensitive field on the primary entity (`$select=<field>` / `fields=<field>`); if denied, (4) re-issue the SAME field selection against EVERY sibling entity type that SHARES that key; (5) any sibling that returns the field has just bypassed the per-entity denylist. Rule: **when field authorization is enforced per entity type, a sibling entity that shares the same KEY and exposes the same property is a second door into the same data — walk the model's shared-key siblings whenever one entity denies a projection.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD (A/B + §17.692): 0 hits across the three write targets for `runtimeForms`, `sibling entit`, `shared entity key`, OData `$select` key-reuse, `entity key` reuse, `formapi`, `createdBy`-as-target. The nearest recorded material REVIEWED and delta'd: ledger ~12856-12917 (`fields=` / response-PROJECTION injection on a search endpoint — a caller-controlled projection that NAMES a field it should not see; a field-NAME injection) and ~9304 (OData `$expand`/decoration-parameter IDOR — write a reference-shaped value into a field and expand it). DELTA: this is neither a projection-name injection nor an expand-reference injection — it is a SIBLING-ENTITY SWAP that reuses a KNOWN KEY to reach a field explicitly DENIED on the primary entity; authorization is entity-scoped, so a key-sharing sibling is an unguarded second door. NEW: the shared-entity-key sibling-swap as its own BAC class.
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over ~12856 = that entry injects a field NAME into ONE endpoint's projection; this swaps the ENTITY TYPE (same key) to escape a per-entity denylist. DELTA over ~9304 = that entry abuses `$expand` resolving a written reference; this abuses `$select` on a key-sharing sibling.
FRESHNESS: Medium post 2021-01-10 / author mirror 2024-10-21 — the writeup is OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window (2021-era), recorded as a BACKFILL because the sibling-entity key-reuse METHOD is genuinely new to this corpus and is not time-sensitive the way a bypass CVE is. Flagged as backfill.
HONESTY: not reproduced this pass; the Medium URL 403'd and `r.jina.ai` failed, so the method is quoted from the author's own public mirror (logicalhunter.me). The request lines are reconstructed from the writeup's own described URL shapes (`formapi/api/<ownerTenantID>/users/<ownerID>/forms(<formID>)/responses` and `.../runtimeForms(<formID>)$select=createdBy`), which are verbatim from that writeup's prose; no response body or PoC screenshot is reproduced here.

SOURCE: https://nechudav.blogspot.com/2020/11/31k-ssrf-in-google-cloud-monitoring.html  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract` returned only the Blogspot nav stub; `r.jina.ai` (via web_extract) returned the first half; the full body was recovered by `curl` of the live Blogspot HTML + local tag-strip (a direct curl of r.jina.ai was IP-reputation-blocked). Article: David Nechuta, "31k$ SSRF in Google Cloud Monitoring led to metadata exposure", posted 2020-11 (Google VRP report June 2020; "Update 25.01.2021: Added Google engineers exploit method for getting access token").
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no GCP project exercised this pass; the author's extraction gist gist.github.com/nechudav/0b2e0217ffe31a3cd1c1743c590595e6 was NOT run).
CLASS: extraction method for a BLIND BOOLEAN READ ORACLE answered by an UNSTABLE / LOAD-BALANCED backend pool — regex character-class BINARY SEARCH with PAIRED POSITIVE/NEGATIVE probes (robustness layer over the comparator-oracle technique already recorded at §17.685).
CORE METHOD (carrier = Google Cloud Monitoring uptime checks, same feature as §17.685 — the SSRF entry and the comparator oracle are already recorded and are NOT re-taught here):
  1. THE ORACLE (verbatim setup): uptime check with "Protocol: HTTP / Hostname: 169.254.169.254 / Path: /computeMetadata/v1/project/project-id / Custom Headers: Metadata-Flavor: Google (required for /v1/ metadata endpoints)" — "Luckily there was an option to add custom headers to the request" (the custom-header capability is what gets past the metadata header gate); the TEST button fires the request ("the check was successful"), and the "Response validation" content-match answers checkPassed/contentMismatch per guess = the §17.685 boolean read oracle ("Because the response code was 200 and the response time was 2 ms, I was sure that the metadata endpoint is reachable").
  2. THE INSTABILITY (verbatim): the check service "is running on multiple instances across the world (there were about 54 running instances) and the requests made to the service are load-balanced. So there was no assurance that multiple requests would be sent to the same instance" — naive char-by-char extraction diverges because consecutive guesses can be answered by DIFFERENT backends holding different values (per-instance data, freshly minted tokens). The original researcher stopped at project-level metadata (public SSH key, project name) for exactly this reason.
  3. THE EXTRACTION MATH (the Google engineers' comment, verbatim): "We actually ended up writing an exploit to get an access token, after struggling with the same limitation. The two main tricks were binary search for each character (to send fewer requests) and probing both positive and negative matches (to get reliably results). For example: foo[a-n] foo[^a-n]. One of those requests must eventually return a success response when we hit the correct backend. We'd repeat queries (up to some limit) until we get any OK response and then adjust the search space based on that."
  4. PARALLELISM (verbatim): "Thanks to regexps you can probe multiple characters in parallel ( foo[a-n] , foo.[a-n] , foo..[a-n] ). In the beginning tokens will overlap, but after ~10 characters or so we usually had a unique prefix."
  5. BUDGET (verbatim): "Access tokens are valid for 60 minutes, so on average you have 30 minutes. In the end the exploit took ~15 minutes to get a full access token, including rate limiting."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a boolean content-match/contains oracle (§17.685) whose answers are UNSTABLE across repeated identical guesses (the pool tell); a rate limit that makes linear extraction infeasible; regex/pattern syntax accepted in the probed string position; target data whose lifetime is shorter than a linear walk (60-min token).
CHAIN: (recorded chain, not re-taught) attacker-controlled server-side fetch WITH custom headers -> GCP metadata 169.254.169.254 + `Metadata-Flavor: Google` -> project/instance metadata -> service-account access token (doctrine §4: SSRF -> cloud metadata -> IAM creds). This entry supplies the EXTRACTION leg that survives the backend pool and the rate limit.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for any blind boolean oracle (content-match validator, contains-check, blind SQLi LIKE/regex oracle) with unstable answers: (1) replace linear char-walking with BINARY SEARCH over the character domain using the oracle's pattern syntax (`^[a-n]`, `foo[a-n]`); (2) PAIR every positive probe with its negative complement (`foo[a-n]` + `foo[^a-n]`) and REPEAT the pair (up to a limit) until one returns OK — from an unstable pool at least one member of the pair lands on the backend that holds the true value; (3) probe several positions in parallel (`x.[a-n]`, `x..[a-n]`) and intersect the overlapping prefixes until unique (~10 chars); (4) budget the extraction against the DATA's lifetime (60-min token -> ~30 min average window) and the rate limit before starting. Rule: **on an unstable boolean oracle every guess ships as a positive/negative pair repeated until one lands — and regex character classes turn the walk into a binary search.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD (A/B + §17.693): 0 hits across the three write targets for `foo[a-n]`, `[^a-n]`, regex character-class probing, positive/negative probe pairs, or load-balanced-backend oracle extraction. `binary search` in the corpus = SQLi ordinal search (§7.9; §17.518's BETWEEN in-browser harness) and the duplicate-detector content search — none addresses an oracle whose ANSWERER CHANGES BETWEEN QUERIES; §17.685 records the same feature's oracle with linear prefix extension assuming stable answers. NEW: paired pos/neg probes + regex-class binary search + overlap intersection as the extraction method for unstable oracles.
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over §17.685 (same carrier; that entry = the oracle + quadzero bypass + linear extraction on stable answers; this = the extraction math that survives ~54 load-balanced instances and a rate limit) and over §7.9/§17.518 (SQL-predicate oracles, stable backends).
FRESHNESS: 2020-11 post (VRP report June 2020; engineer-comment update 2021-01-25) — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; recorded as BACKFILL because the extraction method is version-independent and new to this corpus. Flagged as backfill.
HONESTY: not reproduced this pass; every quote above is verbatim from the fetched article; the Python gist was NOT executed; the SSRF->metadata chain is the article's but is recorded elsewhere and is not claimed as new here.

Article: Rafi Ahamed (Leonidas D. Ace), "Forcing for a bounty$$", 2020-11-03 (reported 2020-09-27, triaged 09-28, resolved 10-18; $500, private HackerOne program).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no target exercised; the result GIFs were not reproduced).
CLASS: business-logic / payment bypass — the preview/trial limit is enforced by serving a SEPARATE PREVIEW RENDITION whose FILENAME carries the limiter (`<id>-thumb.trailer.mp4`) from a DIRECT MEDIA-STORAGE subdomain; the storage host enforces no entitlement, so requesting the full-asset name returns the paid content (CWE-639/CWE-284 family; monetary impact).
CORE METHOD:
  1. SITE (verbatim): "a private site in HackerOne and the site was selling educational videos. So, they allow an user a preview of the video without payment. But the preview was for only 15 seconds or less."
  2. FIND THE MEDIA REQUEST (verbatim): Burp interception; "the endpoint was on another subdomain. By looking at the subdomain name it was understood that the organization uses this subdomain to store all it's videos & other stuffs." — the media is fetched directly from a storage/CDN host, not through an entitlement-checking application endpoint.
  3. THE LIMITER (the author's screenshot, transcribed verbatim): `https://<redacted>/p/user/videos/3587474/3587474-thumb.trailer.mp4` — the served asset is a dedicated PREVIEW FILE whose filename segment (`-thumb.trailer`) names the limitation.
  4. THE BYPASS (verbatim): "Then I noticed that the endpoint has something like this [the URL above]. I thought why not remove it & see what happens. I was surprised that I got the full video. Now I can watch any paid video without payment." — strip the limiter segment from the asset name (request the sibling full-rendition filename for the same id) and the storage host serves the full paid video. "I quickly reported the bug to HackerOne & got a nice $500 bounty."
DETECTION SIGNAL: a paywall/trial/preview enforced by (a) truncated media served from a direct file/CDN/storage host and (b) an asset filename or URL segment encoding the limitation (`thumb.trailer`, `-preview`, `-sample`, `15s`, duration/`?limit=` params); the tell is a SIBLING filename for the same numeric id and a storage host that answers 200 to direct asset requests.
CHAIN: preview-only playback (primitive: direct asset access on the storage host) -> the entitlement is a NAMING CONVENTION, not an access-control decision (bypass: strip the limiter segment / request the full-rendition sibling) -> full paid video for free, any id, repeatable (impact: business-logic error with monetary impact — a §1 class; lost revenue at scale).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every paid/metered media or document feature: (1) intercept the actual asset requests (media/CDN/S3/signed-URL hosts); (2) diff the PREVIEW asset's name/params against plausible full-asset names — strip segments (`-thumb.trailer`, `-preview`, `-sample`, `-trailer`), try `<id>.mp4`, `<id>-full.mp4`, `<id>-1080.mp4`, drop `?duration=`/`?limit=`-style params (and test whether the signature actually covers them); (3) fetch the guessed sibling directly with curl; (4) enumerate ids. Rule: **when the preview is a separate FILE, the entitlement is the filename — strip the limiter and ask the storage host for the sibling it never meant to hand you.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD (A/B + §17.694): 0 hits across the three write targets for `thumb.trailer`, `paid video`, "full video", or preview-rendition filename stripping. Recorded nearest material REVIEWED and delta'd: the UI-only paid-gate family (§17.78; ledger 4821-4831 — a client-side settings gate, server stores the premium value), §17.203 (TOCTOU on a paid install), §17.89 (state-field write skipping a payment gate), the Shopify theme-preview entry ~4738 (unauthenticated preview PATH). None records an entitlement encoded in the ASSET FILENAME on a direct media store. NEW: rendition-name-as-entitlement + sibling-filename enumeration.
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over the client-side-gate family (here the full server-side asset exists and the limit is only which FILE the player points at) and over generic forced browsing (this is a naming-convention bypass on a file store, not a hidden path).

Article: Aseem Shrey, "Abusing 'Report Abuse'", 2020-10-31; a private program on "a foreign financial institution kind of company".
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no forum exercised this pass).
CLASS: BAC / unauthorized read of STATE-GATED content — a per-object ACTION endpoint (Report Abuse) fetches and renders the object's full content WITHOUT the publication/moderation-state check the listing enforces, so content still in the moderation queue (or rejected) is readable; incremental post ids make it cross-user (the platform filed it as Business Logic Errors).
CORE METHOD:
  1. CONTEXT (verbatim): a discussion forum where "The posts in the forum went through a moderation queue.", with a 'report abuse' functionality on each post.
  2. THE LEAK (verbatim): "Above screenshot is of a post that I created and then reported abuse for, it wasn't yet available on the forum but an attacker could still see it's contents because of ' report abuse'." The archived screenshot of the Report Abuse PAGE (browser tab "Report Abuse") shows a "Content" block rendering the PENDING post's full text ("Re: This question will go to moderators, but I can still see it, in the report abuse section :)") and its URL path (`URL: /answers/<slug>`) above the report form (issue radio buttons "Spam and commercial activity / Porn / Offensive content / Hate speech / Copyrighted material / Illegal content / Innacurate Info / It's for the wrong business / It's a fake", "Specific details", Submit/Cancel).
  3. CROSS-USER + ENUMERATION (verbatim): "to verify the bug I created another account and using the report id I sent a ' report abuse' request and yeah I could see the post that wasn't yet posted. Now all I had to do was iterate over the post id, which was conveniently enough, incremental and thus I could see posts which weren't yet posted."
  4. IMPACT (verbatim): "if someone posted something important financially, which the moderators didn't approve ( because it had something sensitive and shouldn't be posted on the forum ), an attacker could see those."
  5. OUTCOME (the report screenshot, transcribed): "An attacker can see posts which are in moderation and haven't yet been approved" — Weakness: Business Logic Errors, Severity Low (0.1~3.9), Bounty $200, State Resolved (Closed).
DETECTION SIGNAL: any per-object secondary action (report/flag/abuse/subscribe/watch/preview) whose response or rendered page echoes the OBJECT's content rather than just a confirmation; objects in non-public states (pending moderation, rejected, draft, scheduled); enumerable/incremental object or report ids; a listing that hides the object while the action still resolves it.
CHAIN: posts sit in a moderation queue (primitive: content exists server-side in a hidden state) -> the report-abuse page fetches the object by id and renders its full content without checking publication state (bypass: the action's fetch path lacks the state check the listing enforces) -> second account + iterate incremental ids (escalation: cross-user, the whole queued backlog) -> read sensitive posts the moderators REJECTED precisely because they were sensitive (impact: sensitive information disclosure with PoC — the content most worth hiding is the content this reads; target's own rating Low/$200, so the ceiling on this program was the forum's queued posts).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every per-object action (report/flag/abuse/moderate/subscribe/watch/share): (1) create your own object in a hidden state (submit it so it is queued/pending); (2) from a SECOND account invoke the action on that object's id (or its report id) and check whether the response/redirect page echoes the object's FULL content; (3) if yes, iterate the id space (incremental ids = the entire backlog) and sweep every hidden state (pending/rejected/draft/scheduled/deleted). Rule: **the action handler often checks CAN-ACT but not CAN-SEE — a report/flag endpoint that echoes the object is a read channel for everything the listing hides; then walk the ids.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD (A/B + §17.695): 0 hits across the three write targets for `report abuse`, `report_abuse`. Hidden-state readers REVIEWED and delta'd: §17.493 (similarity-matcher corpus reads drafts via content probes), #2552205 (draft leak via implicit subscription/notification), #1664920 (drafts inside a CSV export), §17.293 (similarity-score gradient walk), and the preview-path access-control entry (~21861: a preview link trading away the AUTH gate). NEW: the per-object ACTION (report/flag) as a STATE-check-absent read channel with direct id iteration; none of the recorded tests targets report/flag actions or moderation-STATE gates.
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over the hidden-state-reader corpus = the carrier (an action endpoint's render, not a matcher/export/notification) and the gate (publication STATE, not ACL/auth).
FRESHNESS: 2020-10-31 — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; recorded as BACKFILL because the method is new to this corpus. Flagged as backfill.
HONESTY: not reproduced; the Wayback text and the two archived screenshots are quoted/transcribed above; the exact HTTP request is NOT in the writeup's text (it says only "using the report id I sent a ' report abuse' request"; the Report Abuse page URL is partially redacted in the screenshot, visible fragment `where-do-i-see`) — no endpoint or parameter is invented here.

SOURCE: https://tbutler.org/2020/11/01/hinge-hackerone-writeup.html  2026-11-12
ROUTE: live fetch blocked ("URL targets a private or internal network address" — the crawler's SSRF guard; a direct curl from this egress produced no page either); `r.jina.ai` returned the target's 422; the full article was read via the Wayback Machine capture (web.archive.org/web/2021/https://tbutler.org/2020/11/01/hinge-hackerone-writeup.html — web_extract head + curl of the capture + local tag-strip = the full 11,094-char text). Article: Tyler Butler, "Hinge Hackerone Writeup", 2020-11-01 (reported to Hinge via HackerOne March 2020, triaged June 2020; HackerOne severity 3.7, Low).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Cloudinary account/lab exercised this pass; the PoC is the author's own free-Cloudinary-account demo).
CLASS: sensitive information disclosure with PoC / third-party media-store misconfiguration — crop/redaction bypass: the ORIGINAL upload is retrievable from a dynamic image-transformation CDN when the transformation access controls (Strict Transformations / Signed Delivery URLs) are not enabled.
CORE METHOD:
  1. FIND THE ASSET URL: profile photos load from the app's custom Cloudinary delivery domain; the browser-based profile pages reachable from the iOS "share profile" deep link (`https://app.hinge.co/[User profile ID]`) expose them. The exact shape given: `https://hinge-res.cloudinary.com/image/upload/x_0.18,y_0.21,w_0.36,h_0.27,c_crop/w_1055,q_auto/f_webp/[profile number]/[unique profile id].jpg` — the `/image/upload/<TRANSFORMATIONS>/<public_id>.jpg` path carries chained transform segments (`c_crop` with x/y/w/h, `q_auto`, `f_webp`).
  2. THE KEY INSIGHT, verbatim: "When users make a change to an image hosted on Cloudinary, new transformation requests are added on the fly. Original image assets themselves are not changed... both the original asset as it was uploaded to the platform as well as the new requested URL with transformations are able to be requested and exist available to the public."
  3. THE BYPASS (verbatim): "By removing the transformation parameters to the GET request URL, the original asset can be seen as it was uploaded by the user." — request `.../image/upload/[profile number]/[unique profile id].jpg` (delete every transform segment).
  4. WHY IT WORKS (verbatim): "by default, no access controls are implemented on the Cloudinary platform" — Strict Transformations (owner-defined allowed transforms) and Signed Delivery URLs (SHA1 digest of image ID + transformation string chained with the API secret) exist and would close it ("This is an intended function of Cloudinary and a default setting, however, this can be changed through the enforcement of Media Access Controls such as Strict Transformation and Signed Delivery URLS") but neither was enabled.
  5. IMPACT (verbatim): users "uploaded screenshots of their personal mobile devices, and only after upload edited the image to zoom in on a face or body. The full screen shot exposed other information about those users. In one example, a screenshot of the users Instagram profile revealed their name and Instagram handle. Other users uploaded img in various stages of undress and used the crop feature to crop out features other than their face." — the crop IS the user's redaction and the original defeats it.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any displayed image whose URL carries a dynamic transform chain between the store's upload root and the asset id (Cloudinary `image/upload/<transforms>/`, imgix-style query transforms, Thumbor / Fastly image optimizer / Akamai Image Manager segments); the tell is a bare request for the asset id without the transform chain returning 200 with a DIFFERENT (larger/full) rendition. Also: any app that lets users EDIT/REDACT an image — ask where the pre-edit bytes live.
CHAIN: user uploads a photo (primitive: media on a third-party store under a public delivery domain) -> the user redacts sensitive content with the in-app crop/zoom (the redaction is a TRANSFORM applied at request time, not an edit of the stored bytes) -> strip the transform chain from the delivery URL (bypass: the store permanently keeps originals and transforms are URL-driven; no Strict Transformations / Signed URLs) -> the pre-redaction original is public for every user, enumerable at scale (impact: sensitive info disclosure with PoC — screenshots leaking names/handles/PII, intimate photos uncropped; Hinge rated 3.7 because its own corpus was judged minimal-risk, but on a target where users crop out documents/receipts/credentials the same primitive is P2/P3).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every image/media rendered through a dynamic-transformation CDN: (1) capture the asset URL and separate the transform chain from the public id; (2) fetch the bare form with curl (`.../image/upload/<public_id>.<ext>`), then remove each transform segment one at a time and try common alternates (`.../image/upload/original/<id>`, asset-metadata endpoints); (3) diff bytes/dimensions against the displayed rendition — a larger or different image means the original is public; (4) request a transform the app never uses (e.g. `e_grayscale`) — if arbitrary transforms are honoured, the account has neither Strict Transformations nor Signed URLs; (5) enumerate sibling assets (incrementable profile ids). Rule: **on a transform CDN the redaction is a URL parameter — delete it and the store hands you the bytes the user thought they cropped away.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD (A/B + §17.696): `cloudinary`, `strict transformation`, `signed delivery` = 0 hits across the three write targets. Nearest atoms REVIEWED and delta'd: §17.694 (the preview-RENDITION filename as entitlement on a media store — a sibling FILE is fetched) and the pre-signed-S3-URL corpus (where a signature being ABSENT is never the recorded bug). NEW: transform-segment stripping on a dynamic image CDN to retrieve the permanently-retained original upload.
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over §17.694 (rendition-name stripping): here the same file is re-rendered without its URL transforms and the missing control is a CDN account setting, not a filename convention.
FRESHNESS: 2020-11-01 (reported March 2020) — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; recorded as BACKFILL because the Cloudinary default-config behaviour is version-independent and new to this corpus. Flagged as backfill.
HONESTY: not reproduced; every quote above is verbatim from the fetched Wayback text; Hinge's own instance is historical; the 3.7 rating is the writeup's.

Article: "Perform substring search for emails even if Workplace admin hides email profile field." (servicenger, posted 2020-10-21; two Facebook Workplace bugs, $1,000 each; Bug 2 submitted 2020-08-18 -> resolved 2020-09-16; Bug 1 submitted 2020-10-05 -> resolved 2020-10-14).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Workplace instance exercised this pass).
CLASS: BAC / sensitive info disclosure with PoC — a profile-field VISIBILITY toggle enforced only in the profile RENDER while the SEARCH backends still MATCH on the hidden field, turning any search box into a substring email oracle; plus a role-gated mobile ACTIVITY reachable by deep link as a normal user.
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE TOGGLE (verbatim): "As admin From the Admin Panel, goto Settings >> Profile fields >> on Email field Turn visibility off."
  2. BUG 1 — DEEP LINK INTO THE ADMIN ACTIVITY (verbatim): "Login as non-admin user in Workplace4Android" -> "adb shell am start -d "fb-work://at_work_company_dashboard_manage_people"" -> "Workplace launches 'Manage People' activity" — the role-gated admin dashboard opens for a normal user because the deep link reaches the activity directly.
  3. BUG 1 — THE ORACLE (verbatim): "In search box perform any email search query like "@yahoo.com" "@gmail.com" "or random full email in result user associated with searched email will appears." "In this dashboard we can also get Claimed/Deactivated/Invited users."
  4. BUG 2 — THE SAME ORACLE ON THE WEB (verbatim): "In workplace web As non-admin user / Goto Directory >> Search box / In search box perform any email search query like "@yahoo.com" "@gmail.com" "or random full email in result user associated with searched email appears as result." — the substring probe "@yahoo.com" returns every user whose HIDDEN email matches; "@" walks the whole directory.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any profile/contact field with a per-field or per-role VISIBILITY setting; the tell is a SEARCH/DIRECTORY/LOOKUP/AUTOCOMPLETE endpoint returning objects when probed with fragments of the hidden field's VALUE ("@gmail.com", "@", a corporate domain, phone digit prefixes) — the toggle removed the field from the render, not from the query index. On mobile: any role-gated screen reachable by a bare deep link / exported activity as a low-privilege user.
CHAIN: admin hides the email field (primitive: field-level privacy toggle = a RENDER decision) -> the search backend still matches on the field's value (bypass: query-side matching ignores the visibility flag) -> substring probes ("@yahoo.com") return the matching USER OBJECTS to any non-admin (escalation: bulk email enumeration of the whole directory incl. Claimed/Deactivated/Invited accounts) -> on Android the same oracle sits behind an admin "Manage People" activity reached by a plain deep link as a normal user (escalation: role-gate bypass on the mobile surface) -> email enumeration at scale despite an explicit privacy control (impact: sensitive info disclosure with PoC — the platform paid $1,000 per variant).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for every field with a visibility/privacy toggle: (1) confirm it is gone from the profile render for the restricted role; (2) probe EVERY search/directory/lookup/autocomplete endpoint with value FRAGMENTS of that field ("@gmail.com", "@", "corp.com", digit prefixes) from a low-privilege account; (3) if objects come back, the toggle is render-only — harvest the ids and map them to full user objects; (4) on mobile apps, launch role-gated activities directly (`adb shell am start -d "<scheme>://<admin screen>"`, `am start -n <pkg>/<exported activity>`) and repeat the probes there. Rule: **a field-visibility toggle is a RENDER decision — the search index still matches the hidden value, so a substring probe in any lookup box reads what the admin hid.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD (A/B + §17.697): `substring search`, `fb-work`, `Manage People` = 0 hits as recorded techniques (the `Workplace` hits are the Ticket Trick / GitLab-alias entries citing Workplace only as a join-with-corp-email service). Nearest atoms REVIEWED and delta'd: §17.82 (a mobile duplication-CHECK endpoint ignoring an account-level discoverability toggle — an exists/user-id oracle on the INPUT side), the FetLife raw-response entry (a privacy toggle that removes only the UI affordance while the VALUE stays in the response body), §17.692 (OData sibling-entity key-reuse past a per-entity-type denylist). None records the SEARCH-MATCH oracle — the hidden field stays a QUERYABLE index and substring probes return whole objects — and none records the deep link into a role-gated activity as the second carrier.
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over §17.82 (response objects from substring MATCHING vs an exists-oracle; a render-only toggle vs an ignored lookup flag) and over generic user enumeration (this enumerates a field the admin explicitly hid).

SOURCE: https://medium.com/@singh.simran7838/how-i-made-2000-with-url-redirection-b1b5f4e7a678  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract`, one pass, full text. Article: Simran Singh (cybrr_warrior_official), "How I made $2000 with URL REDIRECTION?", 2020-08-12 (reported 2020-08-02, paid 2020-08-11; private program; the title says URL redirection, the class is SQLi).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no target exercised; the writeup shows no request/response pairs, only a PoC video and a payout screenshot).
CLASS: CHAIN-ONLY ENTRY (per the chain rule — the open redirect is the first link, not a finding): an open-redirect parameter used as the PAYLOAD-DELIVERY ENVELOPE that defeats a filter in front of a SQLi parameter — terminal impact = SQLi with DB/table/column enumeration, $2,000.
CORE METHOD:
  1. HIDDEN-PARAMETER DISCOVERY (verbatim): "a tool Arjun hits in my mind and I started discovering some parameters" -> a subdomain blog URI `https://sub.example.com/@someone's_name/blog?pageid=143` with a SQLi-prone parameter (`pageid`).
  2. THE FILTER (verbatim): "I start performing some SQLi attempt using some payloads. And saw there responses in burp suite but all the payloads are getting filtered."
  3. THE REDIRECTOR (verbatim): "let's take a look towards redirect URL if there is any….. And I found something like this: `https://www.example.com/subscribe?r=https://sub.example.com/subscribe_to_newsletter/`" and "the sub domain in the destination URL endpoint is the same Sub domain on which I Tested SQL injections."
  4. THE DELIVERY SWITCH (verbatim): "Let's try whole the SQLi tests with URL Redirections. And I started with Database check, then Table and columns." — the payload series that was filtered in direct requests is delivered nested inside the `r` (destination) parameter of the ROOT domain's redirector and succeeds (DB -> tables -> columns). The author's only explanation, verbatim: "all this happened because some people don't know a domain name is also known as root domain" — i.e. the program's filter/coverage treated the root domain and the subdomain differently.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a parameter where every injection payload is neutralised (filtered/WAF'd) while benign values pass, PLUS anywhere in the same program a first-party URL-forwarding parameter (`?r=`, `?url=`, `?next=`, `?redirect=`, `?continue=`, `?dest=`, `?return=`) whose destination can name the filtered endpoint. The tell is the identical payload succeeding through the forwarder.
CHAIN: hidden parameter on a subdomain with SQLi potential (primitive) -> payloads filtered on direct delivery (the filter is the gate) -> the root domain's own open-redirect parameter `?r=<destination>` carries the payload nested in the destination URL (bypass: the filter inspects the outer request/host, not the nested URL — WHY this passes is NOT explained in the source; empirically it did) -> the SQLi fires through the forwarded request -> DB/table/column enumeration (impact: SQLi data read, $2,000 — a core-ineligible open redirect escalated into a reportable SQLi).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: whenever a parameter eats every payload: (1) enumerate first-party redirector/forwarder/link-preview/webhook params across the program's hosts (`?r=`, `?url=`, `?next=`, `?continue=`, `?dest=`); (2) point the destination at the filtered endpoint with the payload appended INSIDE the nested URL (`?r=https://victim/sub/...?param=PAYLOAD`), trying both the client-followed and the server-fetched variant; (3) diff against direct delivery — the same payload working through the forwarder is the bypass; (4) if the forwarder is server-side, the same hop is also an SSRF primitive. Rule: **a filter guarding one entry path does not guard the same endpoint reached through the program's own redirect parameter — nest the payload in the destination URL and let the forwarder deliver it.**
DEDUPE/DELTA: the redirect-hop-as-WAF-bypass rung IS recorded (ledger 16662/16670 "the target's OWN OUT-OF-SCOPE open redirect is the WAF bypass"; ledger 9800 "ride a whitelisted host's open redirect") — but there in an SSRF ALLOWLIST context where the fetcher FOLLOWS the redirect to the metadata IP. DELTA here: the protected resource is a payload-CHARACTER filter in front of a SQLi parameter, the payload rides ENVELOPED in the redirect parameter's destination URL, and the terminal is an SQLi DB read instead of IMDS. Recorded as a chain/carrier entry with NO §17 slot (the rung is recorded; this is a new carrier + terminal). The Arjun/param-discovery and generic error-based SQLi legs are recorded tooling and are not re-taught.
FRESHNESS: 2020-08 — OUTSIDE the preferred window; recorded as BACKFILL. Flagged as backfill.
HONESTY: not reproduced; no request or payload appears in the source (PoC video only); the writeup does NOT establish why the filter missed the nested payload (client-side vs server-side redirect follow is unstated) — this entry records strictly what the author demonstrates: identical SQLi tests filtered in direct requests, successful via the `r` parameter, DB enumerated, $2,000. No mechanism is invented.

SOURCE: https://medium.com/@jonathanbouman/blind-sql-injection-at-fasteditor-hema-com-6ac140c0d1a3  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract` (head) + the cached full page (read_file of the saved extraction through the omitted middle) = the full article. Article: Jonathan Bouman, "Blind SQL Injection at fasteditor.hema.com", 2020-08-06 (discovered 2020-05-11, vendor hot-fix within hours, €100 gift card + bonus; HEMA approved disclosure).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no target exercised; the technique is quoted from the author's own Burp/Intruder run).
CLASS: SQLi (blind, time-based) in an ORDER BY parameter — the carrier class is RECORDED; the NEW material is the COMMA-FILTER BYPASS (`SUBSTRING(x FROM n FOR m)` comma-free function syntax) that makes extraction possible at all.
CORE METHOD (carrier `https://fasteditor.hema.com/api/user/<userID>/products?offset=0&limit=8&orderby=id+DESC`, a photo-projects list API):
  1. ENTRY: the `orderby` value is spliced into the query (author's reconstruction: `$dbh->prepare('SELECT * FROM photos where userId = :username ORDER BY '.$orderToUse.' LIMIT :limit')` — identifiers cannot be bound in prepared statements). A single quote in `orderby` returns a PDO error carrying query fragments ("The fact that our `'` is not escaped inside this error message is a big red flag").
  2. CLASSIFICATION: sqlmap reports boolean-based blind (sort direction as oracle), stacked queries (`;`), and time-based blind (`SLEEP()`); but sqlmap stalls "because of some firewalls and other limitations", so the payload is handcrafted in Burp Repeater.
  3. THE PAYLOAD, verbatim: `orderby=width+DESC;SELECT+(CASE+WHEN+(SUBSTRING((user())FROM(1)FOR(1))='§h§')+THEN+SLEEP(8)+ELSE+SLEEP(1)+END)` — terminate the original query with `;`, then a stacked `SELECT CASE WHEN <char test> THEN SLEEP(8) ELSE SLEEP(1) END`; `§h§` is the Intruder position over a-z, 0-9 and `_-.,@)`; the ~8s responses are hits; walk `FROM(1)FOR(1)` -> `FROM(2)FOR(1)` -> ... (the `width+DESC` segment is the author's own; he says "it has no use in the payload, so ignore that").
  4. THE BYPASS, verbatim: "Somehow `,` characters are not allowed in this payload. Whatever payload I tried that contained a `,` returned a response without any sleep functions trigger (all response times < 500ms)... Today I learned that you can use `FROM` and `FOR` as a replacement... convert `SUBSTRING(user(),1,1)` to `SUBSTRING((user())FROM(1)FOR(1))`. We just bypassed a firewall (or something else that broke our payload)." (the author credits the zoczus.blogspot.com "SQL injection without comma character" comment thread).
  5. RESULT (verbatim): "we end up with the string `hema_live@10.0.102.192`" — DB user + the database server's internal IP.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a sort/ORDER BY parameter that reflects a SQL error on `'` (or flips sort/timing); and — the bypass tell — a filter that neutralises any payload CONTAINING A COMMA (SLEEP/UNION payloads return baseline timing/status while comma-free payloads behave normally). Comma blocking is a common WAF rule against `UNION SELECT a,b,c` and multi-arg calls.
CHAIN: user-controlled `orderby` (primitive: identifier-context injection, stacked query via `;`) -> a comma filter blocks every standard extraction function (gate) -> comma-free `SUBSTRING(x FROM n FOR m)` rebuilds the character test (bypass) -> time-based blind extraction of `user()` + the DB host's internal IP (impact: SQLi with data read — the author's own words: "one should consider a database compromised"; he stopped at the PoC, though stacked queries imply write/RCE potential).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any injection point where payloads containing `,` are silently dropped (SLEEP/UNION payloads return baseline timing/status while comma-free payloads behave normally): rebuild the payload in SQL's comma-free notations before declaring the sink dead — `SUBSTRING(x FROM n FOR m)`, `MID(x FROM n FOR m)`, `TRIM(LEADING 'c' FROM x)`, `overlay(x PLACING y FROM n)`, `||`/2-arg `CONCAT` where accepted, predicates with `BETWEEN`/`LIKE`/chained `OR` instead of `IN (a,b)` — then reconstruct the boolean/time oracle and extract char-by-char with Burp Intruder. Rule: **when the WAF eats commas, SQL's own `FROM n FOR m` clause syntax is a comma-free arity adapter — the injection never stopped, only the notation did.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD (A/B + §17.698): `FROM(1)FOR`, `without comma`, `comma-free`, `comma filter`, `filtered comma` = 0 hits across the three write targets (the only `MID(... FROM` hit is §17.518's in-browser binary-search harness, which uses ordinary comma-arity `MID(str,pos,len)`). The ORDER BY carrier is NOT re-taught — recorded at ledger 7923-7925 (CASE-driven sort-flip boolean oracle), 15695 (Transposh `orderby` stacked + `BETWEEN` replacing `<`/`>`), 16836-16839 (nested `(select*from(select(sleep(N)))a)` wrapper + `/*!500NN*/` engine fingerprint), 16947-16948 (quote-escaped ORDER BY, error-in-source schema leak). NEW: the comma-filter bypass as the enabler of extraction — filter evasion orthogonal to every recorded tamper trick (`space2comment` ledger 10858-10871, `between`, comment/case splitting).
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over the recorded ORDER BY SQLi entries (carrier recorded; extraction-notation bypass new) and over the recorded sqlmap tamper stack (ledger 10858-10871 + the generic tamper list at Bugbountyskills ~10757) — none covers comma removal.
FRESHNESS: 2020-08 (events May 2020) — OUTSIDE the preferred window; recorded as BACKFILL (SQL syntax is version-independent and the bypass is new to this corpus). Flagged as backfill.
HONESTY: not reproduced; the payload and all quotes are verbatim from the fetched article; the author's own uncertainty about the filter ("a firewall (or something else that broke our payload)") is preserved, not resolved.

SOURCE: https://medium.com/@daoud_youssef/from-host-header-injection-to-sql-injection-e7c61a61b575  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract` returned the head with the middle elided; `r.jina.ai` returned the full text. Article: smacker dodi (daoud_youssef), "From Host Header injection to SQL injection", 2020-07-05 (reported 2020-05-14, resolved 2020-05-24; VDP, no bounty).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no target exercised).
CLASS: CHAIN-ONLY ENTRY (per the chain rule — the header reflection is the first link, not a finding): Host/X-Forwarded-Host header injection -> host-driven CONTENT SELECTION exposes a hidden admin login form -> unfiltered input on the hidden form -> SQLi auth bypass -> admin dashboard access (admin panel access = P1 class).
CORE METHOD:
  1. THE SWEEP (verbatim): an automated recon script iterates subdomains and for each "send curl command ... add custom headers to this curl command then search in the response if these headers exist in response header or response body" — on `dev-test.somedomain.com`, `X-Forwarded-Host: www.bing.com` is reflected in the `Location` header (302 to bing.com; the baseline is a body-less 302 to www.somedomain.com).
  2. THE TELL NOBODY LOOKS FOR (verbatim): "when i inject this header the 302 response has a body which contain a form [ notice that in normal condition the response contain only response header with no response body ]" — the injection doesn't just rewrite `Location`, it changes WHICH PAGE the app renders (host-driven content selection), and the revealed page carries an injected `<meta>` refresh tag plus a FORM.
  3. REACHING THE HIDDEN PAGE (verbatim): "i changed the response code from 302 found to 200 Ok and remove the location header to stop redirect but the subdomain again redirect to www.bing.com" (the meta refresh in the body still fires) -> "So i deleted this meta tag in the burp suite and forwarded this response and in the browser i found my self in front of login form which in normal case i'm not suppose to reach but due to host header injection i could reach and access this form which was admin login form."
  4. THE SINK: the hidden admin login form "was sending the user and password over insecure protocol (HTTP)" and had "no rate limit" (both refused by the program) — and its inputs carried no filtering: `user : administrator' or 1=1 --+` / `pass : any password` -> "bingo i found my self inside the admin dashboard" (dev-test subdomain, "so no sensitive action or data inside the dashboard").
  5. TRIAGE NOTE (verbatim): first closed as NA ("they think that i reported host header injection through MITM"); "when i send a detailed video that i don't need a victim in this scenario and this is access control issue they accepted it and resolve it in 10 days" — resolved, no bounty (VDP).
DETECTION SIGNAL: a header injection (`X-Forwarded-Host`/`Host`) that changes not just `Location` but the response BODY (baseline = empty 302, injected = body with a form/HTML) — that delta means the header selects alternate application content (vhost/route fallback) and the alternate content is a surface nobody fuzzes; an injected `<meta http-equiv=refresh>` or JS redirect in that body keeping a browser off the page; login forms on pages unreachable through normal navigation.
CHAIN: automated header-reflection sweep finds `X-Forwarded-Host` reflected (primitive: P5) -> the injected host changes the RESPONSE BODY and a hidden admin login form appears (bypass: host-driven content selection serves the admin page to a request that looks like another host; the meta refresh hides it from a browser — strip the tag in Burp to interact with it) -> the hidden form's inputs carry no filtering (escalation: `administrator' or 1=1 --+` auth bypass) -> admin dashboard access (impact: admin/internal panel access, P1-class; here on a dev-test host with no sensitive data, so it triaged as access-control on a VDP).

SOURCE: https://medium.com/@keegan.ryan/patched-zoom-exploit-altering-camera-settings-via-remote-sql-injection-4fdf3de8a0d  2026-11-12
ROUTE: `web_extract`, one pass, full article text. Article: Keegan Ryan, "Patched Zoom Exploit: Altering Camera Settings via Remote SQL Injection", 2020-06-29 (found 2020-04-07, reported to Zoom the same day via HackerOne, "triaged as high severity the following day", fixed in Zoom macOS 4.6.11 on 2020-04-12 and Linux 3.5.385850.0413 on 2020-04-14; $2,000 award; Evan Johnson replicated on Mac).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no Zoom binary or lab was exercised this pass).
CLASS: SQLi (client-side SQLite in a desktop application). The carrier (custom-URI-scheme delivery into the desktop client) and the NEW material is the SANITIZER/PARSER DECODE-ORDER BYPASS: quote-doubling defeated by a UTF-8 multibyte lead byte.
CORE METHOD:
  1. SURFACE: any web page can launch the desktop client via the `zoommtg://` custom URI scheme — "These URIs contain several parameters passed in a Base64-encoded blob" — and "A CSRF-style attack from a malicious webpage might then be able to exploit the client."
  2. FIND THE SINK IN A CLOSED BINARY: `strings` shows "several partial SQL queries with format specifiers, which indicates that SQL queries are composed at runtime instead of being properly hardcoded parameterized queries"; the binary's SQLite version string (3.27.2) plus SQLite's public source let the author locate `sqlite3LockAndPrepare` in Ghidra and breakpoint it.
  3. THE SINK CONFIRMED: triggering the URI hits the breakpoint several times; "One of these queries updates a database entry with a long hexadecimal meeting code — the exact same hexadecimal code passed as the 'tid' parameter in the URI's encoded data."
  4. THE FILTER: a lone quote does not inject — "an input sanitization function replaces every single quote with two single quotes, preventing the attack. Common sanitization bypasses, like including a backslash character, also fail."
  5. THE BYPASS, payload verbatim: `success \xC2' or 1=1;` — "Byte 0xC2 in the payload shifts from representing an out-of-range ASCII character to representing the beginning of a two-byte UTF-8 character, preventing the next byte from being interpreted as a single quote. The UTF-8 interpretation contains only the remaining single quote, and the SQL injection attack succeeds." (The sanitizer doubles `'` -> `''` on ASCII bytes; the downstream UTF-8 decode merges 0xC2 with ONE of the doubled quotes into a single multibyte character, leaving one live quote.)
  6. IMPACT PATH (settings rows mapped with DB Browser for SQLite): "automatically joining meetings without user approval and joining meetings with webcam and audio enabled" are stored rows — "A SQL injection attack could surreptitiously modify these values from their default, and, once Zoom has been closed and reopened, Zoom would automatically share the victim's camera and audio with any meeting a malicious web page sends it to."
DETECTION SIGNAL: input neutralization by QUOTE DOUBLING (`'` echoed/neutralized as `''`) instead of parameterization; partial SQL strings with format specifiers inside a desktop binary; any app registering a custom URI scheme handler that writes scheme-supplied values into a local SQLite DB. The bypass tell: behavior changes when a multibyte lead byte (`\xC2`-`\xEF`) immediately precedes the quote.
CHAIN: malicious web page (drive-by) -> `zoommtg://` URI fires with no user action beyond visiting the page (CSRF-style, primitive) -> the Base64 blob's `tid` parameter is concatenated into a runtime-composed SQLite UPDATE (primitive: SQLi sink) -> the quote-doubling sanitizer is defeated by the UTF-8 decode-order trick `\xC2'` (bypass) -> the injection writes the settings rows (auto-join without approval + camera/audio enabled by default) -> on client restart the victim auto-joins any meeting the malicious page names with camera AND microphone live (impact: remote camera/mic capture of the victim, privacy compromise at scale; triaged High, $2,000).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: wherever `'` is neutralized by doubling/escaping (not parameterized), resend `LEAD_BYTE + ' or 1=1` with multibyte lead bytes `\xC2`-`\xEF` (UTF-8), `\x81`-`\xFE` (GBK/Big5 contexts — the classic `%bf%27` addslashes shape), and invalid-sequence variants: if the sanitizer runs on raw bytes/ASCII while the parser decodes a multibyte charset afterwards, one doubled quote is consumed as a continuation byte and the injection fires — verify by diffing DB rows/app state. On desktop apps, enumerate registered custom URI schemes (`zoommtg://`, `slack://`, `teams://`, ...) and replay captured scheme URIs from a local HTML page — scheme handlers are a browser-reachable CSRF surface into the app's local database. Rule: **quote doubling is only safe if the decoder agrees with the sanitizer — put a multibyte lead byte in front of the quote and let the charset eat one of the pair.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD (A/B + §17.699): `zoommtg` / `quote doubling` / `doubled quote` = 0 hits across the three write targets; `0xC2`/`xC2`'s only hits are an unrelated cookie-prefix entry (ledger 7456) and an address offset (15439). The GBK `%bf%27` addslashes family is not recorded either. Nearest atoms REVIEWED and delta'd: the Windows-1252->UTF-8->ASCII pipeline (Bugbountyskills 23833) is strip-then-transcode — a filter REMOVES a char and charset conversion RESURRECTS a lookalike (`‹`->`<`) for XSS; here the sanitizer ESCAPES (doubles) and the decoder MERGES — the escape pair itself is the material the charset eats. V-12 double-encoding and the sqlmap tamper stack (10858-10871, 10757) are request-level WAF evasions, not sanitizer/parser decode-order mismatches. Client-side SQLite injection via a custom scheme handler = 0 hits.
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over the encoding-mismatch corpus (23833) and the tamper stack — new mechanism (escape-then-decode vs strip-then-transcode) and a new surface (desktop-app local DB via scheme handler).
FRESHNESS: 2020-06 (events April 2020) — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; recorded as BACKFILL. Flagged as backfill (the decode-order bypass class is version-independent and new to this corpus).
HONESTY: not reproduced; the payload and every quote are verbatim from the fetched article; the article's screenshots were not re-fetched this pass; no parameter names beyond `tid` are named in the source and none are invented.

STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced — no target exercised).
CLASS: SQLi — auth bypass via CONTEXT-BALANCED TAUTOLOGY on a login form, chained to SQLi data extraction on a post-auth hidden parameter.
CORE METHOD:
  1. ENTRY: Amass + Assetfinder over 30 subdomains found `m***.redacted.com`, an administrative-doctor login — verbatim: "I gave a single quote(') as a value on the user id & password parameter. I got an SQL Error".
  2. THE FLAT TAUTOLOGY FAILS: "I tried with 1' or '1'='1 to bypass the Login, But failed. The failed response to login request was '200 Ok'." — the 200 is the FALSE arm of a ready-made oracle (failure page).
  3. THE ORACLE + THE MATRIX: "Then without wasting time i fired up Burp Intruder having Blind Sqli payloads, and got a response with '302 found.' I cross checked with the succeed Payload `')) or ((‘x’))=((‘` by giving Userid=`')) or ((‘x’))=((‘` &Password=`')) or ((‘x’))=((‘`" — the same wrapper-balanced tautology in BOTH fields at once; login SUCCESS (302 -> panel) vs FAILURE (200) is the boolean oracle. "BBBOOOOMMMMMM…………….. I was Successfully logged in to the administrative account." (admin functions: add blogs, add/delete members, upload/view receipts).
  4. THE ENTRY PARAMS WILL NOT DUMP: "I tried to dump data from the database manually through the 'userid' and 'password' parameter (Result= Failed),fired up Sqlmap and tried to dump database (Result=failed)."
  5. THE ESCALATION — the access gained IS the asset: "I started digging more paths through burp spider, after some time i got a path `m***.redacted.com/ImagingCenter/MailingList.php?personID=1&lang=en&navigation=1&namesOnly=1&view=board`" -> "With the help of Sqlmap, I also get the database and the Vulnerable param was 'personID' and the database was MySql." — data of "all users, members, students and other stuffs".
DETECTION SIGNAL: a login form where `'` returns a SQL error but flat tautologies return the failure page (200) — the fields sit inside quote/paren wrappers the flat payload does not balance; the success/failure responses differ in STATUS (302 vs 200) as well as body; behind the gained role, a spidable parameter surface (id-like query params on listing/export pages).
CHAIN: `'` errors in user id + password (primitive: SQLi) -> flat `1' or '1'='1` returns 200 failure (gate: wrapper mismatch) -> Intruder sweep finds the balanced tautology `')) or ((‘x’))=((‘` in BOTH fields -> 302 = TRUE arm, and the tautology IS the auth bypass -> admin session (escalation) -> login params refuse extraction (sqlmap fails) -> spider the panel -> hidden `personID` on `MailingList.php` -> sqlmap dumps the whole MySQL DB (impact: full user/member/student data extraction + admin functionality; High -> Critical, €1,400).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any login where `'` returns a SQL error: (1) record the failure response (status + body) as the FALSE arm; (2) Intruder a tautology MATRIX matched to wrapper depth over EVERY field pair and both fields together — `' or '1'='1`, `') or ('1'=('1`, `')) or (('x'))=((('`, `')or('x')=('x`, `admin'--`, `" or "1"="1`; (3) the response that flips to the SUCCESS redirect is simultaneously the oracle TRUE arm and an auth bypass; (4) if the authenticated entry params will not extract, spider the unlocked surface for a second injectable id-param (`?personID=`, `?reportId=`, `?id=`) and dump from THERE. Rule: **when a flat `' or 1=1` fails, the query has wrappers the payload must balance — sweep quote/paren-depth-matched tautologies across the field set and let the login's own 302/200 differential be the oracle.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD (A/B + §17.700): `)) or ((` / `') or ('` = 0 hits across the three write targets AND in /root/Myskill/sqli-testing/references/payloads.md (its auth payloads are flat forms only — `1 OR 1=1`); `tautolog`'s only hit is Bugbountyskills 11929 recording the FLAT form (`' OR 1=1; --`). None records the WRAPPER-BALANCE requirement (payload quote/paren depth matched to the query's own wrapping, in both credential fields at once), the login STATUS differential as the built-in boolean oracle, or the "entry params won't dump -> second param behind the gained role" escalation leg.

SOURCE: https://bugwriteups.tech/bug-bounty-write-up-lucky-vulnerability  2026-11-12 (live domain DNS-dead; read via the Wayback capture http://web.archive.org/web/20210126063635/https://bugwriteups.tech/bug-bounty-write-up-lucky-vulnerability)
ROUTE: `web_extract` on the live URL -> "Blocked: URL targets a private or internal network address" (the domain no longer resolves); `r.jina.ai` -> 422 "Domain 'bugwriteups.tech' could not be resolved"; direct curl -> exit 6 (DNS) -> Wayback: availability API found capture 20210126063635, fetched via curl + local tag-strip for the full body (`web_extract` on the same capture returned only the first half). Article: Merbin Russel (Codingest), "Lucky Bug Which Let Me Change Name of Every Accounts at a Single Click", 2020-05-13 (found Dec 2019; "I reported at Hackerone... They understood.").
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced).
CLASS: SQLi — QUERY-TRUNCATION variant: SQL comment injection (`#`) in an UNQUOTED NUMERIC parameter of a bulk UPDATE, commenting out the WHERE clause -> mass cross-account write. (The author labels it "improper input validation" — "This vulnerability is not a sql injection or IDOR, this is a improper input validation flaw" — but the mechanism he demonstrates and reconstructs is SQL comment truncation.)
CORE METHOD (forum profile update on "zsite.xyz"; multipart POST: fullName, countryId, region, postcode, occupation, memberId=99, oldLoginName, submitBtn):
  1. THE FUZZING LEFTOVER, verbatim: "After testing for sql injection, I forgot to remove # after CountryId parameter" -> `countryId = 21#`.
  2. THE IDOR MISREAD (and its differential): memberId is client-supplied — swapping in another account's memberId changed that account's "Name and Country details", but "region and postcode details had not changed, I know if it was a IDOR, I was able to change region and postcode parameters also, So I determined it was not an IDOR." — an IDOR would have applied ALL fields to the one target; only the fields BEFORE the marker moved.
  3. THE REAL EFFECT, verbatim: "Name and Country id of every profiles at that site had been changed with the name an country submitted by me" — one request rewrote name+country of EVERY account; "I removed it then submitted request with another name and country values, But this time Name and Country details of any account wasn't changed."
  4. THE MECHANISM (the author's own reconstruction — "If my understanding is right, following process might be happened at back end"): the save composes `UPDATE forum_profile SET name ="Merbin",country =22, region="Tamil Nadu", postcode ="5555" WHERE id=50`; "Here countryID is a numerical value, so there is no need for single or double quotation" -> with the leftover `#`: `UPDATE forum_profile SET name ="Merbin",country =22#, region="Tamil Nadu", postcode ="5555" WHERE id=50` -> "# is used as comment in SQL, So, query after # is neglected, Where statement is also neglected because it comes after #" -> `UPDATE forum_profile SET name ="Merbin",country =22` — an UPDATE with NO WHERE writes every row.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a numeric/id/enum parameter whose value is spliced unquoted into a composed query; a state change reaching MORE rows than the request should touch (every profile); the FIELDS-BEFORE-MARKER differential — only the columns SET before the injected `#`/`--` change (name+country yes, region/postcode no), which distinguishes query truncation from IDOR; removing the marker restores per-row behavior.
CHAIN: leftover `21#` in the unquoted numeric `countryId` of a profile UPDATE (primitive: SQL comment injection / query truncation) -> `#` comments out the remaining SET columns AND the `WHERE id=50` clause, no quote needed because the parameter is unquoted (bypass) -> the UPDATE executes WITHOUT a WHERE (escalation: a per-row write becomes a full-table write) -> name + country of EVERY account on the site changed with a single click (impact: mass cross-account data modification, account integrity at scale; reported to HackerOne and accepted).
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on every UPDATE/DELETE-shaped action (profile save, settings save, address/bookmark edit) carrying a numeric or enum parameter: (1) append `#`, `-- ` and the encoded `%23`/`-- -` to the value and resubmit; (2) diff WHICH rows and WHICH fields changed — rows beyond your own object changing, or only the fields before the marker changing, means the parameter is spliced unquoted into the query and the truncation ate the WHERE clause; (3) demonstrate on a harmless attribute with a test-account pair and stop — mass writes are destructive, prove the class once, never repeat it. Rule: **an unquoted numeric parameter needs no quote to inject — a trailing `#`/`--` truncates the query, and in an UPDATE the truncation eats the WHERE clause, turning one row's edit into every row's edit.**
WHY IT IS A NEW GENERAL METHOD (A/B + §17.701): the WHERE-clause-comment-truncation mass write = 0 hits across the three write targets; "comment" + "where" greps return only unrelated families (email comment-smuggling Bugbountyskills 22606, the `truncate` corpus 5453/5486/19239 = query/header/path truncation); `every row`/`all rows`/`without where` hits are SELECT-side row over-match (10043 SSN/DOB, `OR 1=1` row over-match). Nearest atoms REVIEWED and delta'd: the recorded tautology/`-- -` SQLi entries use comments to end a SELECT's WHERE for AUTH bypass (which row set you see), never to convert a scoped UPDATE into a full-table WRITE; mass-assignment (V-04 class) is extra body fields reaching a write, not query truncation.
DEDUPE/DELTA: DELTA over tautology/comment SQLi (write-side effect + unquoted-numeric no-quote-needed entry) and over mass assignment (truncation vs extra fields); the fields-before-marker differential is a new detection tell.
FRESHNESS: 2020-05 (found Dec 2019) — OUTSIDE the preferred 6-12 month window; recorded as BACKFILL. Flagged as backfill.
HONESTY: not reproduced; every quote and both reconstructed queries are verbatim from the Wayback text; the author himself frames the backend reconstruction as his understanding ("If my understanding is right, following process might be happened at back end") — the observed facts are the request, the mass name/country change, and the marker A/B; the SQL shown is his reconstruction and is not presented here as observed.
